abstract: Decision making tasks that involve delayed consequences are very common yet difficult to address with supervised learning methods. If there is an accurate model of the underlying dynamical system, then these tasks can be formulated as sequential decision problems and solved by Dynamic Programming. This paper discusses rein(cid:173) forcement learning in terms of the sequential decision framework and shows how a learning algorithm similar to the one implemented by the Adaptive Critic Element used in the pole-balancer of Barto, Sutton, and Anderson (1983), and further developed by Sutton (1984), fits into this framework. Adaptive neural networks can play significant roles as modules for approximating the functions required for solving sequential decision problems.

paragraphs: This paper examines decision-making tasks in which actions have delayed consequences. Such tasks are difficult to handle through supervised learning because the value of a choice depends on what happens later. The sequential decision framework provides a way to express this dependence across a series of actions and outcomes.

When an accurate model of the underlying dynamical system is available, the problem can be formulated for solution by dynamic programming. The paper uses this framework to discuss reinforcement learning and to explain how a learning algorithm related to the Adaptive Critic Element fits within it. This connects a concrete adaptive learning approach to a broader formulation of sequential choice.

Adaptive neural networks enter as modules that approximate functions needed to solve these problems. Their role is therefore tied to particular computational requirements of sequential decision-making. The paper's contribution is a conceptual bridge among delayed-consequence learning, dynamic programming, and neural function approximation, clarifying how neural modules can participate in solving decisions whose effects unfold over time.
summary.tldr: The paper connects reinforcement learning and adaptive critic methods to sequential decision problems and neural function approximation.

title: Sequential Decision Problems and Neural Networks

abstract: We present a new method for obtaining the response function 9 and its average G from which most of the properties of learning and generalization in linear perceptrons can be derived. We first rederive the known results for the 'thermodynamic limit' of infinite perceptron size N and show explicitly that 9 is self-averaging in this limit. We then discuss extensions of our method to more gen(cid:173) eral learning scenarios with anisotropic teacher space priors, input distributions, and weight decay terms. Finally, we use our method to calculate the finite N corrections of order 1/ N to G and discuss the corresponding finite size effects on generalization and learning dynamics. An important spin-off is the observation that results obtained in the thermodynamic limit are often directly relevant to systems of fairly modest, 'real-world' sizes.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for calculating a response function and its average for linear perceptrons. These quantities provide access to much of the behavior of learning and generalization. The main question is how theoretical results for infinitely large systems relate to networks with a finite number of parameters.

The authors first recover known results in the thermodynamic limit, where perceptron size grows without bound. They explicitly show that the response function becomes self-averaging: variation between individual instances loses importance in that limit. They also discuss extensions to settings with direction-dependent assumptions about target weights, different input distributions, and weight-decay terms.

The method then calculates corrections to the average response that scale as the inverse of network size. These corrections allow the authors to examine how finite size affects prediction on new examples and the course of learning. Their stated conclusion is that infinite-size results can often be relevant even for fairly modest systems. The finite-size analysis supplies the connection between the mathematical limit and that practical relevance.
summary.tldr: A response-function analysis shows why infinite-size learning results can remain relevant to linear perceptrons of modest size.

title: Learning in large linear perceptrons and why the thermodynamic limit is relevant to the real world

abstract: A continuous-time, continuous-state version of the temporal differ(cid:173) ence (TD) algorithm is derived in order to facilitate the application of reinforcement learning to real-world control tasks and neurobi(cid:173) ological modeling. An optimal nonlinear feedback control law was also derived using the derivatives of the value function. The per(cid:173) formance of the algorithms was tested in a task of swinging up a pendulum with limited torque. Both the "critic" that specifies the paths to the upright position and the "actor" that works as a non(cid:173) linear feedback controller were successfully implemented by radial basis function (RBF) networks.

paragraphs: This paper derives temporal-difference learning for problems in which both time and state are continuous. The motivation is to make reinforcement learning applicable to physical control tasks and neurobiological modeling. A continuous formulation connects the learning rule directly to systems whose states evolve continuously.

The authors also derive an optimal nonlinear feedback-control law from derivatives of the value function. The critic represents information about paths toward the goal, while the actor uses a nonlinear feedback controller to determine behavior. Both are implemented with radial basis function networks, linking the continuous mathematical formulation to neural representations that can be used in the task.

The algorithms are tested by swinging a pendulum upright with limited torque. The abstract reports successful implementations of both actor and critic. The torque constraint makes the demonstration a constrained control problem, and the contribution combines value learning with a way to derive control actions from that value representation in continuous time and state.
summary.tldr: Continuous-time temporal-difference learning and value-derived feedback control are demonstrated on a torque-limited pendulum swing-up task.

title: Temporal Difference Learning in Continuous Time and Space

abstract: A modular analogue neuro-chip set with on-chip learning capability is developed for active noise canceling. The analogue neuro-chip set incorporates the error backpropagation learning rule for practical applications, and allows pin-to-pin interconnections for multi-chip boards. The developed neuro-board demonstrated active noise canceling without any digital signal processor. Multi-path fading of acoustic channels, random noise, and nonlinear distortion of the loud speaker are compensated by the adaptive learning circuits of the neuro-chips. Experimental results are reported for cancellation of car noise in real time.

Multi-path fading of acoustic channels, random noise, and nonlinear distortion of the loud speaker are compensated by the adaptive learning circuits of the neuro-chips. Experimental results are reported for cancellation of car noise in real time.

paragraphs: This paper develops an analogue neural chip set for active noise cancellation. Learning takes place on the chips themselves through an implementation of error backpropagation. The hardware therefore combines signal processing with the ability to adapt its behavior, making learning part of the operating noise-cancellation system rather than a separate preparation step.

The chips have a modular design, with direct pin connections that allow them to be combined on boards. Their adaptive circuits compensate for several complications in acoustic cancellation: sound traveling through multiple paths, random noise, and nonlinear loudspeaker distortion. These effects matter because the acoustic channel and the loudspeaker both influence the sound that the system must cancel.

The assembled neural board demonstrated active cancellation without a digital signal processor, and the authors report experiments canceling car noise in real time. The finding ties the learning circuitry to a practical acoustic task. It shows that the proposed analogue hardware can perform adaptive cancellation while directly accommodating the stated channel and loudspeaker effects.
summary.tldr: Analogue neural chips with onboard backpropagation learning demonstrate real-time car-noise cancellation without a digital signal processor.

title: Active Noise Canceling Using Analog Neuro-Chip with On-Chip Learning Capability

abstract: A method is described which, like the kernel trick in support vector ma(cid:173) chines (SVMs), lets us generalize distance-based algorithms to operate in feature spaces, usually nonlinearly related to the input space. This is done by identifying a class of kernels which can be represented as norm-based distances in Hilbert spaces. It turns out that common kernel algorithms, such as SVMs and kernel PCA, are actually really distance based algorithms and can be run with that class of kernels, too. As well as providing a useful new insight into how these algorithms work, the present work can form the basis for conceiving new algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper develops a counterpart to the kernel trick for algorithms organized around distances. Its goal is to let such algorithms operate in feature spaces that are usually related nonlinearly to the original input space. This provides a way to change the geometry used by a distance-based method.

The key step is identifying a class of kernels that can be represented as distances derived from norms in Hilbert spaces. This representation connects kernel computations with a distance interpretation. It gives the proposed generalization a mathematical basis: the relevant kernels correspond to distances in an appropriate feature space.

The authors further show that familiar kernel methods, including support vector machines and kernel principal component analysis, can themselves be understood as distance-based algorithms and used with this kernel class. The contribution therefore serves two purposes. It extends the kinds of feature-space computations available to distance methods, and it offers a different interpretation of established kernel algorithms that could support the design of new ones.
summary.tldr: A class of distance-representable kernels extends distance-based algorithms to feature spaces and provides a distance interpretation of familiar kernel methods.

title: The Kernel Trick for Distances

abstract: Multisensory response enhancement (MRE) is the augmentation of the response of a neuron to sensory input of one modality by si(cid:173) multaneous input from another modality. The maximum likelihood (ML) model presented here modifies the Bayesian model for MRE (Anastasio et al.) by incorporating a decision strategy to maximize the number of correct decisions. Thus the ML model can also deal with the important tasks of stimulus discrimination and identifi(cid:173) cation in the presence of incongruent visual and auditory cues. It accounts for the inverse effectiveness observed in neurophysiolog(cid:173) ical recording data, and it predicts a functional relation between uni- and bimodal levels of discriminability that is testable both in neurophysiological and behavioral experiments.

The maximum likelihood (ML) model presented here modifies the Bayesian model for MRE (Anastasio et al.) by incorporating a decision strategy to maximize the number of correct decisions. Thus the ML model can also deal with the important tasks of stimulus discrimination and identifi(cid:173) cation in the presence of incongruent visual and auditory cues. It accounts for the inverse effectiveness observed in neurophysiolog(cid:173) ical recording data, and it predicts a functional relation between uni- and bimodal levels of discriminability that is testable both in neurophysiological and behavioral experiments.

paragraphs: Multisensory enhancement occurs when input through one sense strengthens a neuron's response to input through another. The paper models this phenomenon while also addressing the decisions an observer must make about a stimulus. In particular, the model needs to handle visual and auditory signals that do not agree.

The proposed maximum-likelihood model modifies an earlier Bayesian account by introducing a decision strategy aimed at maximizing correct decisions. This addition lets the model address stimulus discrimination and identification under incongruent sensory cues. The approach connects the size of a neural response with the broader problem of using multiple sources of sensory evidence to decide what is present.

The model accounts for inverse effectiveness reported in neural recordings, where enhancement is related to the effectiveness of the individual sensory inputs. It also predicts a functional relationship between discriminability with one modality and with two. That relationship is presented as testable through both neural recordings and behavioral experiments, giving the model a prediction beyond its account of an existing response pattern.
summary.tldr: A maximum-likelihood model connects multisensory enhancement with stimulus decisions and predicts a testable relationship between single-sense and combined-sense discrimination.

title: A Maximum-Likelihood Approach to Modeling Multisensory Enhancement

abstract: that deals with Monaural speech separation has been studied in previous systems that incorporate auditory scene analysis principles. A major problem for these systems is their inability to deal with speech in the high- frequency range. Psychoacoustic evidence suggests that different perceptual mechanisms are involved in handling resolved and unresolved harmonics. Motivated by this, we propose a model for monaural separation low-frequency and high- frequency signals differently. For resolved harmonics, our model generates segments based on temporal continuity and cross-channel correlation, and groups them according to periodicity. For unresolved harmonics, the model generates segments based on amplitude modulation (AM) in addition to temporal continuity and groups them according to AM repetition rates derived from sinusoidal modeling. Underlying the separation process is a pitch contour obtained according to psychoacoustic constraints. Our model is systematically evaluated, and it yields substantially better performance than previous systems, especially in the high-frequency range.

paragraphs: The paper develops a model for separating speech from a single audio channel. It addresses a weakness of earlier auditory-scene-analysis systems: difficulty handling speech at high frequencies. Motivated by psychoacoustic evidence, the model uses different processing strategies for resolved and unresolved harmonics instead of applying one grouping mechanism throughout the signal.

For resolved harmonics, it forms segments using continuity over time and correlations across channels, then groups those segments by periodicity. For unresolved harmonics, segmentation also uses amplitude modulation, and grouping follows modulation repetition rates estimated through sinusoidal modeling. A pitch contour obtained under psychoacoustic constraints underlies the separation process.

The model is systematically evaluated and substantially outperforms previous systems, with particularly strong improvement in the high-frequency range. The finding supports using distinct signal cues for the two harmonic regimes. Its contribution is not just the presence of a pitch estimate, but the organization of segmentation and grouping around the different information available in low- and high-frequency speech.
summary.tldr: A single-channel speech-separation model uses different cues for resolved and unresolved harmonics, substantially improving performance, especially at high frequencies.

title: Monaural Speech Separation

abstract: Many interesting multiclass problems can be cast in the general frame- work of label ranking defined on a given set of classes. The evaluation for such a ranking is generally given in terms of the number of violated order constraints between classes. In this paper, we propose the Prefer- ence Learning Model as a unifying framework to model and solve a large class of multiclass problems in a large margin perspective. In addition, an original kernel-based method is proposed and evaluated on a ranking dataset with state-of-the-art results.

The evaluation for such a ranking is generally given in terms of the number of violated order constraints between classes. In this paper, we propose the Prefer- ence Learning Model as a unifying framework to model and solve a large class of multiclass problems in a large margin perspective. In addition, an original kernel-based method is proposed and evaluated on a ranking dataset with state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: The paper considers multiclass learning problems that can be expressed by ranking a given set of class labels. In this formulation, the desired prediction contains ordering information about classes. A natural way to evaluate it is to count the ordering requirements that the predicted ranking violates.

The authors introduce the Preference Learning Model as a common framework for a broad collection of these problems. They approach learning from a large-margin perspective, connecting the satisfaction of label preferences to a shared learning principle. This unification matters because several multiclass tasks can then be described through the same language of preferences and ordering constraints.

The paper also proposes an original kernel-based method within this line of work and evaluates it on a ranking dataset. The reported results are state of the art for that evaluation. The contribution therefore includes both a general modeling framework and a concrete method, with the experiment supporting the method's effectiveness on the ranking task studied.
summary.tldr: A large-margin preference-learning framework unifies many multiclass problems and supplies a kernel method with state-of-the-art reported ranking results.

title: Learning Preferences for Multiclass Problems

abstract: This paper presents a new sampling algorithm for approximating func- tions of variables representable as undirected graphical models of arbi- trary connectivity with pairwise potentials, as well as for estimating the notoriously dif(cid:2)cult partition function of the graph. The algorithm (cid:2)ts into the framework of sequential Monte Carlo methods rather than the more widely used MCMC, and relies on constructing a sequence of in- termediate distributions which get closer to the desired one. While the idea of using (cid:147)tempered(cid:148) proposals is known, we construct a novel se- quence of target distributions where, rather than dropping a global tem- perature parameter, we sequentially couple individual pairs of variables that are, initially, sampled exactly from a spanning tree of the variables. We present experimental results on inference and estimation of the parti- tion function for sparse and densely-connected graphs.

paragraphs: Hot Coupling is a sampling method for undirected graphical models with pairwise interactions and arbitrary connectivity. It addresses both approximate inference and estimation of the partition function, the normalization quantity needed to turn the model's weights into probabilities. These tasks become difficult when the graph contains many interacting relationships.

The method uses sequential Monte Carlo, constructing a series of intermediate distributions that approach the desired distribution. It begins with samples drawn exactly from a spanning-tree model. It then progressively couples individual pairs of variables, introducing relationships through the sequence instead of controlling the transition solely by lowering a global temperature parameter.

The distinctive contribution is this construction of the intermediate targets. It organizes the journey from a tractable starting model to the desired model around individual pairwise couplings. The authors present experiments involving both sparse and densely connected graphs, examining inference and partition-function estimation. These experiments evaluate the two intended uses of the method across different patterns of graph connectivity.
summary.tldr: Hot Coupling uses sequential Monte Carlo to approach a pairwise graphical model by progressively coupling variables from a spanning-tree starting point.

title: Hot Coupling: A Particle Approach to Inference and Normalization on Pairwise Undirected Graphs

abstract: We present a novel, semi-supervised approach to training discriminative random fields (DRFs) that efficiently exploits labeled and unlabeled training data to achieve improved accuracy in a variety of image processing tasks. We formulate DRF training as a form of MAP estimation that combines conditional loglikelihood on labeled data, given a data-dependent prior, with a conditional entropy regularizer defined on unlabeled data. Although the training objective is no longer concave, we develop an efficient local optimization procedure that produces classifiers that are more accurate than ones based on standard supervised DRF training. We then apply our semi-supervised approach to train DRFs to segment both synthetic and real data sets, and demonstrate significant improvements over supervised DRFs in each case.

We formulate DRF training as a form of MAP estimation that combines conditional loglikelihood on labeled data, given a data-dependent prior, with a conditional entropy regularizer defined on unlabeled data. Although the training objective is no longer concave, we develop an efficient local optimization procedure that produces classifiers that are more accurate than ones based on standard supervised DRF training. We then apply our semi-supervised approach to train DRFs to segment both synthetic and real data sets, and demonstrate significant improvements over supervised DRFs in each case.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to train discriminative random fields using both labeled and unlabeled data. The goal is to improve image-processing models that capture spatial dependencies. Its semi-supervised formulation allows images without supplied labels to influence training alongside examples whose desired outputs are known.

Training is expressed as maximum a posteriori estimation. The objective combines conditional log-likelihood on labeled data, a data-dependent prior, and a conditional entropy regularizer on unlabeled data. These terms bring supervised evidence and unlabeled examples into a single optimization problem. The resulting objective is no longer concave, so the authors develop an efficient local optimization procedure.

The method is applied to segmentation on synthetic and real datasets. In each case, the authors report significant improvements over supervised discriminative random fields. These findings support the practical benefit of incorporating unlabeled information into training for the tested tasks. The optimization result is a workable local procedure for the new objective, paired with evidence of more accurate classifiers than standard supervised training produces.
summary.tldr: A semi-supervised training objective for discriminative random fields uses unlabeled data to improve segmentation on synthetic and real datasets.

title: Learning to Model Spatial Dependency: Semi-Supervised Discriminative Random Fields

abstract: We show that the relevant information about a classification problem in feature space is contained up to negligible error in a finite number of leading kernel PCA components if the kernel matches the underlying learning problem. Thus, kernels not only transform data sets such that good generalization can be achieved even by linear discriminant functions, but this transformation is also performed in a manner which makes economic use of feature space dimensions. In the best case, kernels provide efficient implicit representations of the data to perform classification. Practically, we propose an algorithm which enables us to recover the subspace and dimensionality relevant for good classification. Our algorithm can therefore be applied (1) to analyze the interplay of data set and kernel in a geometric fashion, (2) to help in model selection, and to (3) de-noise in feature space in order to yield better classification results.

paragraphs: Kernel methods transform the representation of data so that classification can work well using linear decision functions in feature space. This paper asks how much of that space actually carries information relevant to the classification task. Its central result concerns whether a much smaller collection of directions can retain the useful information.

The authors show that a finite set of leading kernel principal components contains the relevant classification information up to negligible error, provided the kernel matches the underlying learning problem. That condition is central: the result describes what a suitably matched kernel can achieve. Such a kernel can both support good generalization and use feature space dimensions economically.

The paper also proposes an algorithm for recovering the relevant subspace and its dimensionality. This gives the theoretical result a practical role: examining the geometry created by a dataset and kernel, supporting model selection, and removing noise in feature space. These applications connect dimension reduction to the classification objective rather than treating compactness as an end in itself.
summary.tldr: When a kernel matches the task, a finite set of leading kernel PCA components can preserve nearly all relevant classification information.

title: Denoising and Dimension Reduction in Feature Space

abstract: We derive an equation for temporal difference learning from statistical principles. Speciﬁcally, we start with the variational principle and then bootstrap to produce an updating rule for discounted state value estimates. The resulting equation is similar to the standard equation for temporal difference learning with eligibil- ity traces, so called TD(λ), however it lacks the parameter α that speciﬁes the learning rate. In the place of this free parameter there is now an equation for the learning rate that is speciﬁc to each state transition. We experimentally test this new learning rule against TD(λ) and ﬁnd that it offers superior performance in various settings. Finally, we make some preliminary investigations into how to extend our new temporal difference algorithm to reinforcement learning. To do this we combine our update equation with both Watkins’ Q(λ) and Sarsa(λ) and ﬁnd that it again offers superior performance without a learning rate parameter.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning updates value estimates using other estimates as part of its target. Standard TD with eligibility traces includes a learning-rate parameter that controls the size of updates. This paper derives a related update from statistical principles, starting with a variational principle and then applying bootstrapping to discounted state values.

The resulting rule resembles TD(lambda), but replaces the freely chosen learning-rate parameter with an equation specific to each state transition. Updates therefore still have a learning rate; its value is determined by the derived rule. This is the concrete meaning of learning without a learning-rate parameter in the proposed method.

Experiments compare the rule with TD(lambda) and report superior performance in various settings. The authors also make preliminary extensions to reinforcement learning by combining it with Watkins’ Q(lambda) and Sarsa(lambda), again reporting improved performance without a free learning-rate parameter. These findings support the usefulness of the derived update in the tested cases, while the control extensions are explicitly presented as preliminary investigations.
summary.tldr: A statistically derived temporal-difference rule replaces a free learning-rate parameter with a transition-specific equation and improves reported experimental performance.

title: Temporal Difference Updating without a Learning Rate

abstract: We combine two threads of research on approximate dynamic programming: random sampling of states and using local trajectory optimizers to globally optimize a policy and associated value function. This combination allows us to replace a dense multidimensional grid with a much sparser adaptive sampling of states. Our focus is on finding steady state policies for the deterministic time invariant discrete time control problems with continuous states and actions often found in robotics. In this paper we show that we can now solve problems we couldn't solve previously with regular grid-based approaches.

This combination allows us to replace a dense multidimensional grid with a much sparser adaptive sampling of states. Our focus is on finding steady state policies for the deterministic time invariant discrete time control problems with continuous states and actions often found in robotics. In this paper we show that we can now solve problems we couldn't solve previously with regular grid-based approaches.

paragraphs: Dynamic programming for continuous-state control often represents the state space with a multidimensional grid. This paper explores a different representation by combining random state sampling with local trajectory optimization. The goal is to optimize a policy and its associated value function while replacing the dense grid with a much sparser, adaptive selection of states.

The two ingredients connect state-space coverage with trajectory-based optimization. Random sampling provides the states used in the approximation, while local trajectory optimizers contribute to optimizing the policy and value function globally. Their combination allows the representation to adapt instead of requiring the regular coverage imposed by a dense grid.

The paper focuses on steady-state policies for deterministic, time-invariant, discrete-time control problems with continuous states and actions, a setting common in robotics. Within that scope, the authors report solving problems that their earlier regular-grid approaches could not solve. The significance is a demonstrated expansion of tractable control problems through a sparser representation and the use of trajectory optimization within approximate dynamic programming.
summary.tldr: Adaptive state sampling combined with local trajectory optimization solves control problems previously beyond the authors' regular-grid methods.

title: Random Sampling of States in Dynamic Programming

abstract: We present a simple and effective approach to learning tractable conditional random fields with structure that depends on the evidence. Our approach retains the advantages of tractable discriminative models, namely efficient exact inference and exact parameter learning. At the same time, our algorithm does not suffer a large expressive power penalty inherent to fixed tractable structures. On real-life relational datasets, our approach matches or exceeds state of the art accuracy of the dense models, and at the same time provides an order of magnitude speedup

paragraphs: This paper addresses a tradeoff in conditional random fields: a structure that permits efficient exact computation can restrict the relationships a model can express. The authors propose learning models whose structure depends on the observed evidence. This makes the organization of dependencies responsive to the input instead of requiring the same fixed tractable structure throughout.

The approach retains efficient exact inference and exact parameter learning. Its flexibility comes from adapting the structure, allowing the model to avoid the large loss of expressive power associated with fixed tractable structures. The central idea is that computationally manageable models can still represent rich relationships when their structure is allowed to vary with the evidence.

On real-world relational datasets, the method matches or exceeds the accuracy of state-of-the-art dense models while delivering an order-of-magnitude speedup. These empirical results show that the proposed structural adaptation can provide both competitive predictions and substantial computational savings in the evaluated settings. The contribution links tractability to input-dependent structure rather than treating expressive power and exact computation as an unavoidable fixed compromise.
summary.tldr: Evidence-dependent CRF structures retain exact computation while matching or improving dense-model accuracy with an order-of-magnitude speedup in relational-data experiments.

title: Evidence-Specific Structures for Rich Tractable CRFs

abstract: To localise the source of a sound, we use location-specific properties of the signals received at the two ears caused by the asymmetric filtering of the original sound by our head and pinnae, the head-related transfer functions (HRTFs). These HRTFs change throughout an organism's lifetime, during development for example, and so the required neural circuitry cannot be entirely hardwired. Since HRTFs are not directly accessible from perceptual experience, they can only be inferred from filtered sounds. We present a spiking neural network model of sound localisation based on extracting location-specific synchrony patterns, and a simple supervised algorithm to learn the mapping between synchrony patterns and locations from a set of example sounds, with no previous knowledge of HRTFs. After learning, our model was able to accurately localise new sounds in both azimuth and elevation, including the difficult task of distinguishing sounds coming from the front and back.

These head-related transfer functions provide localization cues, but they change over an organism's lifetime. A neural system therefore needs a way to learn location cues from the filtered sounds it actually hears, since the filtering functions are not directly available through experience.

This paper proposes a spiking neural network that extracts synchrony patterns specific to sound locations. A simple supervised algorithm learns the relationship between those patterns and locations from example sounds. The model begins without prior knowledge of the head-related transfer functions, so the mapping must be acquired through the examples themselves.

After learning, the model accurately localizes new sounds in both azimuth and elevation. It also handles the difficult distinction between sounds arriving from the front and the back. The results show that learned synchrony patterns can support spatial hearing in this model, connecting experience with spike-based representations of sound location.
summary.tldr: A spiking network learns sound locations from synchrony patterns without prior knowledge of ear filtering, including front-versus-back distinctions.

title: Learning to localise sounds with spiking neural networks

abstract: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death globally, resulting in 17 million deaths each year. Despite the availability of various treatment options, existing techniques based upon conventional medical knowledge often fail to identify patients who might have benefited from more aggressive therapy. In this paper, we describe and evaluate a novel unsupervised machine learning approach for cardiac risk stratification. The key idea of our approach is to avoid specialized medical knowledge, and assess patient risk using symbolic mismatch, a new metric to assess similarity in long-term time-series activity. We hypothesize that high risk patients can be identified using symbolic mismatch, as individuals in a population with unusual long-term physiological activity. We describe related approaches that build on these ideas to provide improved medical decision making for patients who have recently suffered coronary attacks. We first describe how to compute the symbolic mismatch between pairs of long term electrocardiographic (ECG) signals. This algorithm maps the original signals into a symbolic domain, and provides a quantitative assessment of the difference between these symbolic representations of the original signals. We then show how this measure can be used with each of a one-class SVM, a nearest neighbor classifier, and hierarchical clustering to improve risk stratification. We evaluated our methods on a population of 686 cardiac patients with available long-term electrocardiographic data. In a univariate analysis, all of the methods provided a statistically significant association with the occurrence of a major adverse cardiac event in the next 90 days. In a multivariate analysis that incorporated the most widely used clinical risk variables, the nearest neighbor and hierarchical clustering approaches were able to statistically significantly distinguish patients with a roughly two-fold risk of suffering a major adverse cardiac event in the next 90 days.

summary.tldr: Symbolic comparisons of long-term ECG signals identified groups with elevated 90-day cardiac-event risk in a study of 686 patients.

title: Identifying Patients at Risk of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events Using Symbolic Mismatch

abstract: We develop a Bayesian nonparametric extension of the popular Plackett-Luce choice model that can handle an infinite number of choice items. Our framework is based on the theory of random atomic measures, with the prior specified by a gamma process. We derive a posterior characterization and a simple and effective Gibbs sampler for posterior simulation. We then develop a time-varying extension of our model, and apply our model to the New York Times lists of weekly bestselling books.
originalAbstract: We develop a Bayesian nonparametric extension of the popular Plackett-Luce choice model that can handle an infinite number of choice items. Our framework is based on the theory of random atomic measures, with the prior specified by a gamma process. We derive a posterior characterization and a simple and effective Gibbs sampler for posterior simulation. We then develop a time-varying extension of our model, and apply our model to the New York Times lists of weekly bestselling books.

paragraphs: This paper extends the Plackett–Luce choice model to ranked data with an infinite collection of possible items. The distinction concerns the space of available choices: the model can accommodate an unbounded item universe while describing observed rankings. This gives ranked-data modeling a Bayesian nonparametric formulation.

The mathematical construction uses random atomic measures, with a gamma process specifying the prior. These measures provide a way to associate statistical weight with individual items. The authors derive a characterization of the posterior, describing how the model changes after rankings are observed, and develop a Gibbs sampler for drawing from that posterior. The inference procedure makes the proposed model usable for posterior simulation.

The authors also extend the model so that it can vary over time and apply it to weekly New York Times bestseller lists. This application brings together ranking and temporal change within one framework. The stated contribution consists of the expanded choice model, its posterior analysis, a sampling method, and a time-varying version demonstrated on ranked book data.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric extension of Plackett–Luce models rankings over infinitely many possible items and supports temporal variation.

title: Bayesian nonparametric models for ranked data

abstract: The interaction between the patient's expected outcome of an intervention and the inherent effects of that intervention can have extraordinary effects. Thus in clinical trials an effort is made to conceal the nature of the administered intervention from the participants in the trial i.e. to blind it. Yet, in practice perfect blinding is impossible to ensure or even verify. The current standard is follow up the trial with an auxiliary questionnaire, which allows trial participants to express their belief concerning the assigned intervention and which is used to compute a measure of the extent of blinding in the trial. If the estimated extent of blinding exceeds a threshold the trial is deemed sufficiently blinded; otherwise, the trial is deemed to have failed. In this paper we make several important contributions. Firstly, we identify a series of fundamental problems of the aforesaid practice and discuss them in context of the most commonly used blinding measures. Secondly, motivated by the highlighted problems, we formulate a novel method for handling imperfectly blinded trials. We too adopt a post-trial feedback questionnaire but interpret the collected data using an original approach, fundamentally different from those previously proposed. Unlike previous approaches, ours is void of any ad hoc free parameters, is robust to small changes in auxiliary data and is not predicated on any strong assumptions used to interpret participants' feedback.

paragraphs: Clinical trial blinding aims to conceal which intervention participants receive because their expectations can interact with the intervention's effects. The paper starts from the difficulty of ensuring or verifying perfect blinding. It examines the practice of asking participants afterward which intervention they believe they received, converting their answers into a blinding score, and applying a pass-or-fail threshold.

The authors identify fundamental problems with this practice and discuss them in relation to commonly used blinding measures. They then propose a different method for handling trials whose blinding is imperfect. Their approach still uses a questionnaire after the trial, so the central change is how participants' responses are interpreted and used.

The proposed interpretation avoids ad hoc adjustable parameters and is reported to be robust to small changes in the questionnaire data. It also does not rely on strong assumptions for interpreting participants' feedback. These properties address weaknesses in judging a trial through a thresholded blinding score and provide a different way to use evidence about participants' beliefs when blinding is incomplete.
summary.tldr: The paper critiques threshold-based blinding assessments and proposes a robust, parameter-free interpretation of post-trial participant feedback.

title: Assessing Blinding in Clinical Trials

abstract: The Dawid-Skene estimator has been widely used for inferring the true labels from the noisy labels provided by non-expert crowdsourcing workers. However, since the estimator maximizes a non-convex log-likelihood function, it is hard to theoretically justify its performance. In this paper, we propose a two-stage efficient algorithm for multi-class crowd labeling problems. The first stage uses the spectral method to obtain an initial estimate of parameters. Then the second stage refines the estimation by optimizing the objective function of the Dawid-Skene estimator via the EM algorithm. We show that our algorithm achieves the optimal convergence rate up to a logarithmic factor. We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is comparable to the most accurate empirical approach, while outperforming several other recently proposed methods.

Then the second stage refines the estimation by optimizing the objective function of the Dawid-Skene estimator via the EM algorithm. We show that our algorithm achieves the optimal convergence rate up to a logarithmic factor. We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic and real datasets. paragraphs: Crowdsourcing combines labels from workers who may make mistakes, so recovering the underlying labels requires accounting for noisy responses. The Dawid-Skene estimator is widely used for this task, but its non-convex likelihood makes performance difficult to justify theoretically. This paper develops an efficient two-stage algorithm for problems with multiple possible classes.

The first stage uses a spectral method to estimate the model parameters. The second refines that estimate by applying expectation-maximization to the Dawid-Skene objective. This division gives initialization an explicit role in the overall procedure: the algorithm begins with a spectral estimate and then uses likelihood optimization to improve it.

The authors prove that the combined algorithm achieves an optimal convergence rate up to a logarithmic factor. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show accuracy comparable to the strongest empirical approach considered, while outperforming several other recent methods. The paper thus joins a near-optimal theoretical rate with competitive observed performance, without claiming to surpass the most accurate comparator.
summary.tldr: Spectral initialization followed by EM yields a crowdsourcing estimator with a near-optimal convergence rate and competitive empirical accuracy.

title: Spectral Methods meet EM: A Provably Optimal Algorithm for Crowdsourcing

abstract: Several problems such as network intrusion, community detection, and disease outbreak can be described by observations attributed to nodes or edges of a graph. In these applications presence of intrusion, community or disease outbreak is characterized by novel observations on some unknown connected subgraph. These problems can be formulated in terms of optimization of suitable objectives on connected subgraphs, a problem which is generally computationally difficult. We overcome the combinatorics of connectivity by embedding connected subgraphs into linear matrix inequalities (LMI). Computationally efficient tests are then realized by optimizing convex objective functions subject to these LMI constraints. We prove, by means of a novel Euclidean embedding argument, that our tests are minimax optimal for exponential family of distributions on 1-D and 2-D lattices. We show that internal conductance of the connected subgraph family plays a fundamental role in characterizing detectability.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to detect unusual observations concentrated on an unknown connected part of a graph. Network intrusions, communities, and disease outbreaks motivate this setting. Connectivity is valuable information about where a signal might occur, but searching over connected subgraphs creates a difficult combinatorial optimization problem.

The authors represent connected subgraphs through linear matrix inequalities, turning connectivity into constraints that can be used in an optimization framework. They then construct computationally efficient tests by optimizing convex objectives subject to those constraints. This approach makes the graph’s structural information usable without treating detection solely as a direct search over candidate connected regions.

Using a new Euclidean embedding argument, the paper proves minimax optimality for exponential-family distributions on one- and two-dimensional lattices. This means the tests attain the best worst-case detection performance in the analyzed settings. The analysis also identifies internal conductance, a measure of connectivity within a region, as fundamental to detectability. The optimality claim is specific to those distributions and lattice settings, while the formulation addresses the broader difficulty posed by connectivity.
summary.tldr: Matrix-inequality constraints enable efficient graph-signal tests with minimax guarantees for exponential-family observations on one- and two-dimensional lattices.

title: Efficient Minimax Signal Detection on Graphs

abstract: The modern scale of data has brought new challenges to Bayesian inference. In particular, conventional MCMC algorithms are computationally very expensive for large data sets. A promising approach to solve this problem is embarrassingly parallel MCMC (EP-MCMC), which first partitions the data into multiple subsets and runs independent sampling algorithms on each subset. The subset posterior draws are then aggregated via some combining rules to obtain the final approximation. Existing EP-MCMC algorithms are limited by approximation accuracy and difficulty in resampling. In this article, we propose a new EP-MCMC algorithm PART that solves these problems. The new algorithm applies random partition trees to combine the subset posterior draws, which is distribution-free, easy to resample from and can adapt to multiple scales. We provide theoretical justification and extensive experiments illustrating empirical performance.

The subset posterior draws are then aggregated via some combining rules to obtain the final approximation. Existing EP-MCMC algorithms are limited by approximation accuracy and difficulty in resampling. In this article, we propose a new EP-MCMC algorithm PART that solves these problems. paragraphs: Large datasets make conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo expensive for Bayesian inference. Embarrassingly parallel MCMC distributes the work by splitting the data, running independent samplers on the subsets, and combining their posterior draws. The combination step determines the final approximation and can create difficulties for accuracy and subsequent resampling.

The proposed PART algorithm uses random partition trees to combine the subset draws. The authors describe this construction as distribution-free, adaptable to multiple scales, and easy to resample from. These properties target both the quality of the combined approximation and the practical ability to generate draws from it.

The paper supplies theoretical justification and extensive experiments illustrating empirical performance. Its central contribution is therefore a new aggregation mechanism within the parallel sampling workflow. Independent subset sampling already provides the division of computational labor; PART addresses how the resulting samples can be brought together into a usable final approximation while tackling the shortcomings identified in existing combining methods.
summary.tldr: PART combines independently sampled subset posteriors using random partition trees to improve aggregation and simplify resampling.

title: Parallelizing MCMC with Random Partition Trees

abstract: We study the problem of multi-party interactive function computation under differential privacy. In this setting, each party is interested in computing a function on its private bit and all the other parties' bits. The function to be computed can vary from one party to the other. Moreover, there could be a central observer who is interested in computing a separate function on all the parties' bits. Differential privacy ensures that there remains an uncertainty in any party's bit even when given the transcript of interactions and all other parties' bits. Performance at each party is measured via the accuracy of the function to be computed. We allow for an arbitrary cost metric to measure the distortion between the true and the computed function values. Our main result is the optimality of a simple non-interactive protocol: each party randomizes its bit (sufficiently) and shares the privatized version with the other parties. This optimality result is very general: it holds for all types of functions, heterogeneous privacy conditions on the parties, all types of cost metrics, and both average and worst-case (over the inputs) measures of accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper considers parties that each hold a private bit and want to compute a function involving everyone's bits. Different parties may want different functions, and a central observer may have a separate objective. Privacy must leave uncertainty about an individual's bit even when the interaction transcript and every other bit are known.

The main result establishes the optimality of a simple noninteractive protocol in this setting. Each participant sufficiently randomizes their own bit and shares the privatized result. Despite allowing interactive computation in the problem formulation, the authors show that this direct sharing procedure attains optimal accuracy under the privacy requirements they study.

The result covers arbitrary functions and distortion measures, different privacy requirements for different participants, and both average and worst-case accuracy over inputs. Its breadth means that the optimality does not rely on all participants wanting the same computation or measuring error identically. The scope remains the stated private-bit setting, within which the theorem gives a strong justification for a particularly simple communication protocol.
summary.tldr: For the studied private-bit computation setting, sharing independently privatized bits is optimal across broad function, privacy, and accuracy requirements.

title: Secure Multi-party Differential Privacy

abstract: A $k$-submodular function is a generalization of a submodular function, where the input consists of $k$ disjoint subsets, instead of a single subset, of the domain.Many machine learning problems, including influence maximization with $k$ kinds of topics and sensor placement with $k$ kinds of sensors, can be naturally modeled as the problem of maximizing monotone $k$-submodular functions.In this paper, we give constant-factor approximation algorithms for maximizing monotone $k$-submodular functions subject to several size constraints.The running time of our algorithms are almost linear in the domain size.We experimentally demonstrate that our algorithms outperform baseline algorithms in terms of the solution quality.

paragraphs: Some selection problems require choosing several different kinds of items while keeping the resulting groups disjoint. A k-submodular function models this situation by taking k disjoint subsets as its input, extending the single-subset formulation of ordinary submodularity. The paper studies maximizing monotone functions of this kind under restrictions on set sizes.

The authors develop constant-factor approximation algorithms for several size-constrained settings. Such guarantees establish that the returned solution achieves a fixed fraction of the optimum, without requiring exact optimization. The algorithms run in time that is almost linear in the size of the domain, making the computational cost grow relatively gently as the pool of possible items expands.

The formulation naturally covers influence maximization with multiple topics and sensor placement with multiple sensor types. Experiments report better solution quality than the baseline algorithms considered. The contribution combines three useful properties for these structured selection problems: support for multiple disjoint groups, explicit approximation guarantees, and running times suited to larger domains.
summary.tldr: Nearly linear-time algorithms provide constant-factor guarantees for monotone k-submodular maximization under several size constraints.

title: Monotone k-Submodular Function Maximization with Size Constraints

abstract: Clustering graphs under the Stochastic Block Model (SBM) and extensions are well studied. Guarantees of correctness exist under the assumption that the data is sampled from a model. In this paper, we propose a framework, in which we obtain "correctness" guarantees without assuming the data comes from a model. The guarantees we obtain depend instead on the statistics of the data that can be checked. We also show that this framework ties in with the existing model-based framework, and that we can exploit results in model-based recovery, as well as strengthen the results existing in that area of research.
originalAbstract: Clustering graphs under the Stochastic Block Model (SBM) and extensions are well studied. Guarantees of correctness exist under the assumption that the data is sampled from a model. In this paper, we propose a framework, in which we obtain "correctness" guarantees without assuming the data comes from a model. The guarantees we obtain depend instead on the statistics of the data that can be checked. We also show that this framework ties in with the existing model-based framework, and that we can exploit results in model-based recovery, as well as strengthen the results existing in that area of research.

paragraphs: Graph clustering aims to identify groups within a network. Many correctness guarantees rely on assuming that the observed graph was generated by a particular probabilistic model, such as a stochastic block model. This paper develops a framework that changes the basis on which clustering results can receive theoretical support.

The proposed guarantees depend on statistics of the observed data that can be checked, without requiring the data to have been sampled from a model. This shifts attention toward properties of the graph actually being analyzed. The guarantees still depend on those properties; removing a generative-model assumption does not make the correctness statement unconditional.

The framework also connects with existing model-based analysis. The authors show that it can use established recovery results and strengthen results in that research area. Its significance is therefore twofold: it provides a route to guarantees grounded in checkable data statistics, and it preserves a useful relationship with the substantial theory already developed for model-based graph clustering.
summary.tldr: A graph-clustering framework bases correctness guarantees on checkable data statistics while connecting with and strengthening model-based recovery theory.

title: Graph Clustering: Block-models and model free results

abstract: We consider the problem of jointly inferring the $M$-best diverse labelings for a binary (high-order) submodular energy of a graphical model. Recently, it was shown that this problem can be solved to a global optimum, for many practically interesting diversity measures. It was noted that the labelings are, so-called, nested. This nestedness property also holds for labelings of a class of parametric submodular minimization problems, where different values of the global parameter $\gamma$ give rise to different solutions. The popular example of the parametric submodular minimization is the monotonic parametric max-flow problem, which is also widely used for computing multiple labelings. As the main contribution of this work we establish a close relationship between diversity with submodular energies and the parametric submodular minimization. In particular, the joint $M$-best diverse labelings can be obtained by running a non-parametric submodular minimization (in the special case - max-flow) solver for $M$ different values of $\gamma$ in parallel, for certain diversity measures. Importantly, the values for~$\gamma$ can be computed in a closed form in advance, prior to any optimization. These theoretical results suggest two simple yet efficient algorithms for the joint $M$-best diverse problem, which outperform competitors in terms of runtime and quality of results. In particular, as we show in the paper, the new methods compute the exact $M$-best diverse labelings faster than a popular method of Batra et al., which in some sense only obtains approximate solutions.

paragraphs: A graphical model can be used to produce several plausible labelings while encouraging those answers to differ. This paper studies jointly finding M such labelings for binary submodular energies, including higher-order interactions. Its central insight connects this diversity objective to a family of submodular optimization problems controlled by one parameter.

The connection relies on a shared nested structure in the solutions. For certain diversity measures, the desired labelings can be recovered by solving M ordinary submodular minimization problems at different parameter values. Those values have closed-form expressions that can be computed before optimization begins, allowing the individual problems to run in parallel. In a special case, the required solver is max-flow.

The theory leads to two algorithms that the authors report outperform competitors in runtime and result quality. In particular, they compute exact jointly diverse labelings faster than a popular approach that yields approximate solutions in the sense discussed by the paper. The result makes a structured diversity objective accessible through existing optimization machinery under the specified conditions.
summary.tldr: For certain diversity measures, exact jointly diverse labelings reduce to independent submodular optimizations with parameters computed in advance.

title: Joint M-Best-Diverse Labelings as a Parametric Submodular Minimization

abstract: We present a factorized hierarchical variational autoencoder, which learns disentangled and interpretable representations from sequential data without supervision. Specifically, we exploit the multi-scale nature of information in sequential data by formulating it explicitly within a factorized hierarchical graphical model that imposes sequence-dependent priors and sequence-independent priors to different sets of latent variables. The model is evaluated on two speech corpora to demonstrate, qualitatively, its ability to transform speakers or linguistic content by manipulating different sets of latent variables; and quantitatively, its ability to outperform an i-vector baseline for speaker verification and reduce the word error rate by as much as 35% in mismatched train/test scenarios for automatic speech recognition tasks.
originalAbstract: We present a factorized hierarchical variational autoencoder, which learns disentangled and interpretable representations from sequential data without supervision. Specifically, we exploit the multi-scale nature of information in sequential data by formulating it explicitly within a factorized hierarchical graphical model that imposes sequence-dependent priors and sequence-independent priors to different sets of latent variables. The model is evaluated on two speech corpora to demonstrate, qualitatively, its ability to transform speakers or linguistic content by manipulating different sets of latent variables; and quantitatively, its ability to outperform an i-vector baseline for speaker verification and reduce the word error rate by as much as 35% in mismatched train/test scenarios for automatic speech recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Sequential data contains information that varies over different timescales. This paper uses that structure to learn separate, interpretable representations without supervision. It introduces a factorized hierarchical variational autoencoder whose graphical model explicitly distinguishes different groups of latent variables through sequence-dependent and sequence-independent prior distributions.

The design gives the model a structural basis for separating kinds of information that coexist in a sequence. On two speech corpora, qualitative experiments manipulate different latent-variable groups to transform either the speaker or the linguistic content. These demonstrations show that the learned variables can provide distinct controls over meaningful properties of speech.

Quantitative evaluations report better speaker verification than an i-vector baseline and reductions in speech-recognition word error rate of as much as 35% when training and testing conditions are mismatched. These findings connect interpretability to task utility: the representations support both controlled changes to speech and improvements in the evaluated applications. The largest reported error reduction belongs specifically to the mismatched train/test scenarios.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical variational autoencoder separates speech factors without supervision and improves evaluated speaker-verification and mismatched speech-recognition tasks.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Disentangled and Interpretable Representations from Sequential Data

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning algorithms have been shown to learn complex tasks using highly general policy classes. However, sparse reward problems remain a significant challenge. Exploration methods based on novelty detection have been particularly successful in such settings but typically require generative or predictive models of the observations, which can be difficult to train when the observations are very high-dimensional and complex, as in the case of raw images. We propose a novelty detection algorithm for exploration that is based entirely on discriminatively trained exemplar models, where classifiers are trained to discriminate each visited state against all others. Intuitively, novel states are easier to distinguish against other states seen during training. We show that this kind of discriminative modeling corresponds to implicit density estimation, and that it can be combined with count-based exploration to produce competitive results on a range of popular benchmark tasks, including state-of-the-art results on challenging egocentric observations in the vizDoom benchmark.

paragraphs: EX2 addresses exploration when reinforcement learning rewards are sparse. Novelty can guide an agent toward states it has not adequately explored, but many novelty methods require generating or predicting observations. Training those models can be difficult when observations are complex and high-dimensional, including raw images.

The paper instead learns discriminative exemplar models. These classifiers try to distinguish each visited state from the other states encountered during training. The intuition is that an unusual state should be easier to distinguish from the agent’s previous experience. The authors show that this discriminative procedure corresponds to an implicit form of density estimation, connecting classification-based novelty to how frequently states occur.

They combine this novelty mechanism with count-based exploration and obtain competitive results across several popular benchmarks. On challenging egocentric observations in vizDoom, they report state-of-the-art results. The significance is that exploration can use a density-related novelty signal learned entirely through discrimination, providing an alternative to explicitly modeling how observations are generated or predicting their contents.
summary.tldr: EX2 guides exploration using classifiers that identify distinctive states, linking discriminative novelty detection to implicit density estimation.

title: EX2: Exploration with Exemplar Models for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce a solid harmonic wavelet scattering representation, invariant to rigid motion and stable to deformations, for regression and classification of 2D and 3D signals. Solid harmonic wavelets are computed by multiplying solid harmonic functions with Gaussian windows dilated at different scales. Invariant scattering coefficients are obtained by cascading such wavelet transforms with the complex modulus nonlinearity. We study an application of solid harmonic scattering invariants to the estimation of quantum molecular energies, which are also invariant to rigid motion and stable with respect to deformations. A multilinear regression over scattering invariants provides close to state of the art results over small and large databases of organic molecules.

paragraphs: A useful representation of a molecule should reflect properties that remain unchanged when the molecule is translated or rotated. This paper introduces solid harmonic wavelet scattering, a representation for two- and three-dimensional signals that is invariant to rigid motion and stable under deformation. It is designed for regression and classification.

The construction combines solid harmonic functions with Gaussian windows at multiple scales to form wavelets. Cascading wavelet transforms with a complex-modulus nonlinearity produces invariant scattering coefficients. These coefficients describe signals while respecting the stated transformation properties, providing inputs for prediction that do not depend on an arbitrary rigid placement of the signal.

The authors apply the representation to molecular electronic densities to estimate quantum molecular energies, which share the relevant invariance and stability properties. Multilinear regression using the scattering coefficients achieves results close to the state of the art on small and large organic-molecule databases. The findings support pairing a carefully structured representation with a comparatively simple regression model.
summary.tldr: Rigid-motion-invariant wavelet scattering descriptors support near-state-of-the-art molecular energy prediction using multilinear regression.

title: Solid Harmonic Wavelet Scattering: Predicting Quantum Molecular Energy from Invariant Descriptors of 3D Electronic Densities

abstract: Here, we present a novel approach to solve the problem of reconstructing perceived stimuli from brain responses by combining probabilistic inference with deep learning. Our approach first inverts the linear transformation from latent features to brain responses with maximum a posteriori estimation and then inverts the nonlinear transformation from perceived stimuli to latent features with adversarial training of convolutional neural networks. We test our approach with a functional magnetic resonance imaging experiment and show that it can generate state-of-the-art reconstructions of perceived faces from brain activations.
originalAbstract: Here, we present a novel approach to solve the problem of reconstructing perceived stimuli from brain responses by combining probabilistic inference with deep learning. Our approach first inverts the linear transformation from latent features to brain responses with maximum a posteriori estimation and then inverts the nonlinear transformation from perceived stimuli to latent features with adversarial training of convolutional neural networks. We test our approach with a functional magnetic resonance imaging experiment and show that it can generate state-of-the-art reconstructions of perceived faces from brain activations.

paragraphs: This paper reconstructs perceived faces from measured brain responses by combining probabilistic inference with deep learning. It divides reconstruction into two linked inverse problems: recovering latent features from brain activity and then recovering an image from those features. The latent representation provides the connection between neural measurements and visual content.

The first stage reverses a linear transformation from latent features to brain responses using maximum a posteriori estimation. This selects a feature estimate through probabilistic inference. The second stage reverses the nonlinear transformation from a perceived stimulus to its latent features, using convolutional neural networks trained through an adversarial approach.

The authors test the combined method in a functional magnetic resonance imaging experiment and report state-of-the-art reconstructions of perceived faces. The finding supports the complete decoding pipeline in that experimental setting. Its methodological significance is the division of labor between a probabilistic estimate of the hidden representation and a learned nonlinear reconstruction stage, allowing each part of the brain-to-image mapping to be addressed separately.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic latent-feature inference and adversarial convolutional networks reconstruct perceived faces from fMRI responses.

title: Reconstructing perceived faces from brain activations with deep adversarial neural decoding

abstract: In pattern recognition, a random label Y is to be predicted based upon observing a random vector X valued in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with d>1 by means of a classification rule with minimum probability of error. In a wide variety of applications, ranging from finance/insurance to environmental sciences through teletraffic data analysis for instance, extreme (i.e. very large) observations X are of crucial importance, while contributing in a negligible manner to the (empirical) error however, simply because of their rarity. As a consequence, empirical risk minimizers generally perform very poorly in extreme regions. It is the purpose of this paper to develop a general framework for classification in the extremes. Precisely, under non-parametric heavy-tail assumptions for the class distributions, we prove that a natural and asymptotic notion of risk, accounting for predictive performance in extreme regions of the input space, can be defined and show that minimizers of an empirical version of a non-asymptotic approximant of this dedicated risk, based on a fraction of the largest observations, lead to classification rules with good generalization capacity, by means of maximal deviation inequalities in low probability regions. Beyond theoretical results, numerical experiments are presented in order to illustrate the relevance of the approach developed.

paragraphs: Very large observations may be crucial to a classification problem while contributing little to average training error because they are rare. This paper argues that ordinary empirical risk minimization can consequently perform poorly in extreme regions. It develops a classification framework whose objective specifically accounts for prediction quality in those regions.

Under nonparametric heavy-tail assumptions on the class distributions, the authors define an asymptotic notion of risk for extreme observations. They then construct a non-asymptotic approximation and an empirical version based on a fraction of the largest observations. Learning with that objective directs attention toward the part of the input space that an overall error measure can underweight.

The theoretical analysis uses maximal deviation inequalities in low-probability regions to establish good generalization capacity for the resulting classifiers. Numerical experiments illustrate the approach's relevance. The key contribution is a dedicated learning objective and supporting theory for classification in the extremes, with the guarantees grounded in the stated heavy-tail assumptions.
summary.tldr: A tail-focused classification objective provides generalization guarantees for extreme observations under heavy-tail assumptions.

title: On Binary Classification in Extreme Regions

abstract: We introduce a family of implicit probabilistic integrators for initial value problems (IVPs), taking as a starting point the multistep Adams–Moulton method. The implicit construction allows for dynamic feedback from the forthcoming time-step, in contrast to previous probabilistic integrators, all of which are based on explicit methods. We begin with a concise survey of the rapidly-expanding field of probabilistic ODE solvers. We then introduce our method, which builds on and adapts the work of Conrad et al. (2016) and Teymur et al. (2016), and provide a rigorous proof of its well-definedness and convergence. We discuss the problem of the calibration of such integrators and suggest one approach. We give an illustrative example highlighting the effect of the use of probabilistic integrators—including our new method—in the setting of parameter inference within an inverse problem.

paragraphs: An initial value problem specifies how a system changes and where its trajectory begins. Numerical integration approximates that trajectory through successive time steps. This paper develops probabilistic integrators for such problems, using the multistep Adams–Moulton method as the starting point for a new family of implicit constructions.

The defining feature is that a step can incorporate feedback from the forthcoming time point. The abstract contrasts this with earlier probabilistic integrators, which used explicit methods. The authors adapt previous probabilistic-solver work to this implicit setting and rigorously establish that their construction is well defined and convergent. This provides mathematical support for the method alongside its algorithmic description.

The paper also discusses calibration: how the probabilistic treatment should be set, rather than merely introducing randomness into a solver. It suggests one approach and illustrates the effects of probabilistic integration in an inverse problem involving parameter inference. That example connects the solver to a downstream task, showing why the treatment of numerical integration can matter when estimating the parameters of a dynamical system.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces implicit probabilistic ODE integrators, proves their convergence, and illustrates their role in parameter inference.

title: Implicit Probabilistic Integrators for ODEs

abstract: Gaussian processes (GPs) are flexible non-parametric models, with a capacity that grows with the available data. However, computational constraints with standard inference procedures have limited exact GPs to problems with fewer than about ten thousand training points, necessitating approximations for larger datasets. In this paper, we develop a scalable approach for exact GPs that leverages multi-GPU parallelization and methods like linear conjugate gradients, accessing the kernel matrix only through matrix multiplication. By partitioning and distributing kernel matrix multiplies, we demonstrate that an exact GP can be trained on over a million points, a task previously thought to be impossible with current computing hardware. Moreover, our approach is generally applicable, without constraints to grid data or specific kernel classes. Enabled by this scalability, we perform the first-ever comparison of exact GPs against scalable GP approximations on datasets with $10^4 \!-\! 10^6$ data points, showing dramatic performance improvements.
