paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible models whose capacity grows with the data, but standard exact inference becomes computationally demanding as datasets expand. This paper develops a scalable computational approach that makes exact Gaussian-process training possible on more than a million points, substantially extending the scale discussed for standard procedures.

The approach combines multiple GPUs with methods such as linear conjugate gradients. It accesses the kernel matrix through matrix multiplication and partitions those multiplications across devices. This organization distributes the expensive computation while retaining the exact Gaussian-process model. The method is broadly applicable: it does not require data arranged on a grid or restrict use to particular kernel classes.

The increased scale enables comparisons between exact Gaussian processes and scalable approximations on datasets ranging from ten thousand to one million points. The authors report dramatic performance improvements in those comparisons. The contribution is therefore both computational and empirical: it makes a previously difficult model feasible at larger scales and uses that capability to examine the performance consequences of approximation.
summary.tldr: Distributed kernel-matrix multiplication and iterative methods enable exact Gaussian-process training on more than a million data points.

title: Exact Gaussian Processes on a Million Data Points

abstract: Several important families of computational and statistical results in machine learning and randomized algorithms rely on uniform bounds on quadratic forms of random vectors or matrices. Such results include the Johnson-Lindenstrauss (J-L) Lemma, the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP), randomized sketching algorithms, and approximate linear algebra. The existing results critically depend on statistical independence, e.g., independent entries for random vectors, independent rows for random matrices, etc., which prevent their usage in dependent or adaptive modeling settings. In this paper, we show that such independence is in fact not needed for such results which continue to hold under fairly general dependence structures. In particular, we present uniform bounds on random quadratic forms of stochastic processes which are conditionally independent and sub-Gaussian given another (latent) process. Our setup allows general dependencies of the stochastic process on the history of the latent process and the latent process to be influenced by realizations of the stochastic process. The results are thus applicable to adaptive modeling settings and also allows for sequential design of random vectors and matrices. We also discuss stochastic process based forms of J-L, RIP, and sketching, to illustrate the generality of the results.

Our setup allows general dependencies of the stochastic process on the history of the latent process and the latent process to be influenced by realizations of the stochastic process. paragraphs: Many guarantees for random projections, matrix sketches, and approximate linear algebra rely on controlling quadratic forms of random vectors or matrices. Standard results often assume independent entries or rows. That assumption restricts their use when later random choices depend on earlier observations, as happens in adaptive or sequential construction.

The paper establishes uniform bounds under a broader, structured form of dependence. The processes must be conditionally independent and sub-Gaussian given a latent process. Within that setup, the observed process may depend on the latent process's history, and the latent process may itself respond to observed realizations. This permits feedback while retaining assumptions sufficient for the bounds.

The authors discuss stochastic-process versions of the Johnson-Lindenstrauss result, restricted isometry, and sketching to illustrate the consequences. The contribution extends familiar mathematical tools to adaptive modeling and sequentially designed random vectors or matrices. Independence is therefore not indispensable in its usual unconditional form, but the result does not cover arbitrary dependence: the conditional independence and tail assumptions define the setting in which the extension applies.
summary.tldr: Uniform bounds for random quadratic forms extend to structured dependent processes, supporting adaptive versions of projection, isometry, and sketching guarantees.

title: Random Quadratic Forms with Dependence: Applications to Restricted Isometry and Beyond

abstract: This paper studies a curious phenomenon in learning energy-based model (EBM) using MCMC. In each learning iteration, we generate synthesized examples by running a non-convergent, non-mixing, and non-persistent short-run MCMC toward the current model, always starting from the same initial distribution such as uniform noise distribution, and always running a fixed number of MCMC steps. After generating synthesized examples, we then update the model parameters according to the maximum likelihood learning gradient, as if the synthesized examples are fair samples from the current model. We treat this non-convergent short-run MCMC as a learned generator model or a flow model. We provide arguments for treating the learned non-convergent short-run MCMC as a valid model. We show that the learned short-run MCMC is capable of generating realistic images. More interestingly, unlike traditional EBM or MCMC, the learned short-run MCMC is capable of reconstructing observed images and interpolating between images, like generator or flow models. The code can be found in the Appendix.

paragraphs: The paper studies an unusual way to train an energy-based model: generate examples using only a fixed, short run of Markov chain Monte Carlo, even though that run does not converge or mix. Every run starts afresh from the same initial distribution, such as uniform noise, rather than continuing a previous chain.

After generating these examples, training updates the energy model using the maximum-likelihood gradient as if the examples were representative samples from the current model. The authors propose interpreting the short sampling procedure itself as a learned generator or flow model. They provide arguments for treating this non-convergent procedure as a valid model in its own right.

The learned short-run process produces realistic images in the reported results. It also reconstructs observed images and interpolates between images, capabilities the authors associate with generator and flow models. The significance is that useful generative behavior can emerge from the finite sampling dynamics themselves. The claim does not depend on the chain having reached the energy model's equilibrium distribution; its deliberate lack of convergence is central to the phenomenon under study.
summary.tldr: A fixed, non-convergent MCMC procedure can learn to act as an image generator that also supports reconstruction and interpolation.

title: Learning Non-Convergent Non-Persistent Short-Run MCMC Toward Energy-Based Model

abstract: Reinforcement learning demands a reward function, which is often difficult to provide or design in real world applications. While inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) holds promise for automatically learning reward functions from demonstrations, several major challenges remain. First, existing IRL methods learn reward functions from scratch, requiring large numbers of demonstrations to correctly infer the reward for each task the agent may need to perform. Second, and more subtly, existing methods typically assume demonstrations for one, isolated behavior or task, while in practice, it is significantly more natural and scalable to provide datasets of heterogeneous behaviors. To this end, we propose a deep latent variable model that is capable of learning rewards from unstructured, multi-task demonstration data, and critically, use this experience to infer robust rewards for new, structurally-similar tasks from a single demonstration. Our experiments on multiple continuous control tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to state-of-the-art imitation and inverse reinforcement learning methods.

Our experiments on multiple continuous control tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared to state-of-the-art imitation and inverse reinforcement learning methods.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning needs a reward function, but specifying a useful reward can be difficult in real applications. Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer rewards from demonstrations. This paper addresses two obstacles: learning each task from scratch can require many demonstrations, and demonstration datasets naturally contain mixtures of behaviors rather than one isolated task.

The authors propose a deep latent variable model that learns rewards from unstructured demonstrations covering multiple tasks. Probabilistic context variables provide the model's way to represent the task context within this mixed experience. The aim is to reuse what has been learned across tasks when interpreting a demonstration of a new one.

The model can infer robust rewards from a single demonstration for new tasks that are structurally similar to those represented in its experience. Experiments across multiple continuous control tasks demonstrate effectiveness compared with state-of-the-art imitation and inverse reinforcement learning methods. The contribution is therefore both learning from heterogeneous behavior and reducing the demonstration requirement for related new tasks.
summary.tldr: A latent variable model learns from mixed-task demonstrations and uses that experience to infer rewards for structurally similar new tasks from one demonstration.

title: Meta-Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Probabilistic Context Variables

abstract: We integrate information-theoretic concepts into the design and analysis of optimistic algorithms and Thompson sampling. By making a connection between information-theoretic quantities and confidence bounds, we obtain results that relate the per-period performance of the agent with its information gain about the environment, thus explicitly characterizing the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. The resulting cumulative regret bound depends on the agent's uncertainty over the environment and quantifies the value of prior information. We show applicability of this approach to several environments, including linear bandits, tabular MDPs, and factored MDPs. These examples demonstrate the potential of a general information-theoretic approach for the design and analysis of reinforcement learning algorithms.

By making a connection between information-theoretic quantities and confidence bounds, we obtain results that relate the per-period performance of the agent with its information gain about the environment, thus explicitly characterizing the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. The resulting cumulative regret bound depends on the agent's uncertainty over the environment and quantifies the value of prior information. We show applicability of this approach to several environments, including linear bandits, tabular MDPs, and factored MDPs. These examples demonstrate the potential of a general information-theoretic approach for the design and analysis of reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning requires balancing decisions that perform well now with decisions that reveal useful information. This paper connects that tradeoff to confidence bounds through information-theoretic quantities. It develops the connection for optimistic algorithms and Thompson sampling, providing a common way to reason about how uncertainty affects their decisions.

The resulting analysis relates an agent’s performance in each period to the information it gains about the environment. Across periods, the cumulative regret bound depends on how uncertain the agent is about that environment. This gives prior information an explicit role in the guarantee: the analysis quantifies its value through the uncertainty that remains for the agent to resolve.

The authors demonstrate applicability to linear bandits, tabular Markov decision processes, and factored Markov decision processes. These examples show that the approach reaches several different models of sequential decision making. The contribution is a connection useful for algorithm design and analysis, with the examples supporting the potential of a broader information-theoretic framework rather than establishing a universal performance improvement across all reinforcement learning problems.
summary.tldr: Information-theoretic confidence bounds connect reinforcement learning performance to information gain and quantify the value of prior knowledge.

title: Information-Theoretic Confidence Bounds for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study how recurrent neural networks (RNNs) solve a hierarchical inference task involving two latent variables and disparate timescales separated by 1-2 orders of magnitude. The task is of interest to the International Brain Laboratory, a global collaboration of experimental and theoretical neuroscientists studying how the mammalian brain generates behavior. We make four discoveries. First, RNNs learn behavior that is quantitatively similar to ideal Bayesian baselines. Second, RNNs perform inference by learning a two-dimensional subspace defining beliefs about the latent variables. Third, the geometry of RNN dynamics reflects an induced coupling between the two separate inference processes necessary to solve the task. Fourth, we perform model compression through a novel form of knowledge distillation on hidden representations -- Representations and Dynamics Distillation (RADD)-- to reduce the RNN dynamics to a low-dimensional, highly interpretable model. This technique promises a useful tool for interpretability of high dimensional nonlinear dynamical systems. Altogether, this work yields predictions to guide exploration and analysis of mouse neural data and circuity.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how recurrent neural networks solve an inference task involving two hidden variables that evolve on substantially different timescales. The task is relevant to studies of mouse behavior and neural processing. The authors examine both the networks' performance and the internal dynamics that support their solutions.

The trained networks behave quantitatively similarly to ideal Bayesian baselines. Within their hidden activity, the authors identify a two-dimensional subspace representing beliefs about the two latent variables. The geometry of the dynamics also reveals coupling between the separate inference processes, explaining how the network's internal organization connects the two levels of the task.

To make the solution easier to interpret, the paper introduces Representations and Dynamics Distillation, which compresses hidden representations and dynamics into a low-dimensional model. The resulting model is highly interpretable, and the technique is presented as promising for studying other high-dimensional nonlinear systems. The work yields predictions for investigations of mouse neural data and circuitry; the reported network mechanisms serve as guides for that biological exploration.
summary.tldr: Analysis and distillation reveal a low-dimensional belief representation underlying RNN solutions to a hierarchical inference task relevant to mouse neuroscience.

title: Reverse-engineering recurrent neural network solutions to a hierarchical inference task for mice

abstract: Among existing uncertainty estimation approaches, Dirichlet Prior Network (DPN) distinctly models different predictive uncertainty types. However, for in-domain examples with high data uncertainties among multiple classes, even a DPN model often produces indistinguishable representations from the out-of-distribution (OOD) examples, compromising their OOD detection performance. We address this shortcoming by proposing a novel loss function for DPN to maximize the representation gap between in-domain and OOD examples. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach consistently improves OOD detection performance.
originalAbstract: Among existing uncertainty estimation approaches, Dirichlet Prior Network (DPN) distinctly models different predictive uncertainty types. However, for in-domain examples with high data uncertainties among multiple classes, even a DPN model often produces indistinguishable representations from the out-of-distribution (OOD) examples, compromising their OOD detection performance. We address this shortcoming by proposing a novel loss function for DPN to maximize the representation gap between in-domain and OOD examples. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach consistently improves OOD detection performance.

paragraphs: An uncertain prediction can arise because an example is ambiguous among familiar classes or because it comes from outside the model's domain. This paper focuses on separating these cases. Dirichlet Prior Networks model different types of predictive uncertainty, but their representations can still become difficult to distinguish in an important setting.

The problematic setting involves in-domain examples with substantial uncertainty across multiple classes. Their representations can resemble those of out-of-distribution examples, weakening the network's ability to detect unfamiliar inputs. The authors propose a new loss function for Dirichlet Prior Networks that aims to maximize the representation gap between in-domain and out-of-distribution examples.

Experiments show consistent improvements in out-of-distribution detection with the proposed objective. The finding supports training explicitly for separation between these two kinds of examples, particularly when ambiguity within the known domain otherwise resembles unfamiliarity. The contribution targets a specific failure of uncertainty representation: a model may express uncertainty while still failing to distinguish why that uncertainty has arisen.
summary.tldr: A new Dirichlet Prior Network loss improves out-of-distribution detection by separating unfamiliar inputs from ambiguous in-domain examples.

title: Towards Maximizing the Representation Gap between In-Domain & Out-of-Distribution Examples

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning algorithms with probabilistic dynamical models are amongst the most data-efficient learning methods. This is often attributed to their ability to distinguish between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. However, while most algorithms distinguish these two uncertainties for learning the model, they ignore it when optimizing the policy, which leads to greedy and insufficient exploration. At the same time, there are no practical solvers for optimistic exploration algorithms. In this paper, we propose a practical optimistic exploration algorithm (H-UCRL). H-UCRL reparameterizes the set of plausible models and hallucinates control directly on the epistemic uncertainty. By augmenting the input space with the hallucinated inputs, H-UCRL can be solved using standard greedy planners. Furthermore, we analyze H-UCRL and construct a general regret bound for well-calibrated models, which is provably sublinear in the case of Gaussian Process models. Based on this theoretical foundation, we show how optimistic exploration can be easily combined with state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms and different probabilistic models. Our experiments demonstrate that optimistic exploration significantly speeds-up learning when there are penalties on actions, a setting that is notoriously difficult for existing model-based reinforcement learning algorithms.
originalAbstract: Model-based reinforcement learning algorithms with probabilistic dynamical models are amongst the most data-efficient learning methods. This is often attributed to their ability to distinguish between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. However, while most algorithms distinguish these two uncertainties for learning the model, they ignore it when optimizing the policy, which leads to greedy and insufficient exploration. At the same time, there are no practical solvers for optimistic exploration algorithms. In this paper, we propose a practical optimistic exploration algorithm (H-UCRL). H-UCRL reparameterizes the set of plausible models and hallucinates control directly on the epistemic uncertainty. By augmenting the input space with the hallucinated inputs, H-UCRL can be solved using standard greedy planners. Furthermore, we analyze H-UCRL and construct a general regret bound for well-calibrated models, which is provably sublinear in the case of Gaussian Process models. Based on this theoretical foundation, we show how optimistic exploration can be easily combined with state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms and different probabilistic models. Our experiments demonstrate that optimistic exploration significantly speeds-up learning when there are penalties on actions, a setting that is notoriously difficult for existing model-based reinforcement learning algorithms.

paragraphs: A learned dynamics model can be uncertain because it lacks knowledge or because outcomes contain inherent randomness. These are epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty, respectively. The paper argues that many model-based reinforcement learning methods distinguish them during model learning but fail to exploit the distinction when choosing actions, leading to insufficient exploration.

H-UCRL makes optimistic exploration practical by reparameterizing plausible dynamics models and adding imagined control inputs that act on epistemic uncertainty. These extra inputs let planning consider favorable possibilities within what the model does not yet know. By augmenting the input space this way, the method can use standard greedy planners to solve the resulting optimistic planning problem.

The analysis gives a general regret bound for well-calibrated models and proves sublinear regret for Gaussian Process models. The authors also combine the approach with different probabilistic models and existing reinforcement learning algorithms. Experiments show substantially faster learning when actions incur penalties. In that setting, optimism helps exploration despite the immediate cost of taking actions, addressing a reported weakness of existing model-based methods.
summary.tldr: H-UCRL turns uncertainty about dynamics into optimistic planning inputs, enabling practical exploration and faster learning in experiments with action penalties.

title: Efficient Model-Based Reinforcement Learning through Optimistic Policy Search and Planning

abstract: Constrained submodular maximization problems encompass a wide variety of applications, including personalized recommendation, team formation, and revenue maximization via viral marketing. The massive instances occurring in modern-day applications can render existing algorithms prohibitively slow. Moreover, frequently those instances are also inherently stochastic. Focusing on these challenges, we revisit the classic problem of maximizing a (possibly non-monotone) submodular function subject to a knapsack constraint. We present a simple randomized greedy algorithm that achieves a $5.83$ approximation and runs in $O(n \log n)$ time, i.e., at least a factor $n$ faster than other state-of-the-art algorithms. The robustness of our approach allows us to further transfer it to a stochastic version of the problem. There, we obtain a 9-approximation to the best adaptive policy, which is the first constant approximation for non-monotone objectives. Experimental evaluation of our algorithms showcases their improved performance on real and synthetic data.

The objective may also be non-monotone, so adding an item can reduce value. This paper targets the computational difficulty of solving such problems at large scale, including settings with stochastic outcomes.

The stated running time is at least a factor of n faster than other state-of-the-art algorithms, addressing the cost of applying existing methods to massive instances.

The approach also extends to a stochastic version, where decisions can adapt as information becomes available. Experiments on real and synthetic data show improved performance, complementing the theoretical tradeoff between efficient computation and solution quality.
summary.tldr: A fast randomized greedy method provides approximation guarantees for budgeted non-monotone submodular selection and an adaptive stochastic extension.

title: Fast Adaptive Non-Monotone Submodular Maximization Subject to a Knapsack Constraint

abstract: We propose to learn to distinguish reversible from irreversible actions for better informed decision-making in Reinforcement Learning (RL). From theoretical considerations, we show that approximate reversibility can be learned through a simple surrogate task: ranking randomly sampled trajectory events in chronological order. Intuitively, pairs of events that are always observed in the same order are likely to be separated by an irreversible sequence of actions. Conveniently, learning the temporal order of events can be done in a fully self-supervised way, which we use to estimate the reversibility of actions from experience, without any priors.We propose two different strategies that incorporate reversibility in RL agents, one strategy for exploration (RAE) and one strategy for control (RAC). We demonstrate the potential of reversibility-aware agents in several environments, including the challenging Sokoban game. In synthetic tasks, we show that we can learn control policies that never fail and reduce to zero the side-effects of interactions, even without access to the reward function.

paragraphs: An agent's decisions can have very different consequences depending on whether their effects can be undone. This paper develops a way for reinforcement-learning agents to estimate that distinction from experience. Its theoretical starting point is that approximate reversibility can be learned through a surrogate task: determining the chronological order of randomly sampled trajectory events.

The intuition is that events consistently observed in the same order are likely to be separated by an irreversible sequence of actions. Temporal ordering supplies its own training information, so the reversibility estimate can be learned without prior knowledge. The authors incorporate this estimate into two strategies, one guiding exploration and another guiding control.

Experiments demonstrate the potential of these strategies in several environments, including Sokoban. In synthetic tasks, the authors learn control policies that never fail and produce no interaction side effects, even without access to the reward function. Those outcomes are specific to the reported tasks. More broadly, the work shows how a self-supervised temporal signal can inform decisions about actions whose consequences may be difficult to reverse.
summary.tldr: Learning the temporal order of experienced events provides a self-supervised signal for reversibility that can guide exploration and control.

title: There Is No Turning Back: A Self-Supervised Approach for Reversibility-Aware Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) methods for Reinforcement Learning (RL) problems, where the goal is to find a policy using data from several tasks represented by Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) that can be updated by one step of \textit{stochastic} policy gradient for the realized MDP. In particular, using stochastic gradients in MAML update steps is crucial for RL problems since computation of exact gradients requires access to a large number of possible trajectories. For this formulation, we propose a variant of the MAML method, named Stochastic Gradient Meta-Reinforcement Learning (SG-MRL), and study its convergence properties. We derive the iteration and sample complexity of SG-MRL to find an $\epsilon$-first-order stationary point, which, to the best of our knowledge, provides the first convergence guarantee for model-agnostic meta-reinforcement learning algorithms. We further show how our results extend to the case where more than one step of stochastic policy gradient method is used at test time. Finally, we empirically compare SG-MRL and MAML in several deep RL environments.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning seeks a policy that can adapt quickly after learning from several tasks. Here, each task is a Markov decision process, and adaptation initially consists of one stochastic policy-gradient step. Stochastic updates are central to the formulation because computing exact gradients would require access to many possible trajectories.

The authors introduce Stochastic Gradient Meta-Reinforcement Learning, or SG-MRL, as a variant of Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning. They derive the iteration and sample requirements for reaching an epsilon-first-order stationary point. This establishes a convergence target where the first-order signal is sufficiently small; it does not assert that the procedure finds a globally best policy.

The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first convergence guarantee for model-agnostic meta-reinforcement learning algorithms. They extend the results to multiple stochastic adaptation steps at test time and compare SG-MRL with MAML in several deep reinforcement learning environments. The central contribution is a convergence analysis that explicitly accommodates the sampled adaptation updates needed in reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: SG-MRL provides convergence and sample-complexity guarantees for meta-reinforcement learning with stochastic policy-gradient adaptation.

title: On the Convergence Theory of Debiased Model-Agnostic Meta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Language is an interface to the outside world. In order for embodied agents to use it, language must be grounded in other, sensorimotor modalities. While there is an extended literature studying how machines can learn grounded language, the topic of how to learn spatio-temporal linguistic concepts is still largely uncharted. To make progress in this direction, we here introduce a novel spatio-temporal language grounding task where the goal is to learn the meaning of spatio-temporal descriptions of behavioral traces of an embodied agent. This is achieved by training a truth function that predicts if a description matches a given history of observations. The descriptions involve time-extended predicates in past and present tense as well as spatio-temporal references to objects in the scene. To study the role of architectural biases in this task, we train several models including multimodal Transformer architectures; the latter implement different attention computations between words and objects across space and time. We test models on two classes of generalization: 1) generalization to new sentences, 2) generalization to grammar primitives. We observe that maintaining object identity in the attention computation of our Transformers is instrumental to achieving good performance on generalization overall, and that summarizing object traces in a single token has little influence on performance. We then discuss how this opens new perspectives for language-guided autonomous embodied agents.

This paper introduces a task focused on descriptions that refer to space and time: a model must determine whether a description matches an agent's observation history. The descriptions include past and present tense, events extending over time, and references to objects in a scene.

The authors train a truth function for this matching task and compare several architectures. Their multimodal Transformers differ in how attention connects words and objects across spatial and temporal information. Evaluation examines two kinds of generalization: handling new sentences and generalizing to grammar primitives. This makes architectural choices part of the investigation into grounded language learning.

By comparison, summarizing an object's trace in a single token has little effect on performance. These findings suggest that how the model maintains the connection to a particular object matters more in the tested task than that trace-summary choice. The paper discusses implications for language-guided autonomous embodied agents.
summary.tldr: A language-grounding task shows that preserving object identity in Transformer attention helps generalization across space and time.

title: Grounding Spatio-Temporal Language with Transformers

abstract: Estimating Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence from samples of two distributions is essential in many machine learning problems. Variational methods using neural network discriminator have been proposed to achieve this task in a scalable manner. However, we noticed that most of these methods using neural network discriminators suffer from high fluctuations (variance) in estimates and instability in training. In this paper, we look at this issue from statistical learning theory and function space complexity perspective to understand why this happens and how to solve it. We argue that the cause of these pathologies is lack of control over the complexity of the neural network discriminator function and could be mitigated by controlling it. To achieve this objective, we 1) present a novel construction of the discriminator in the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), 2) theoretically relate the error probability bound of the KL estimates to the complexity of the discriminator in the RKHS space, 3) present a scalable way to control the complexity (RKHS norm) of the discriminator for a reliable estimation of KL divergence, and 4) prove the consistency of the proposed estimator. In three different applications of KL divergence -- estimation of KL, estimation of mutual information and Variational Bayes -- we show that by controlling the complexity as developed in the theory, we are able to reduce the variance of KL estimates and stabilize the training.

Across these applications, controlling complexity as prescribed by the analysis reduces estimate variance and stabilizes training. The results support the paper's diagnosis and proposed remedy: managing the discriminator's flexibility can improve the reliability of the estimates produced through it.
summary.tldr: Controlling an RKHS discriminator's complexity yields a consistent KL estimator and reduces variance and training instability in the reported applications.

title: Reliable Estimation of KL Divergence using a Discriminator in Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space

abstract: Privacy-protected microdata are often the desired output of a differentially private algorithm since microdata is familiar and convenient for downstream users. However, there is a statistical price for this kind of convenience. We show that an uncertainty principle governs the trade-off between accuracy for a population of interest (``sum query'') vs. accuracy for its component sub-populations (``point queries''). Compared to differentially private query answering systems that are not required to produce microdata, accuracy can degrade by a logarithmic factor. For example, in the case of pure differential privacy, without the microdata requirement, one can provide noisy answers to the sum query and all point queries while guaranteeing that each answer has squared error $O(1/\epsilon^2)$. With the microdata requirement, one must choose between allowing an additional $\log^2(d)$ factor ($d$ is the number of point queries) for some point queries or allowing an extra $O(d^2)$ factor for the sum query. We present lower bounds for pure, approximate, and concentrated differential privacy. We propose mitigation strategies and create a collection of benchmark datasets that can be used for public study of this problem.

paragraphs: Privacy-protected microdata provide a familiar record-based format that downstream users can analyze. This paper shows that requiring this format can carry an additional statistical cost. Its central trade-off concerns accurately representing a population total while also accurately representing the individual subpopulations that make up that total.

The authors compare private query-answering systems with systems required to output microdata. Under pure differential privacy, a system without that requirement can answer both the sum query and every point query with squared error O(1/ε²). Requiring microdata forces a choice: some point queries incur an additional log²(d) factor, or the sum query incurs an extra O(d²) factor, where d counts the point queries.

These results show that the output format itself can restrict accuracy, even when the desired statistics are the same. The paper establishes lower bounds for pure, approximate, and concentrated differential privacy. It also proposes mitigation strategies and supplies benchmark datasets for studying the problem publicly. The practical message is that convenient records and accurate answers to multiple kinds of queries need not be interchangeable privacy products.
summary.tldr: Requiring differentially private microdata introduces an accuracy trade-off between population totals and their component subpopulations.

title: An Uncertainty Principle is a Price of Privacy-Preserving Microdata

abstract: Robust principal component analysis (RPCA) is a critical tool in modern machine learning, which detects outliers in the task of low-rank matrix reconstruction. In this paper, we propose a scalable and learnable non-convex approach for high-dimensional RPCA problems, which we call Learned Robust PCA (LRPCA). LRPCA is highly efficient, and its free parameters can be effectively learned to optimize via deep unfolding. Moreover, we extend deep unfolding from finite iterations to infinite iterations via a novel feedforward-recurrent-mixed neural network model. We establish the recovery guarantee of LRPCA under mild assumptions for RPCA. Numerical experiments show that LRPCA outperforms the state-of-the-art RPCA algorithms, such as ScaledGD and AltProj, on both synthetic datasets and real-world applications.

The paper targets high-dimensional versions of this problem, where an approach needs both effective recovery and scalable computation. It introduces Learned Robust PCA, or LRPCA, as an efficient, learnable non-convex method.

LRPCA uses deep unfolding to learn free parameters of its optimization procedure. This connects an iterative algorithm with a neural network whose parameters can be trained to improve optimization. The authors also introduce a mixed feedforward and recurrent architecture, extending unfolding beyond a fixed finite sequence of iterations to an infinite-iteration formulation. This broadens how the learned iterative process can be represented.

The paper establishes a recovery guarantee under assumptions described as mild for robust PCA. That guarantee gives conditional theoretical support alongside the learned design. Numerical experiments show improvements over state-of-the-art methods, including ScaledGD and AltProj, on synthetic data and real-world applications. Together, these results support LRPCA as a scalable approach that combines trainable optimization parameters with a formal recovery analysis.
summary.tldr: LRPCA combines learnable non-convex optimization with an extended deep-unfolding architecture for scalable robust matrix recovery and outlier detection.

title: Learned Robust PCA: A Scalable Deep Unfolding Approach for High-Dimensional Outlier Detection

abstract: We present an approach for generating natural language explanations of high-level behavior of autonomous agents navigating in partially-revealed environments. Our counterfactual explanations communicate changes to interpratable statistics of the belief (e.g., the likelihood an exploratory action will reach the unseen goal) that are estimated from visual input via a deep neural network and used (via a Bellman equation variant) to inform planning far into the future. Additionally, our novel training procedure mimics explanation generation, allowing us to use planning performance as an objective measure of explanation quality. Simulated experiments validate that our explanations are both high quality and can be used in interventions to directly correct bad behavior; agents trained via our training-by-explaining procedure achieve 9.1% lower average cost than a non-learned baseline (12.7% after interventions) in environments derived from real-world floor plans.

This paper explains those high-level decisions through interpretable quantities in the agent's beliefs, such as the estimated likelihood that an exploratory action will reach an unseen goal. A neural network estimates these quantities from visual observations.

The explanations are counterfactual: they describe changes to belief statistics relevant to the agent's behavior. Those same statistics feed a variant of the Bellman equation used for planning far into the future. The training procedure mimics explanation generation, allowing the quality of the explanations to be assessed through their connection to planning performance.

Agents trained through this procedure achieve 9.1% lower average cost than a non-learned baseline, rising to 12.7% after interventions. The results tie explanations to measurable improvements in navigation and behavior correction.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual explanations of a navigator's beliefs support planning and corrective interventions, with lower navigation costs in simulated environments.

title: Generating High-Quality Explanations for Navigation in Partially-Revealed Environments

abstract: Following their success in natural language processing, transformers have recently shown much promise for computer vision. The self-attention operation underlying transformers yields global interactions between all tokens ,i.e. words or image patches, and enables flexible modelling of image data beyond the local interactions of convolutions. This flexibility, however, comes with a quadratic complexity in time and memory, hindering application to long sequences and high-resolution images. We propose a “transposed” version of self-attention that operates across feature channels rather than tokens, where the interactions are based on the cross-covariance matrix between keys and queries. The resulting cross-covariance attention (XCA) has linear complexity in the number of tokens, and allows efficient processing of high-resolution images.Our cross-covariance image transformer (XCiT) is built upon XCA. It combines the accuracy of conventional transformers with the scalability of convolutional architectures. We validate the effectiveness and generality of XCiT by reporting excellent results on multiple vision benchmarks, including image classification and self-supervised feature learning on ImageNet-1k, object detection and instance segmentation on COCO, and semantic segmentation on ADE20k.We will opensource our code and trained models to reproduce the reported results.

paragraphs: Standard self-attention lets every image token interact with every other token, providing flexible global modeling. Its time and memory costs grow quadratically with the number of tokens, making long sequences and high-resolution images expensive to process.

The paper changes the direction of attention. Cross-covariance attention operates between feature channels rather than between tokens, using a cross-covariance matrix derived from keys and queries to determine the interactions. Its complexity grows linearly with the number of tokens.

The resulting XCiT architecture is built around this operation. It aims to retain conventional transformers' accuracy while achieving scalability associated with convolutional architectures. The change directly targets the token-count bottleneck that becomes more severe as image resolution increases.

The authors report strong results for ImageNet-1k classification and self-supervised feature learning, COCO object detection and instance segmentation, and ADE20k semantic segmentation. These evaluations support the architecture's usefulness across several visual tasks, while the linear token complexity explains its appeal for efficiently handling higher-resolution inputs.
summary.tldr: XCiT moves attention from token pairs to feature channels, achieving linear token complexity and strong results across several vision tasks.

title: XCiT: Cross-Covariance Image Transformers

abstract: In few-shot domain adaptation (FDA), classifiers for the target domain are trained with \emph{accessible} labeled data in the source domain (SD) and few labeled data in the target domain (TD). However, data usually contain private information in the current era, e.g., data distributed on personal phones. Thus, the private data will be leaked if we directly access data in SD to train a target-domain classifier (required by FDA methods). In this paper, to prevent privacy leakage in SD, we consider a very challenging problem setting, where the classifier for the TD has to be trained using few labeled target data and a well-trained SD classifier, named few-shot hypothesis adaptation (FHA). In FHA, we cannot access data in SD, as a result, the private information in SD will be protected well. To this end, we propose a target-oriented hypothesis adaptation network (TOHAN) to solve the FHA problem, where we generate highly-compatible unlabeled data (i.e., an intermediate domain) to help train a target-domain classifier. TOHAN maintains two deep networks simultaneously, in which one focuses on learning an intermediate domain and the other takes care of the intermediate-to-target distributional adaptation and the target-risk minimization. Experimental results show that TOHAN outperforms competitive baselines significantly.

paragraphs: Ordinary few-shot domain adaptation assumes access to labeled source data along with a few labeled target examples. This paper studies a more restricted setting: the source data cannot be accessed, but a well-trained source classifier is available. Called few-shot hypothesis adaptation, this setup is motivated by avoiding direct exposure of private source-domain records.

TOHAN adapts the classifier by generating compatible unlabeled data that form an intermediate domain. It maintains two deep networks simultaneously. One learns the intermediate domain, while the other handles adaptation from that domain to the target and minimizes target risk. The generated data thus provide a bridge between the available source classifier and the small labeled target set.

Experiments show significant improvements over competitive baselines. The contribution is a way to adapt using a source hypothesis rather than accessible source training examples. Its privacy motivation is specifically tied to keeping those source records inaccessible during adaptation; the mechanism described is the removal of direct source-data access from the training setup.
summary.tldr: TOHAN adapts a source classifier using few labeled target examples and a generated intermediate domain, without accessing source data.

title: TOHAN: A One-step Approach towards Few-shot Hypothesis Adaptation

abstract: Single image reflection separation (SIRS), as a representative blind source separation task, aims to recover two layers, $\textit{i.e.}$, transmission and reflection, from one mixed observation, which is challenging due to the highly ill-posed nature. Existing deep learning based solutions typically restore the target layers individually, or with some concerns at the end of the output, barely taking into account the interaction across the two streams/branches. In order to utilize information more efficiently, this work presents a general yet simple interactive strategy, namely $\textit{your trash is my treasure}$ (YTMT), for constructing dual-stream decomposition networks. To be specific, we explicitly enforce the two streams to communicate with each other block-wisely. Inspired by the additive property between the two components, the interactive path can be easily built via transferring, instead of discarding, deactivated information by the ReLU rectifier from one stream to the other. Both ablation studies and experimental results on widely-used SIRS datasets are conducted to demonstrate the efficacy of YTMT, and reveal its superiority over other state-of-the-art alternatives. The implementation is quite simple and our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mingcv/YTMT-Strategy.

paragraphs: Separating a reflection from a single image requires recovering two layers from one mixed observation: the transmitted scene and the reflection. The problem is highly ill-posed. Existing deep-learning approaches often reconstruct the layers largely independently, leaving limited interaction between the two processing branches until late in the network.

The proposed YTMT strategy makes the branches communicate at each block. It draws on the additive relationship between the two components: information that is unhelpful for reconstructing one layer may still help reconstruct the other. Specifically, information deactivated by a ReLU operation is transferred to the other stream instead of being discarded.

Ablation studies and experiments on commonly used reflection-separation datasets demonstrate the strategy's effectiveness and superiority over the compared state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution is a simple way to make dual-stream decomposition use intermediate information more efficiently. By exchanging information throughout processing, the two branches participate in a connected reconstruction procedure rather than relying mainly on separate estimates or late interaction.
summary.tldr: YTMT improves reflection separation by transferring ReLU-deactivated information between the branches reconstructing transmission and reflection.

title: Trash or Treasure? An Interactive Dual-Stream Strategy for Single Image Reflection Separation

abstract: The theory of spectral filtering is a remarkable tool to understand the statistical properties of learning with kernels. For least squares, it allows to derive various regularization schemes that yield faster convergence rates of the excess risk than with Tikhonov regularization. This is typically achieved by leveraging classical assumptions called source and capacity conditions, which characterize the difficulty of the learning task. In order to understand estimators derived from other loss functions, Marteau-Ferey et al. have extended the theory of Tikhonov regularization to generalized self concordant loss functions (GSC), which contain, e.g., the logistic loss. In this paper, we go a step further and show that fast and optimal rates can be achieved for GSC by using the iterated Tikhonov regularization scheme, which is intrinsically related to the proximal point method in optimization, and overcomes the limitation of the classical Tikhonov regularization.

paragraphs: In kernel learning, regularization shapes how a model balances fitting observations with controlling the solution. For least-squares problems, spectral filtering theory explains why some regularization schemes achieve faster statistical learning rates than standard Tikhonov regularization. Those improvements use source and capacity conditions, assumptions that describe the difficulty of the learning problem.

This paper extends the search for faster rates beyond least squares. It studies generalized self-concordant losses, a class that includes logistic loss. Earlier work had extended the analysis of standard Tikhonov regularization to this class; the authors instead analyze an iterated version of the regularization scheme, which is closely connected to the proximal point method in optimization.

The result is that iterated Tikhonov regularization can achieve fast, optimal excess-risk rates for this broader loss class. Excess risk measures the statistical gap between the learned predictor and the target optimum. The significance is therefore about how efficiently prediction quality improves with learning, rather than simply how quickly an optimization routine runs. The analysis shows how iteration can overcome a limitation of classical Tikhonov regularization.
summary.tldr: Iterated Tikhonov regularization achieves fast, optimal statistical rates for generalized self-concordant losses, extending improvements beyond least squares.

title: Beyond Tikhonov: faster learning with self-concordant losses, via iterative regularization

abstract: We consider the exploration-exploitation trade-off in reinforcement learning and show that an agent endowed with an exponential epistemic-risk-seeking utility function explores efficiently, as measured by regret. The state-action values induced by the exponential utility satisfy a Bellman recursion, so we can use dynamic programming to compute them. We call the resulting algorithm K-learning (for knowledge) and the risk-seeking utility ensures that the associated state-action values (K-values) are optimistic for the expected optimal Q-values under the posterior. The exponential utility function induces a Boltzmann exploration policy for which the 'temperature' parameter is equal to the risk-seeking parameter and is carefully controlled to yield a Bayes regret bound of $\tilde O(L^{3/2} \sqrt{S A T})$, where $L$ is the time horizon, $S$ is the number of states, $A$ is the number of actions, and $T$ is the total number of elapsed timesteps. We conclude with a numerical example demonstrating that K-learning is competitive with other state-of-the-art algorithms in practice.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents must balance exploiting known rewards with exploring actions whose value remains uncertain. This paper develops K-learning using an exponential utility that seeks epistemic risk, meaning uncertainty arising from incomplete knowledge. The utility encourages exploration and produces K-values that are optimistic relative to posterior expected optimal Q-values.

The resulting state-action values obey a Bellman recursion, allowing them to be computed with dynamic programming. The exponential utility also induces a Boltzmann exploration policy. Its temperature equals the risk-seeking parameter, connecting the amount of exploration directly to the utility used to value uncertainty.

Carefully controlling that parameter yields a Bayes regret bound of approximately L^(3/2) times sqrt(SAT), with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here L is the horizon, S the number of states, A the number of actions, and T the elapsed timesteps. This supplies a formal efficiency guarantee for exploration. A numerical example also shows competitive performance against other state-of-the-art algorithms, offering practical support alongside the theoretical result rather than a broad empirical comparison.
summary.tldr: K-learning turns epistemic risk seeking into optimistic values and a Boltzmann exploration policy with a controlled Bayes regret bound.

title: Variational Bayesian Reinforcement Learning with Regret Bounds

abstract: Differential equations in general and neural ODEs in particular are an essential technique in continuous-time system identification. While many deterministic learning algorithms have been designed based on numerical integration via the adjoint method, many downstream tasks such as active learning, exploration in reinforcement learning, robust control, or filtering require accurate estimates of predictive uncertainties. In this work, we propose a novel approach towards estimating epistemically uncertain neural ODEs, avoiding the numerical integration bottleneck. Instead of modeling uncertainty in the ODE parameters, we directly model uncertainties in the state space. Our algorithm distributional gradient matching (DGM) jointly trains a smoother and a dynamics model and matches their gradients via minimizing a Wasserstein loss. Our experiments show that, compared to traditional approximate inference methods based on numerical integration, our approach is faster to train, faster at predicting previously unseen trajectories, and in the context of neural ODEs, significantly more accurate.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe how a system changes continuously over time. Many learning methods produce deterministic models, but applications such as exploration, filtering, and robust control also need predictive uncertainty. This paper targets epistemic uncertainty, the uncertainty associated with what the model has learned, while avoiding a numerical-integration bottleneck.

Distributional gradient matching represents uncertainty directly in the system's state space instead of placing it on the differential equation's parameters. It jointly trains a smoother and a dynamics model. Their gradients are matched by minimizing a Wasserstein loss, so learning aligns distributions of changes rather than relying on parameter uncertainty propagated through the usual integration-based approach.

Compared with traditional approximate-inference methods that use numerical integration, the experiments show faster training and faster prediction of previously unseen trajectories. In the neural-ODE setting, the authors also report substantially greater accuracy. These findings support matching uncertain state-space dynamics as a way to combine predictive uncertainty with computational efficiency. The reported speed and accuracy advantages are experimental comparisons, rather than universal guarantees for every continuous-time system.
summary.tldr: Distributional gradient matching learns uncertain neural dynamics in state space and improves speed and accuracy in the reported comparisons.

title: Distributional Gradient Matching for Learning Uncertain Neural Dynamics Models

abstract: Most existing video-and-language (VidL) research focuses on a single dataset, or multiple datasets of a single task. In reality, a truly useful VidL system is expected to be easily generalizable to diverse tasks, domains, and datasets. To facilitate the evaluation of such systems, we introduce Video-And-Language Understanding Evaluation (VALUE) benchmark, an assemblage of 11 VidL datasets over 3 popular tasks: (i) text-to-video retrieval; (ii) video question answering; and (iii) video captioning. VALUE benchmark aims to cover a broad range of video genres, video lengths, data volumes, and task difficulty levels. Rather than focusing on single-channel videos with visual information only, VALUE promotes models that leverage information from both video frames and their associated subtitles, as well as models that share knowledge across multiple tasks. We evaluate various baseline methods with and without large-scale VidL pre-training, and systematically investigate the impact of video input channels, fusion methods, and different video representations. We also study the transferability between tasks, and conduct multi-task learning under different settings. The significant gap between our best model and human performance calls for future study for advanced VidL models. VALUE is available at https://value-benchmark.github.io/.

paragraphs: VALUE evaluates video-and-language systems across a wider range of demands than a single dataset or task. It combines 11 datasets covering text-to-video retrieval, video question answering, and video captioning. The collection spans different genres, video lengths, dataset sizes, and difficulty levels to support evaluation of broader generalization.

These comparisons make the sources and organization of information explicit parts of the evaluation.

Its best model remains substantially below human performance, identifying considerable room for improvement within the benchmark. VALUE's contribution is therefore both a broad evaluation resource and an experimental examination of design choices. It offers a setting for assessing whether progress extends across video-and-language uses rather than being confined to one dataset.
summary.tldr: VALUE evaluates video-and-language models across 11 datasets and three tasks, revealing a substantial gap between its best model and human performance.

title: VALUE: A Multi-Task Benchmark for Video-and-Language Understanding Evaluation

abstract: Learning in deep neural networks is known to depend critically on the knowledge embedded in the initial network weights. However, few theoretical results have precisely linked prior knowledge to learning dynamics. Here we derive exact solutions to the dynamics of learning with rich prior knowledge in deep linear networks by generalising Fukumizu's matrix Riccati solution \citep{fukumizu1998effect}. We obtain explicit expressions for the evolving network function, hidden representational similarity, and neural tangent kernel over training for a broad class of initialisations and tasks. The expressions reveal a class of task-independent initialisations that radically alter learning dynamics from slow non-linear dynamics to fast exponential trajectories while converging to a global optimum with identical representational similarity, dissociating learning trajectories from the structure of initial internal representations. We characterise how network weights dynamically align with task structure, rigorously justifying why previous solutions successfully described learning from small initial weights without incorporating their fine-scale structure. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for continual learning, reversal learning and learning of structured knowledge. Taken together, our results provide a mathematical toolkit for understanding the impact of prior knowledge on deep learning.

paragraphs: Initial network weights encode information that can strongly influence subsequent learning. This paper makes that connection mathematically explicit for deep linear networks. By extending a matrix Riccati solution, the authors derive exact descriptions of training with rich prior knowledge across a broad class of tasks and initializations.

The formulas track the network's input-output function, similarities within hidden representations, and the neural tangent kernel over time. They reveal task-independent initializations that change slow nonlinear learning into fast exponential trajectories while reaching a global optimum with identical representational similarity. This separates the path taken during learning from what the structure of internal representations alone might suggest.

The analysis also describes how weights align with task structure as training proceeds. It rigorously explains why earlier solutions captured learning from small initial weights without modeling their fine-grained structure. The authors discuss implications for continual learning, reversal learning, and structured knowledge. The resulting toolkit provides exact insight within deep linear networks into how prior knowledge shapes learning speed and trajectory.
summary.tldr: Exact solutions for deep linear networks reveal how initialization can radically alter learning trajectories and speed.

title: Exact learning dynamics of deep linear networks with prior knowledge

abstract: Personalized Federated Learning (pFL), which utilizes and deploys distinct local models, has gained increasing attention in recent years due to its success in handling the statistical heterogeneity of FL clients. However, standardized evaluation and systematical analysis of diverse pFL methods remain a challenge. Firstly, the highly varied datasets, FL simulation settings and pFL implementations prevent easy and fair comparisons of pFL methods. Secondly, the current pFL literature diverges in the adopted evaluation and ablation protocols. Finally, the effectiveness and robustness of pFL methods are under-explored in various practical scenarios, such as the generalization to new clients and the participation of resource-limited clients. To tackle these challenges, we propose the first comprehensive pFL benchmark, pFL-Bench, for facilitating rapid, reproducible, standardized and thorough pFL evaluation. The proposed benchmark contains more than 10 dataset variants in various application domains with a unified data partition and realistic heterogeneous settings; a modularized and easy-to-extend pFL codebase with more than 20 competitive pFL method implementations; and systematic evaluations under containerized environments in terms of generalization, fairness, system overhead, and convergence. We highlight the benefits and potential of state-of-the-art pFL methods and hope pFL-Bench enables further pFL research and broad applications that would otherwise be difficult owing to the absence of a dedicated benchmark. The code is released at https://github.com/alibaba/FederatedScope/tree/master/benchmark/pFL-Bench.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning gives different clients distinct local models, helping accommodate differences in their data. Comparing methods is difficult when studies use different datasets, client simulations, implementations, and evaluation protocols. The paper introduces pFL-Bench to make these comparisons more standardized, reproducible, and comprehensive.

The benchmark includes more than ten dataset variants across application areas, with unified data partitioning and realistic heterogeneous settings. A modular codebase supplies more than twenty competitive method implementations and is designed for extension. Evaluations run in containerized environments, providing a common setup for investigating methods whose published results might otherwise be difficult to compare directly.

The evaluation covers generalization, fairness, system overhead, and convergence. The motivation also includes practical questions such as whether a method works for new clients or accommodates participants with limited resources. These concerns broaden assessment beyond performance for the clients already involved in training. The paper highlights the benefits and potential of existing personalized methods, while its main contribution is shared infrastructure for examining their behavior under consistent and practically relevant conditions.
summary.tldr: pFL-Bench standardizes datasets, implementations, and evaluations for comparing personalized federated learning methods under heterogeneous conditions.

title: pFL-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Personalized Federated Learning

abstract: This paper presents HierSpeech, a high-quality end-to-end text-to-speech (TTS) system based on a hierarchical conditional variational autoencoder (VAE) utilizing self-supervised speech representations. Recently, single-stage TTS systems, which directly generate raw speech waveform from text, have been getting interest thanks to their ability in generating high-quality audio within a fully end-to-end training pipeline. However, there is still a room for improvement in the conventional TTS systems. Since it is challenging to infer both the linguistic and acoustic attributes from the text directly, missing the details of attributes, specifically linguistic information, is inevitable, which results in mispronunciation and over-smoothing problem in their synthetic speech. To address the aforementioned problem, we leverage self-supervised speech representations as additional linguistic representations to bridge an information gap between text and speech. Then, the hierarchical conditional VAE is adopted to connect these representations and to learn each attribute hierarchically by improving the linguistic capability in latent representations. Compared with the state-of-the-art TTS system, HierSpeech achieves +0.303 comparative mean opinion score, and reduces the phoneme error rate of synthesized speech from 9.16% to 5.78% on the VCTK dataset. Furthermore, we extend our model to HierSpeech-U, an untranscribed text-to-speech system. Specifically, HierSpeech-U can adapt to a novel speaker by utilizing self-supervised speech representations without text transcripts. The experimental results reveal that our method outperforms publicly available TTS models, and show the effectiveness of speaker adaptation with untranscribed speech.

paragraphs: Generating speech directly from text requires a model to recover both linguistic content and acoustic characteristics. The paper argues that losing information along this route can produce mispronunciations and overly smooth speech. HierSpeech addresses this gap by incorporating self-supervised speech representations as additional linguistic information in an end-to-end text-to-speech system.

A hierarchical conditional variational autoencoder connects these representations and learns the relevant attributes at different levels. The purpose of the hierarchy is to strengthen linguistic information within the model's latent representations, giving waveform generation a richer basis than the direct text-to-speech mapping alone. This connects the architecture to the pronunciation and detail problems motivating the work.

On VCTK, HierSpeech reports a comparative mean opinion score improvement of 0.303 and reduces phoneme error from 9.16% to 5.78% against the stated comparison system. The authors also introduce HierSpeech-U, which adapts to a new speaker using speech without transcripts. Their experiments support both improved synthesis and the usefulness of self-supervised representations for adaptation from untranscribed recordings.
summary.tldr: HierSpeech combines hierarchical latent modeling with self-supervised speech representations to improve synthesis and enable speaker adaptation without transcripts.

title: HierSpeech: Bridging the Gap between Text and Speech by Hierarchical Variational Inference using Self-supervised Representations for Speech Synthesis

abstract: The conventional sliced Wasserstein is defined between two probability measures that have realizations as \textit{vectors}. When comparing two probability measures over images, practitioners first need to vectorize images and then project them to one-dimensional space by using matrix multiplication between the sample matrix and the projection matrix. After that, the sliced Wasserstein is evaluated by averaging the two corresponding one-dimensional projected probability measures. However, this approach has two limitations. The first limitation is that the spatial structure of images is not captured efficiently by the vectorization step; therefore, the later slicing process becomes harder to gather the discrepancy information. The second limitation is memory inefficiency since each slicing direction is a vector that has the same dimension as the images. To address these limitations, we propose novel slicing methods for sliced Wasserstein between probability measures over images that are based on the convolution operators. We derive \emph{convolution sliced Wasserstein} (CSW) and its variants via incorporating stride, dilation, and non-linear activation function into the convolution operators. We investigate the metricity of CSW as well as its sample complexity, its computational complexity, and its connection to conventional sliced Wasserstein distances. Finally, we demonstrate the favorable performance of CSW over the conventional sliced Wasserstein in comparing probability measures over images and in training deep generative modeling on images.

paragraphs: Sliced Wasserstein compares distributions through one-dimensional projections. For images, the conventional procedure first flattens each image into a vector. The authors identify two drawbacks: this does not efficiently capture spatial structure, and every projection direction requires a vector as large as the flattened image, creating a memory burden.

The paper replaces this slicing procedure with methods based on convolution operators. It derives convolution sliced Wasserstein, or CSW, along with variants that incorporate stride, dilation, and nonlinear activation. This brings the slicing operation closer to the spatial organization of image data. The authors investigate metric properties, sample requirements, computational complexity, and connections to conventional sliced Wasserstein distances.

Experiments show favorable performance compared with conventional sliced Wasserstein for comparing image distributions and training deep generative models on images. The contribution is both a new family of image-oriented comparisons and an analysis of their mathematical and computational behavior. The reported findings support convolution as a useful way to construct slices when the samples being compared have image structure.
summary.tldr: Convolution sliced Wasserstein replaces flattened-image projections with convolutional slicing to better accommodate image structure and memory demands.

title: Revisiting Sliced Wasserstein on Images: From Vectorization to Convolution

abstract: Unsupervised distribution alignment estimates a transformation that maps two or more source distributions to a shared aligned distribution given only samples from each distribution. This task has many applications including generative modeling, unsupervised domain adaptation, and socially aware learning. Most prior works use adversarial learning (i.e., min-max optimization), which can be challenging to optimize and evaluate. A few recent works explore non-adversarial flow-based (i.e., invertible) approaches, but they lack a unified perspective and are limited in efficiently aligning multiple distributions. Therefore, we propose to unify and generalize previous flow-based approaches under a single non-adversarial framework, which we prove is equivalent to minimizing an upper bound on the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD). Importantly, our problem reduces to a min-min, i.e., cooperative, problem and can provide a natural evaluation metric for unsupervised distribution alignment. We show empirical results on both simulated and real-world datasets to demonstrate the benefits of our approach. Code is available at https://github.com/inouye-lab/alignment-upper-bound.

We show empirical results on both simulated and real-world datasets to demonstrate the benefits of our approach. Code is available at https://github.com/inouye-lab/alignment-upper-bound.

paragraphs: Unsupervised distribution alignment learns transformations that bring samples from different source distributions into a shared distribution. It appears in generative modeling, domain adaptation, and socially aware learning. Many existing methods use adversarial optimization, where one component minimizes an objective while another maximizes it, making both optimization and evaluation challenging.

This paper unifies and extends approaches based on invertible transformations within a non-adversarial framework. The authors prove that the proposed formulation is equivalent to minimizing an upper bound on Jensen-Shannon divergence, a measure of distributional difference. Its optimization is cooperative: the participating components minimize rather than compete over the objective.

The framework also supplies a natural evaluation measure for unsupervised alignment and addresses limitations in efficiently aligning multiple distributions. Experiments on simulated and real-world data demonstrate benefits of the approach. The theoretical connection matters because it gives the cooperative objective a distribution-comparison interpretation, joining optimization and evaluation within one formulation instead of leaving them as separate design choices.
summary.tldr: A unified invertible-transformation framework aligns distributions cooperatively by minimizing an upper bound on Jensen-Shannon divergence.

title: Cooperative Distribution Alignment via JSD Upper Bound

abstract: The automation of the medical evidence acquisition and diagnosis process has recently attracted increasing attention in order to reduce the workload of doctors and democratize access to medical care. However, most works proposed in the machine learning literature focus solely on improving the prediction accuracy of a patient's pathology. We argue that this objective is insufficient to ensure doctors' acceptability of such systems. In their initial interaction with patients, doctors do not only focus on identifying the pathology a patient is suffering from; they instead generate a differential diagnosis (in the form of a short list of plausible diseases) because the medical evidence collected from patients is often insufficient to establish a final diagnosis. Moreover, doctors explicitly explore severe pathologies before potentially ruling them out from the differential, especially in acute care settings. Finally, for doctors to trust a system's recommendations, they need to understand how the gathered evidences led to the predicted diseases. In particular, interactions between a system and a patient need to emulate the reasoning of doctors. We therefore propose to model the evidence acquisition and automatic diagnosis tasks using a deep reinforcement learning framework that considers three essential aspects of a doctor's reasoning, namely generating a differential diagnosis using an exploration-confirmation approach while prioritizing severe pathologies. We propose metrics for evaluating interaction quality based on these three aspects. We show that our approach performs better than existing models while maintaining competitive pathology prediction accuracy.

The authors formulate evidence acquisition and diagnosis using deep reinforcement learning. summary.tldr: A reinforcement learning diagnosis framework improves measured interaction quality by maintaining differential diagnoses, exploring and confirming evidence, and prioritizing severe diseases.

title: Towards Trustworthy Automatic Diagnosis Systems by Emulating Doctors' Reasoning with Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) is an emerging paradigm that addresses distributional shifts between training and testing phases without additional data acquisition or labeling cost; only unlabeled test data streams are used for continual model adaptation. Previous TTA schemes assume that the test samples are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), even though they are often temporally correlated (non-i.i.d.) in application scenarios, e.g., autonomous driving. We discover that most existing TTA methods fail dramatically under such scenarios. Motivated by this, we present a new test-time adaptation scheme that is robust against non-i.i.d. test data streams. Our novelty is mainly two-fold: (a) Instance-Aware Batch Normalization (IABN) that corrects normalization for out-of-distribution samples, and (b) Prediction-balanced Reservoir Sampling (PBRS) that simulates i.i.d. data stream from non-i.i.d. stream in a class-balanced manner. Our evaluation with various datasets, including real-world non-i.i.d. streams, demonstrates that the proposed robust TTA not only outperforms state-of-the-art TTA algorithms in the non-i.i.d. setting, but also achieves comparable performance to those algorithms under the i.i.d. assumption. Code is available at https://github.com/TaesikGong/NOTE.
