paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using an unlabeled stream encountered after training, helping it respond to distribution shifts without collecting new labels. Many existing methods assume that incoming samples are independent and identically distributed. This paper examines the more realistic possibility that nearby samples are temporally related and finds dramatic failures among most existing methods in those scenarios.

NOTE addresses this problem with two components. Instance-Aware Batch Normalization corrects normalization for out-of-distribution samples. Prediction-balanced Reservoir Sampling selects stored samples to simulate a more independent, class-balanced stream from the correlated observations. Together, these mechanisms address both how individual inputs are normalized and which observations are used during adaptation.

Evaluations include multiple datasets and real-world streams with temporal correlation. NOTE outperforms state-of-the-art adaptation methods in the non-independent setting while achieving comparable performance under the usual independent-sample assumption. The findings make the ordering and composition of test data central to adaptation design: a method that works on shuffled observations may behave very differently when observations arrive in correlated sequences.
summary.tldr: NOTE combines instance-aware normalization and prediction-balanced sampling to improve continual adaptation on temporally correlated test streams.

title: NOTE: Robust Continual Test-time Adaptation Against Temporal Correlation

abstract: Autoformalization is the process of automatically translating from natural language mathematics to formal specifications and proofs. A successful autoformalization system could advance the fields of formal verification, program synthesis, and artificial intelligence.While the long-term goal of autoformalization seemed elusive for a long time, we show large language models provide new prospects towards this goal. We make the surprising observation that LLMs can correctly translate a significant portion ($25.3\%$) of mathematical competition problems perfectly to formal specifications in Isabelle/HOL. We demonstrate the usefulness of this process by improving a previously introduced neural theorem prover via training on these autoformalized theorems. Our methodology results in a new state-of-the-art result on the MiniF2F theorem proving benchmark, improving the proof rate from~$29.6\%$ to~$35.2\%$.

paragraphs: Autoformalization translates mathematical writing into precise statements and proofs that formal systems can process. This paper investigates whether large language models can help with that translation. Its central result concerns formal specifications: the models correctly translate 25.3% of the mathematical competition problems studied into Isabelle/HOL, showing that a meaningful portion of these informal statements can be formalized automatically.

The authors then use the automatically formalized theorems as training material for an existing neural theorem prover. This connects two stages of mathematical automation. A language model converts informal problems into formal statements, and a theorem prover learns from those statements to improve its ability to produce proofs.

On the MiniF2F benchmark, this methodology raises the proof rate from 29.6% to 35.2%, which the paper reports as a new state of the art. The findings support autoformalization as a useful source of training material for theorem proving. They also distinguish successful statement translation from proof production: the translation result supplies theorems, while the downstream evaluation measures how often the prover solves problems.
summary.tldr: Language models correctly formalize some competition mathematics problems, and training on those statements improves a neural theorem prover.

title: Autoformalization with Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce chefs' random tables (CRTs), a new class of non-trigonometric random features (RFs) to approximate Gaussian and softmax kernels. CRTs are an alternative to standard random kitchen sink (RKS) methods, which inherently rely on the trigonometric maps. We present variants of CRTs where RFs are positive, a key requirement for applications in recent low-rank Transformers. Further variance reduction is possible by leveraging statistics which are simple to compute. One instantiation of CRTs, the optimal positive random features (OPRFs), is to our knowledge the first RF method for unbiased softmax kernel estimation with positive and bounded RFs, resulting in exponentially small tails and much lower variance than its counterparts. As we show, orthogonal random features applied in OPRFs provide additional variance reduction for any dimensionality $d$ (not only asymptotically for sufficiently large $d$, as for RKS). We test CRTs on many tasks ranging from non-parametric classification to training Transformers for text, speech and image data, obtaining new state-of-the-art results for low-rank text Transformers, while providing linear space and time complexity.

title: Chefs' Random Tables: Non-Trigonometric Random Features

abstract: Learning effective reinforcement learning (RL) policies to solve real-world complex tasks can be quite challenging without a high-fidelity simulation environment. In most cases, we are only given imperfect simulators with simplified dynamics, which inevitably lead to severe sim-to-real gaps in RL policy learning. The recently emerged field of offline RL provides another possibility to learn policies directly from pre-collected historical data. However, to achieve reasonable performance, existing offline RL algorithms need impractically large offline data with sufficient state-action space coverage for training. This brings up a new question: is it possible to combine learning from limited real data in offline RL and unrestricted exploration through imperfect simulators in online RL to address the drawbacks of both approaches? In this study, we propose the Dynamics-Aware Hybrid Offline-and-Online Reinforcement Learning (H2O) framework to provide an affirmative answer to this question. H2O introduces a dynamics-aware policy evaluation scheme, which adaptively penalizes the Q function learning on simulated state-action pairs with large dynamics gaps, while also simultaneously allowing learning from a fixed real-world dataset. Through extensive simulation and real-world tasks, as well as theoretical analysis, we demonstrate the superior performance of H2O against other cross-domain online and offline RL algorithms. H2O provides a brand new hybrid offline-and-online RL paradigm, which can potentially shed light on future RL algorithm design for solving practical real-world tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning faces a trade-off when real data is scarce and simulators are imperfect. Simulation allows extensive exploration, but simplified dynamics can produce policies that transfer poorly. Offline learning uses historical real-world data, yet effective learning can require broad coverage of states and actions. H2O combines these two sources.

The framework learns from a fixed real-world dataset while also exploring in simulation. Its central mechanism is dynamics-aware policy evaluation: it adaptively penalizes Q-function learning on simulated state-action pairs that have large dynamics gaps. This makes the influence of simulated experience depend on how strongly its dynamics differ from the real environment.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and evaluate H2O in simulation and real-world tasks. They report stronger performance than the compared cross-domain online and offline reinforcement learning algorithms. The findings support using limited real data together with simulator exploration, while adjusting for disagreement between their dynamics. H2O offers a hybrid learning approach in which simulation remains useful even when it is imperfect.
summary.tldr: H2O combines fixed real-world data with simulator exploration and penalizes simulated learning where dynamics gaps are large.

title: When to Trust Your Simulator: Dynamics-Aware Hybrid Offline-and-Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Text-conditioned image generation models have recently shown immense qualitative success using denoising diffusion processes. However, unlike discriminative vision-and-language models, it is a non-trivial task to subject these diffusion-based generative models to automatic fine-grained quantitative evaluation of high-level phenomena such as compositionality.Towards this goal, we perform two innovations. First, we transform diffusion-based models (in our case, Stable Diffusion) for any image-text matching (ITM) task using a novel method called DiffusionITM.Second, we introduce the Generative-Discriminative Evaluation Benchmark (GDBench) benchmark with 7 complex vision-and-language tasks, bias evaluation and detailed analysis.We find that Stable Diffusion + DiffusionITM is competitive on many tasks and outperforms CLIP on compositional tasks like like CLEVR and Winoground.We further boost its compositional performance with a transfer setup by fine-tuning on MS-COCO while retaining generative capabilities. We also measure the stereotypical bias in diffusion models, and find that Stable Diffusion 2.1 is, for the most part, less biased than Stable Diffusion 1.5.Overall, our results point in an exciting direction bringing discriminative and generative model evaluation closer. We will release code and benchmark setup soon.

paragraphs: Producing convincing images does not directly reveal how well a model understands relationships between objects and language. This paper makes that question more measurable by adapting Stable Diffusion to image–text matching. The resulting method, DiffusionITM, lets a generative model participate in tasks designed to test whether images and descriptions agree.

The authors also introduce GDBench, which combines seven complex vision-and-language tasks with bias evaluation and detailed analysis. This creates a shared evaluation route for generative and discriminative models. Stable Diffusion paired with DiffusionITM is competitive on many evaluated tasks and exceeds CLIP on compositional tasks including CLEVR and Winoground.

Fine-tuning on MS-COCO further improves compositional performance while preserving image generation capabilities. The bias analysis finds that Stable Diffusion 2.1 is generally, though not uniformly, less stereotypically biased than version 1.5. Together, these findings show that diffusion models contain capabilities that can be assessed through matching tasks, giving a more specific picture of their strengths than image quality alone.
summary.tldr: DiffusionITM turns Stable Diffusion into an image–text matcher, revealing competitive performance and particular strengths on evaluated compositional tasks.

title: Are Diffusion Models Vision-And-Language Reasoners?

abstract: Reference features from a template or historical frames are crucial for visual object tracking. Prior works utilize all features from a fixed template or memory for visual object tracking. However, due to the dynamic nature of videos, the required reference historical information for different search regions at different time steps is also inconsistent. Therefore, using all features in the template and memory can lead to redundancy and impair tracking performance. To alleviate this issue, we propose a novel tracking paradigm, consisting of a relevance attention mechanism and a global representation memory, which can adaptively assist the search region in selecting the most relevant historical information from reference features. Specifically, the proposed relevance attention mechanism in this work differs from previous approaches in that it can dynamically choose and build the optimal global representation memory for the current frame by accessing cross-frame information globally. Moreover, it can flexibly read the relevant historical information from the constructed memory to reduce redundancy and counteract the negative effects of harmful information. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving competitive performance on five challenging datasets with 71 FPS.

paragraphs: Visual tracking uses a template or earlier video frames to help locate an object in the current frame. However, the historical information useful for one search region or moment may be unhelpful for another. Using every available reference feature can introduce redundancy and information that harms tracking.

This paper proposes a tracker built around relevance attention and a global representation memory. The attention mechanism accesses information across frames to dynamically construct a memory suited to the current frame. It then lets the search region read relevant historical information from that memory. Both memory construction and retrieval therefore adapt to the current tracking problem.

The authors evaluate the method on five challenging datasets and report competitive tracking performance at 71 frames per second. These results support selective use of history as an effective tracking strategy. The contribution goes beyond retaining reference features: it makes decisions about which past information to organize and retrieve, with the aim of reducing redundant features and limiting the influence of harmful ones.
summary.tldr: A relevance-guided memory helps a visual tracker select useful historical features, achieving competitive results at 71 frames per second.

title: Reading Relevant Feature from Global Representation Memory for Visual Object Tracking

abstract: Text-to-Image diffusion models have made tremendous progress over the past two years, enabling the generation of highly realistic images based on open-domain text descriptions. However, despite their success, text descriptions often struggle to adequately convey detailed controls, even when composed of long and complex texts. Moreover, recent studies have also shown that these models face challenges in understanding such complex texts and generating the corresponding images. Therefore, there is a growing need to enable more control modes beyond text description. In this paper, we introduce Uni-ControlNet, a unified framework that allows for the simultaneous utilization of different local controls (e.g., edge maps, depth map, segmentation masks) and global controls (e.g., CLIP image embeddings) in a flexible and composable manner within one single model. Unlike existing methods, Uni-ControlNet only requires the fine-tuning of two additional adapters upon frozen pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models, eliminating the huge cost of training from scratch. Moreover, thanks to some dedicated adapter designs, Uni-ControlNet only necessitates a constant number (i.e., 2) of adapters, regardless of the number of local or global controls used. This not only reduces the fine-tuning costs and model size, making it more suitable for real-world deployment, but also facilitate composability of different conditions. Through both quantitative and qualitative comparisons, Uni-ControlNet demonstrates its superiority over existing methods in terms of controllability, generation quality and composability. Code is available at https://github.com/ShihaoZhaoZSH/Uni-ControlNet.

paragraphs: Text prompts can struggle to communicate detailed image requirements, and longer descriptions do not necessarily solve the problem. Uni-ControlNet gives text-to-image diffusion models additional control inputs within one framework. It supports local information such as edges, depth, and segmentation masks, together with global information such as CLIP image embeddings.

Their design allows different controls to be combined while keeping the adapter count fixed at two, regardless of how many local or global controls are used. This reduces fine-tuning costs and model size relative to approaches that require more extensive training or additional control-specific components.

Quantitative and qualitative comparisons report better controllability, generation quality, and composability than existing methods. Composability matters because users may need several constraints to influence the same image simultaneously. The contribution is a unified way to combine those conditions with a small, fixed adapter setup, making richer image control more practical without retraining the underlying diffusion model from scratch.
summary.tldr: Uni-ControlNet combines local and global image controls through two trainable adapters attached to a frozen text-to-image diffusion model.

title: Uni-ControlNet: All-in-One Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models

abstract: Meta learning is a promising paradigm to enable skill transfer across tasks.Most previous methods employ the empirical risk minimization principle in optimization.However, the resulting worst fast adaptation to a subset of tasks can be catastrophic in risk-sensitive scenarios.To robustify fast adaptation, this paper optimizes meta learning pipelines from a distributionally robust perspective and meta trains models with the measure of tail task risk.We take the two-stage strategy as heuristics to solve the robust meta learning problem, controlling the worst fast adaptation cases at a certain probabilistic level. Experimental results show that our simple method can improve the robustness of meta learning to task distributions and reduce the conditional expectation of the worst fast adaptation risk.

paragraphs: Meta learning aims to transfer experience across tasks so that a model can adapt quickly to a new one. Optimizing average training performance, however, can leave a subset of tasks with very poor adaptation outcomes. This paper focuses on those difficult cases, which matter especially when a bad outcome carries substantial risk.

The authors formulate meta learning from a distributionally robust perspective and train using tail task risk. This shifts attention toward the high-risk portion of the task distribution. They use a two-stage strategy as a heuristic for solving the robust learning problem, with the aim of controlling the worst adaptation cases at a specified probabilistic level.

Experiments show that the method can improve robustness to task distributions and lower the conditional average risk among the worst adaptation outcomes. The contribution is therefore about improving the unfavorable end of the performance distribution, rather than reporting only its overall average. The probabilistic framing matters: the stated objective concerns a selected level of tail risk, not a guarantee that every possible task will adapt successfully.
summary.tldr: Training meta learners on tail task risk can reduce poor adaptation outcomes and improve robustness across task distributions.

title: A Simple Yet Effective Strategy to Robustify the Meta Learning Paradigm

abstract: This paper seeks to address a gap in optimizing Average Precision (AP) while ensuring adversarial robustness, an area that has not been extensively explored to the best of our knowledge. AP maximization for deep learning has widespread applications, particularly when there is a significant imbalance between positive and negative examples. Although numerous studies have been conducted on adversarial training, they primarily focus on robustness concerning accuracy, ensuring that the average accuracy on adversarially perturbed examples is well maintained. However, this type of adversarial robustness is insufficient for many applications, as minor perturbations on a single example can significantly impact AP while not greatly influencing the accuracy of the prediction system. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel formulation that combines an AP surrogate loss with a regularization term representing adversarial ranking robustness, which maintains the consistency between ranking of clean data and that of perturbed data. We then devise an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm to optimize the resulting objective. Our empirical studies, which compare our method to current leading adversarial training baselines and other robust AP maximization strategies, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Notably, our methods outperform a state-of-the-art method (TRADES) by more than 4\% in terms of robust AP against PGD attacks while achieving 7\% higher AP on clean data simultaneously on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.The code is available at: <https://github.com/GangLii/Adversarial-AP>

Notably, our methods outperform a state-of-the-art method (TRADES) by more than 4\% in terms of robust AP against PGD attacks while achieving 7\% higher AP on clean data simultaneously on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100.The code is available at: <https://github.com/GangLii/Adversarial-AP>

paragraphs: Average precision evaluates the ordering of predictions and is useful when positive and negative examples are heavily imbalanced. This paper argues that adversarial robustness measured through classification accuracy can miss important ranking failures. A small perturbation to one example may substantially change average precision while barely affecting overall prediction accuracy.

The proposed objective combines a surrogate loss for average precision with a regularization term for adversarial ranking robustness. That term encourages the ordering of clean examples to remain consistent with the ordering after perturbation. The authors also develop an efficient stochastic optimization algorithm for this objective, making ranking consistency a direct part of training.

Empirical comparisons against leading adversarial training methods and robust average-precision approaches support the method's effectiveness. On CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, the paper reports more than 4% higher robust average precision under PGD attacks and 7% higher clean-data average precision than TRADES. These results show improvements in both clean and attacked rankings in the evaluated setting, supporting robustness objectives that directly reflect the ranking metric of interest.
summary.tldr: A ranking-consistency regularizer improves average precision on both clean and adversarially perturbed data in the reported experiments.

title: Maximization of Average Precision for Deep Learning with Adversarial Ranking Robustness

abstract: This paper investigates methods for improving generative data augmentation for deep learning. Generative data augmentation leverages the synthetic samples produced by generative models as an additional dataset for classification with small dataset settings. A key challenge of generative data augmentation is that the synthetic data contain uninformative samples that degrade accuracy. This can be caused by the synthetic samples not perfectly representing class categories in real data and uniform sampling not necessarily providing useful samples for tasks. In this paper, we present a novel strategy for generative data augmentation called *meta generative regularization* (MGR). To avoid the degradation of generative data augmentation, MGR utilizes synthetic samples for regularizing feature extractors instead of training classifiers. These synthetic samples are dynamically determined to minimize the validation losses through meta-learning. We observed that MGR can avoid the performance degradation of naive generative data augmentation and boost the baselines. Experiments on six datasets showed that MGR is effective particularly when datasets are smaller and stably outperforms baselines by up to 7 percentage points on test accuracy.

Generated samples may represent real classes imperfectly, and uniform sampling may supply examples that contribute little to the task. This paper addresses the resulting risk that generative data augmentation can reduce accuracy instead of improving it.

The proposed method, meta generative regularization, changes how synthetic examples are used. They regularize the feature extractor rather than directly train the classifier. A meta-learning process dynamically determines the synthetic samples to minimize validation loss. This connects the use of generated data to evidence of its usefulness for the learning task.

The benefits are particularly strong for smaller datasets, with reported test-accuracy improvements of up to seven percentage points. These findings support using synthetic data to shape learned features and adapting that regularization through validation feedback, rather than assuming every generated example will help.
summary.tldr: Meta generative regularization uses validation-guided synthetic samples to improve feature learning, especially with small datasets.

title: Regularizing Neural Networks with Meta-Learning Generative Models

abstract: We propose the Quantization Model of neural scaling laws, explaining both the observed power law dropoff of loss with model and data size, and also the sudden emergence of new capabilities with scale. We derive this model from what we call the Quantization Hypothesis, where network knowledge and skills are "quantized" into discrete chunks (quanta). We show that when quanta are learned in order of decreasing use frequency, then a power law in use frequencies explains observed power law scaling of loss. We validate this prediction on toy datasets, then study how scaling curves decompose for large language models. Using language model gradients, we automatically decompose model behavior into a diverse set of skills (quanta). We tentatively find that the frequency at which these quanta are used in the training distribution roughly follows a power law corresponding with the empirical scaling exponent for language models, a prediction of our theory.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a shared explanation for two observations about larger neural networks: loss often decreases according to a power law, while particular capabilities can appear suddenly. Its starting hypothesis is that knowledge and skills are acquired in discrete units, called quanta. Scaling then changes which of these units a model has learned.

The authors derive a relationship between the frequency of those units and the overall scaling curve. If units are learned from most frequently used to least frequently used, a power-law distribution of use frequencies explains power-law loss scaling. They validate this prediction on toy datasets before investigating how language-model behavior can be decomposed into skills.

For language models, they use gradients to automatically identify a diverse collection of candidate quanta. They tentatively find that the frequency of their use roughly follows a power law aligned with the observed language-model scaling exponent. That language-model evidence remains qualified, while the framework provides a concrete hypothesis linking gradual aggregate improvement to the acquisition of discrete capabilities.
summary.tldr: The Quantization Model explains scaling through discrete skills learned by frequency, with toy-data validation and tentative supporting evidence from language models.

title: The Quantization Model of Neural Scaling

abstract: Recent advancements in masked image modeling (MIM) have made it a prevailing framework for self-supervised visual representation learning. The MIM pretrained models, like most deep neural network methods, remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks, limiting their practical application, and this issue has received little research attention. In this paper, we investigate how this powerful self-supervised learning paradigm can provide adversarial robustness to downstream classifiers. During the exploration, we find that noisy image modeling (NIM), a simple variant of MIM that adopts denoising as the pre-text task, reconstructs noisy images surprisingly well despite severe corruption. Motivated by this observation, we propose an adversarial defense method, referred to as De^3, by exploiting the pretrained decoder for denoising. Through De^3, NIM is able to enhance adversarial robustness beyond providing pretrained features. Furthermore, we incorporate a simple modification, sampling the noise scale hyperparameter from random distributions, and enable the defense to achieve a better and tunable trade-off between accuracy and robustness. Experimental results demonstrate that, in terms of adversarial robustness, NIM is superior to MIM thanks to its effective denoising capability. Moreover, the defense provided by NIM achieves performance on par with adversarial training while offering the extra tunability advantage. Source code and models are available at https://github.com/youzunzhi/NIM-AdvDef.

paragraphs: Masked image modelling trains a visual model by asking it to reconstruct missing image content, but the resulting representations can still be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper investigates whether a related self-supervised task can contribute more directly to defence. The authors study noisy image modelling, which learns to reconstruct images after noise has been added.

They observe that this denoising task produces strong reconstruction even under severe corruption. Their defence, called De^3, uses the pretrained decoder's denoising capability to improve downstream classifiers' adversarial robustness. The decoder therefore contributes to defence alongside the features learned during pretraining. A further modification samples the noise-scale setting from random distributions, allowing adjustment of the balance between accuracy and robustness.

In the reported experiments, noisy image modelling provides stronger adversarial robustness than masked image modelling because of its denoising ability. Its defence performs on par with adversarial training while offering the additional tuning flexibility. These findings support using reconstruction capabilities learned during pretraining as an active component of a defensive system.
summary.tldr: A pretrained image-denoising decoder provides an adversarial defence with experimentally competitive robustness and an adjustable accuracy–robustness trade-off.

title: Beyond Pretrained Features: Noisy Image Modeling Provides Adversarial Defense

abstract: For some hypothesis classes and input distributions, \emph{active} agnostic learning needs exponentially fewer samples than passive learning; for other classes and distributions, it offers little to no improvement. The most popular algorithms for agnostic active learning express their performance in terms of a parameter called the disagreement coefficient, but it is known that these algorithms are inefficient on some inputs. We take a different approach to agnostic active learning, getting an algorithm that is \emph{competitive} with the optimal algorithm for any binary hypothesis class $H$ and distribution $\mathcal{D}_X$ over $X$. In particular, if any algorithm can use $m^*$ queries to get $O(\eta)$ error, then our algorithm uses $O(m^* \log H)$ queries to get $O(\eta)$ error. Our algorithm lies in the vein of the splitting-based approach of Dasgupta [2004], which gets a similar result for the realizable ($\eta = 0$) setting. We also show that it is NP-hard to do better than our algorithm's $O(\log H)$ overhead in general.

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples to request labels for, so its value depends on how much those choices reduce the labeling burden. In the agnostic setting, the learner must accommodate imperfect prediction. Some hypothesis classes and input distributions allow enormous savings over passive learning, while others offer little benefit. This paper seeks a guarantee that adapts to that variation.

The proposed algorithm competes with the best achievable query count for a given binary hypothesis class and input distribution. If some algorithm can reach error O(η) with m* queries, this algorithm reaches error of the same order using O(m* log H) queries. Its approach builds on splitting-based active learning, extending a style of guarantee previously obtained for the realizable setting.

The result measures performance against what is possible on the particular learning problem, rather than relying on the disagreement coefficient used by many existing algorithms. The paper also proves that improving the logarithmic overhead is NP-hard in general. Together, these results provide a competitive query guarantee and a computational obstacle to strengthening it universally.
summary.tldr: A new agnostic active-learning algorithm achieves the target error with a logarithmic query overhead relative to the optimum.

title: A Competitive Algorithm for Agnostic Active Learning

abstract: Modern machine learning paradigms, such as deep learning, occur in or close to the interpolation regime, wherein the number of model parameters is much larger than the number of data samples. In this work, we propose a regularity condition within the interpolation regime which endows the stochastic gradient method with the same worst-case iteration complexity as the deterministic gradient method, while using only a single sampled gradient (or a minibatch) in each iteration. In contrast, all existing guarantees require the stochastic gradient method to take small steps, thereby resulting in a much slower linear rate of convergence. Finally, we demonstrate that our condition holds when training sufficiently wide feedforward neural networks with a linear output layer.

paragraphs: This paper studies why stochastic gradient descent can converge quickly in heavily overparameterized learning problems. Its focus is the interpolation regime, where models have many more parameters than training samples and can fit the training data. The theoretical question is whether using a sampled gradient must impose a worse iteration requirement than using the deterministic gradient.

The authors propose a regularity condition under which the stochastic method has the same worst-case iteration complexity as the deterministic method. Each stochastic iteration still uses only one sampled gradient or a minibatch. This matters because the earlier guarantees described in the abstract require small stochastic steps, leading to a substantially slower linear convergence rate.

The paper also shows that its condition holds when training sufficiently wide feedforward neural networks with a linear output layer. The result therefore identifies a concrete class of networks where the analysis applies. Its claim is conditional on this regularity and the stated setting: it establishes when fast stochastic convergence is possible, rather than asserting that overparameterization alone always guarantees it.
summary.tldr: A regularity condition lets SGD match deterministic gradient descent’s worst-case iteration complexity in certain overparameterized problems.

title: Aiming towards the minimizers: fast convergence of SGD for overparametrized problems

abstract: In this paper, we hypothesize that gradient-based meta-learning (GBML) implicitly suppresses the Hessian along the optimization trajectory in the inner loop. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce an algorithm called SHOT (Suppressing the Hessian along the Optimization Trajectory) that minimizes the distance between the parameters of the target and reference models to suppress the Hessian in the inner loop. Despite dealing with high-order terms, SHOT does not increase the computational complexity of the baseline model much. It is agnostic to both the algorithm and architecture used in GBML, making it highly versatile and applicable to any GBML baseline. To validate the effectiveness of SHOT, we conduct empirical tests on standard few-shot learning tasks and qualitatively analyze its dynamics. We confirm our hypothesis empirically and demonstrate that SHOT outperforms the corresponding baseline.

paragraphs: Gradient-based meta-learning learns through an inner optimization process that adapts model parameters. This paper proposes that such methods implicitly suppress the Hessian along that adaptation trajectory. The Hessian describes how gradients change around the current parameters, so the hypothesis concerns the curvature encountered during learning, rather than only the final parameter values.

SHOT turns this hypothesis into an explicit algorithm by minimizing the distance between the parameters of a target model and a reference model. This objective is intended to suppress the Hessian during the inner loop. Although it addresses higher-order quantities, the authors report that it adds relatively little computational complexity to the underlying method.

The method is described as independent of the particular gradient-based meta-learning algorithm and architecture. Tests on standard few-shot learning tasks show improvements over the corresponding baselines, while qualitative analysis examines the learning dynamics. The authors report empirical confirmation of their hypothesis. The evidence therefore supports the proposed curvature-related explanation experimentally, alongside demonstrating the usefulness of the resulting training modification.
summary.tldr: SHOT explicitly encourages Hessian suppression during meta-learning adaptation and improves the tested few-shot baselines with modest added complexity.

title: SHOT: Suppressing the Hessian along the Optimization Trajectory for Gradient-Based Meta-Learning

abstract: Multi-objective learning (MOL) often arises in emerging machine learning problems when multiple learning criteria or tasks need to be addressed. Recent works have developed various _dynamic weighting_ algorithms for MOL, including MGDA and its variants, whose central idea is to find an update direction that _avoids conflicts_ among objectives. Albeit its appealing intuition, empirical studies show that dynamic weighting methods may not always outperform static alternatives. To bridge this gap between theory and practice, we focus on a new variant of stochastic MGDA - the Multi-objective gradient with Double sampling (MoDo) algorithm and study its generalization performance and the interplay with optimization through the lens of algorithm stability. We find that the rationale behind MGDA -- updating along conflict-avoidant direction - may \emph{impede} dynamic weighting algorithms from achieving the optimal ${\cal O}(1/\sqrt{n})$ population risk, where $n$ is the number of training samples. We further highlight the variability of dynamic weights and their impact on the three-way trade-off among optimization, generalization, and conflict avoidance that is unique in MOL. Code is available at https://github.com/heshandevaka/Trade-Off-MOL.

paragraphs: When a model serves several objectives, an update that helps one can conflict with another. Dynamic weighting methods such as MGDA try to find directions that avoid these conflicts. Despite that appealing rationale, they do not always outperform fixed weighting in experiments. This paper examines why avoiding conflict can have costs elsewhere in learning.

The analysis focuses on MoDo, a stochastic MGDA variant using double sampling. Through algorithm stability, the authors study generalization and its interaction with optimization. They find that choosing conflict-avoidant directions may prevent dynamic weighting methods from attaining an optimal population-risk rate of order one over the square root of the training sample count.

The paper also highlights how variability in the changing objective weights influences this behavior. Its central message is a three-way trade-off among optimizing the training objectives, generalizing beyond the training data, and avoiding conflicts between objectives. The result does not establish that dynamic weighting always fails. It explains why stronger conflict avoidance need not translate into the best learning performance.
summary.tldr: Analysis of MoDo shows how avoiding conflicts between learning objectives can trade off against optimization and generalization.

title: Three-Way Trade-Off in Multi-Objective Learning: Optimization, Generalization and Conflict-Avoidance

abstract: Recent studies have discovered that Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) can dramatically improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when dealing with complex tasks involving mathematics or reasoning. Despite the enormous empirical success, the underlying mechanisms behind CoT and how it unlocks the potential of LLMs remain elusive. In this paper, we take a first step towards theoretically answering these questions. Specifically, we examine the expressivity of LLMs with CoT in solving fundamental mathematical and decision-making problems. By using circuit complexity theory, we first give impossibility results showing that bounded-depth Transformers are unable to directly produce correct answers for basic arithmetic/equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length. In contrast, we then prove by construction that autoregressive Transformers of constant size suffice to solve both tasks by generating CoT derivations using a commonly used math language format. Moreover, we show LLMs with CoT can handle a general class of decision-making problems known as Dynamic Programming, thus justifying their power in tackling complex real-world tasks. Finally, an extensive set of experiments show that, while Transformers always fail to directly predict the answers, they can consistently learn to generate correct solutions step-by-step given sufficient CoT demonstrations.

paragraphs: This paper asks how producing intermediate reasoning steps changes what a Transformer can compute. It studies chain-of-thought through expressivity: whether a model architecture can represent solutions to particular problems. Circuit-complexity arguments establish barriers for bounded-depth Transformers that must directly output answers to basic arithmetic and equation tasks.

For those direct-answer settings, the authors show that model size must grow super-polynomially with input length. They then construct constant-size autoregressive Transformers that solve both tasks by generating intermediate derivations in a commonly used mathematical format. The distinction is that the model can carry out a sequence of reasoning steps as it generates text. The analysis also extends to a general class of dynamic-programming problems.

Experiments complement the constructions: in the tested settings, Transformers fail at direct answer prediction but consistently learn correct step-by-step solutions given sufficient demonstrations. The results connect intermediate generation to increased computational capability. They establish what the studied constructions can express and what the experiments learn, rather than guaranteeing that any prompted language model will reason correctly.
summary.tldr: Theoretical constructions show how generating intermediate steps lets constant-size autoregressive Transformers solve tasks that challenge bounded-depth direct-answer models.

title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) is a popular uncertainty quantification method that provides distribution-free, statistically valid prediction sets, assuming that training and test data are exchangeable. In such a case, CP's prediction sets are guaranteed to cover the (unknown) true test output with a user-specified probability. Nevertheless, this guarantee is violated when the data is subjected to adversarial attacks, which often result in a significant loss of coverage. Recently, several approaches have been put forward to recover CP guarantees in this setting. These approaches leverage variations of randomised smoothing to produce conservative sets which account for the effect of the adversarial perturbations. They are, however, limited in that they only support $\ell_2$-bounded perturbations and classification tasks. This paper introduces VRCP (Verifiably Robust Conformal Prediction), a new framework that leverages recent neural network verification methods to recover coverage guarantees under adversarial attacks. Our VRCP method is the first to support perturbations bounded by arbitrary norms including $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_\infty$, as well as regression tasks. We evaluate and compare our approach on image classification tasks (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet) and regression tasks for deep reinforcement learning environments. In every case, VRCP achieves above nominal coverage and yields significantly more efficient and informative prediction regions than the SotA.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets intended to contain the true output with a user-chosen probability. Its standard coverage guarantee relies on exchangeability of training and test data. Adversarial perturbations can undermine that guarantee, motivating methods that account explicitly for how attacks affect predictions.

VRCP uses neural network verification methods to recover coverage guarantees under adversarial attacks. Earlier approaches described in the paper rely on randomized smoothing and support classification with L2-bounded perturbations. VRCP extends support to regression and perturbations bounded by arbitrary norms, including L1, L2, and L-infinity. This broadens both the kinds of output that can receive protection and the ways an allowed attack can be bounded.

The authors evaluate image classification on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet, together with regression tasks from deep reinforcement learning environments. In every evaluated case, coverage exceeds the nominal target, and the prediction regions are more efficient and informative than those of the state-of-the-art methods compared. The empirical results complement the framework’s guarantees by showing useful prediction regions in the tested attack settings.
summary.tldr: VRCP uses neural network verification to provide adversarially robust conformal prediction for classification and regression under arbitrary norm-bounded perturbations.

title: Verifiably Robust Conformal Prediction

abstract: We introduce VideoLISA, a video-based multimodal large language model designed to tackle the problem of language-instructed reasoning segmentation in videos. Leveraging the reasoning capabilities and world knowledge of large language models, and augmented by the Segment Anything Model, VideoLISA generates temporally consistent segmentation masks in videos based on language instructions. Existing image-based methods, such as LISA, struggle with video tasks due to the additional temporal dimension, which requires temporal dynamic understanding and consistent segmentation across frames. VideoLISA addresses these challenges by integrating a Sparse Dense Sampling strategy into the video-LLM, which balances temporal context and spatial detail within computational constraints. Additionally, we propose a One-Token-Seg-All approach using a specially designed <TRK> token, enabling the model to segment and track objects across multiple frames. Extensive evaluations on diverse benchmarks, including our newly introduced ReasonVOS benchmark, demonstrate VideoLISA's superior performance in video object segmentation tasks involving complex reasoning, temporal understanding, and object tracking. While optimized for videos, VideoLISA also shows promising generalization to image segmentation, revealing its potential as a unified foundation model for language-instructed object segmentation. Code and model will be available at: https://github.com/showlab/VideoLISA.

paragraphs: VideoLISA addresses language-instructed video segmentation: identifying the requested object and marking its pixels consistently across frames. Instructions may require reasoning and understanding events over time. Methods designed for individual images face an additional challenge here because they must preserve object identity and segmentation consistency as the video changes.

The model combines a video-capable multimodal language model with the Segment Anything Model. A Sparse Dense Sampling strategy balances information about temporal context with spatial detail under computational constraints. A dedicated tracking token, <TRK>, supports the One-Token-Seg-All approach, enabling segmentation and tracking across multiple frames through a shared token mechanism.

Evaluations across several benchmarks, including the newly introduced ReasonVOS benchmark, report superior performance on tasks involving complex reasoning, temporal understanding, and tracking. VideoLISA also shows promising transfer to image segmentation despite being optimized for video. These findings support combining language-model reasoning with explicit mechanisms for temporal processing and segmentation, and suggest potential for a unified model spanning both image and video instructions.
summary.tldr: VideoLISA combines language reasoning, video sampling, and a tracking token to segment instructed objects consistently across frames.

title: One Token to Seg Them All: Language Instructed Reasoning Segmentation in Videos

abstract: In this paper, we study Adam in non-convex smooth scenarios with potential unbounded gradients and affine variance noise. We consider a general noise model which governs affine variance noise, bounded noise, and sub-Gaussian noise. We show that Adam with a specific hyper-parameter setup can find a stationary point with a $\mathcal{O}(\text{poly}(\log T)/\sqrt{T})$ rate in high probability under this general noise model where $T$ denotes total number iterations, matching the lower rate of stochastic first-order algorithms up to logarithm factors. We also provide a probabilistic convergence result for Adam under a generalized smooth condition which allows unbounded smoothness parameters and has been illustrated empirically to capture the smooth property of many practical objective functions more accurately.

title: On Convergence of Adam for Stochastic Optimization under Relaxed Assumptions

abstract: Probabilistic integral circuits (PICs) have been recently introduced as probabilistic models enjoying the key ingredient behind expressive generative models: continuous latent variables (LVs). PICs are symbolic computational graphs defining continuous LV models as hierarchies of functions that are summed and multiplied together, or integrated over some LVs. They are tractable if LVs can be analytically integrated out, otherwise they can be approximated by tractable probabilistic circuits (PC) encoding a hierarchical numerical quadrature process, called QPCs.So far, only tree-shaped PICs have been explored, and training them via numerical quadrature requires memory-intensive processing at scale. In this paper, we address these issues, and present: (i) a pipeline for building DAG-shaped PICs out of arbitrary variable decompositions, (ii) a procedure for training PICs using tensorized circuit architectures, and (iii) neural functional sharing techniques to allow scalable training. In extensive experiments, we showcase the effectiveness of functional sharing and the superiority of QPCs over traditional PCs.

paragraphs: Probabilistic integral circuits represent models with continuous latent variables through graphs of sums, products, and integration operations. When the latent variables can be integrated out analytically, the models are tractable. Otherwise, numerical quadrature can approximate them through tractable probabilistic circuits called QPCs, turning continuous integration into a structured computational approximation.

Earlier work explored only tree-shaped integral circuits, and quadrature-based training could require substantial memory at scale. This paper expands the architecture to directed acyclic graphs built from arbitrary variable decompositions. It also introduces a training procedure based on tensorized circuit architectures and neural functional sharing techniques intended to make training scale more effectively.

The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of functional sharing and report that QPCs outperform traditional probabilistic circuits. These findings support combining continuous latent-variable modeling with tractable circuit approximations. The contribution addresses both structural flexibility and training cost, allowing the explored circuit family to extend beyond trees while making the associated numerical integration approach more practical to train.
summary.tldr: Graph-shaped integral circuits, tensorized training, and functional sharing make continuous latent-variable circuit models more scalable.

title: Scaling Continuous Latent Variable Models as Probabilistic Integral Circuits

abstract: The advent of Federated Learning (FL) highlights the practical necessity for the ’right to be forgotten’ for all clients, allowing them to request data deletion from the machine learning model’s service provider. This necessity has spurred a growing demand for Federated Unlearning (FU). Feature unlearning has gained considerable attention due to its applications in unlearning sensitive, backdoor, and biased features. Existing methods employ the influence function to achieve feature unlearning, which is impractical for FL as it necessitates the participation of other clients, if not all, in the unlearning process. Furthermore, current research lacks an evaluation of the effectiveness of feature unlearning. To address these limitations, we define feature sensitivity in evaluating feature unlearning according to Lipschitz continuity. This metric characterizes the model output’s rate of change or sensitivity to perturbations in the input feature. We then propose an effective federated feature unlearning framework called Ferrari, which minimizes feature sensitivity. Extensive experimental results and theoretical analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of Ferrari across various feature unlearning scenarios, including sensitive, backdoor, and biased features. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/OngWinKent/Federated-Feature-Unlearning

paragraphs: Feature unlearning aims to remove a model's reliance on particular input features, including sensitive attributes, backdoor signals, or biased cues. In federated learning, this is complicated by methods that require other clients to participate in the removal process. The paper identifies that participation requirement as a practical obstacle for existing influence-function approaches.

Ferrari introduces feature sensitivity as a way to evaluate and pursue unlearning. Defined through Lipschitz continuity, the measure describes how quickly model outputs change when the targeted input feature is perturbed. The framework then minimizes this sensitivity, making reduced responsiveness to the feature the central optimization objective.

This connects the desired behavior after unlearning to a measurable property of the model: changes in the targeted feature should have less influence on its outputs. The authors support Ferrari with theoretical analysis and extensive experiments covering sensitive, backdoor, and biased features. Their findings indicate that sensitivity optimization can provide an effective framework for feature unlearning in federated settings.
summary.tldr: Ferrari pursues federated feature unlearning by measuring and minimizing how strongly model outputs respond to targeted features.

title: Ferrari: Federated Feature Unlearning via Optimizing Feature Sensitivity

abstract: Scalarization is a general, parallizable technique that can be deployed in any multiobjective setting to reduce multiple objectives into one, yet some have dismissed this versatile approach because linear scalarizations cannot explore concave regions of the Pareto frontier. To that end, we aim to find simple non-linear scalarizations that provably explore a diverse set of $k$ objectives on the Pareto frontier, as measured by the dominated hypervolume. We show that hypervolume scalarizations with uniformly random weights achieves an optimal sublinear hypervolume regret bound of $O(T^{-1/k})$, with matching lower bounds that preclude any algorithm from doing better asymptotically. For the setting of multiobjective stochastic linear bandits, we utilize properties of hypervolume scalarizations to derive a novel non-Euclidean analysis to get regret bounds of $\tilde{O}( d T^{-1/2} + T^{-1/k})$, removing unnecessary $\text{poly}(k)$ dependencies. We support our theory with strong empirical performance of using non-linear scalarizations that outperforms both their linear counterparts and other standard multiobjective algorithms in a variety of natural settings.

paragraphs: Multiobjective optimization seeks useful trade-offs among several goals. Scalarization combines those goals into one objective, but linear combinations cannot explore concave portions of the Pareto frontier. This paper studies simple nonlinear scalarizations designed to cover diverse trade-offs, measuring their quality through dominated hypervolume, which captures how much objective-space volume the obtained solutions dominate.

The authors prove that hypervolume scalarizations with uniformly random weights achieve a regret bound of O(T^(-1/k)) for k objectives. Matching lower bounds establish that no algorithm can improve the asymptotic rate under the analyzed setting. This gives the proposed scalarization strategy a guarantee about the quality of its coverage, beyond its convenience as a way to combine objectives.

Experiments also show strong performance against linear scalarizations and standard multiobjective algorithms across several settings. Together, the theory and empirical results support nonlinear scalarization as an effective approach to exploring objective trade-offs.
summary.tldr: Randomly weighted nonlinear hypervolume scalarizations achieve an asymptotically optimal regret rate for exploring multiple objectives.

title: Optimal Scalarizations for Sublinear Hypervolume Regret

abstract: Online free-viewpoint video (FVV) streaming is a challenging problem, which is relatively under-explored. It requires incremental on-the-fly updates to a volumetric representation, fast training and rendering to satisfy realtime constraints and a small memory footprint for efficient transmission. If acheived, it can enhance user experience by enabling novel applications, e.g., 3D video conferencing and live volumetric video broadcast, among others. In this work, we propose a novel framework for QUantized and Efficient ENcoding (QUEEN) for streaming FVV using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS). QUEEN directly learns Gaussian attribute residuals between consecutive frames at each time-step without imposing any structural constraints on them, allowing for high quality reconstruction and generalizability. To efficiently store the residuals, we further propose a quantization-sparsity framework, which contains a learned latent-decoder for effectively quantizing attribute residuals other than Gaussian positions and a learned gating module to sparsify position residuals. We propose to use the Gaussian viewspace gradient difference vector as a signal to separate the static and dynamic content of the scene. It acts as a guide for effective sparsity learning and speeds up training. On diverse FVV benchmarks, QUEEN outperforms the state-of-the-art online FVV methods on all metrics. Notably, for several highly dynamic scenes, it reduces the model size to just 0.7 MB per frame while training in under 5 sec and rendering at ~350 FPS.

paragraphs: QUEEN targets online video that viewers can inspect from different viewpoints. Streaming this kind of content requires a 3D representation that updates as frames arrive, renders quickly, and remains compact enough to transmit. The method uses 3D Gaussian Splatting and learns changes in Gaussian attributes between consecutive frames without imposing structural constraints on those changes.

Its compression strategy treats different attributes differently. A learned latent decoder quantizes changes to attributes other than position, while a learned gating module makes position changes sparse. These results show how learning and compressing frame-to-frame changes can jointly improve reconstruction, storage, and processing efficiency in the evaluated streaming setting.
summary.tldr: QUEEN compresses frame-to-frame Gaussian changes to deliver compact, fast, high-quality free-viewpoint video representations.

title: QUEEN: QUantized Efficient ENcoding of Dynamic Gaussians for Streaming Free-viewpoint Videos

abstract: The high-dimensional single index model (SIM), which assumes that the response is independent of the predictors given a linear combination of predictors, has drawn attention due to its flexibility and interpretability, but its efficiency is adversely affected by outlying observations and heavy-tailed distributions. This paper introduces a robust procedure by recasting the SIM into a pseudo-linear model with transformed responses. It relaxes the distributional conditions on random errors from sub-Gaussian to more general distributions and thus it is robust with substantial efficiency gain for heavy-tailed random errors. Under this paradigm, we provide asymptotically honest group inference procedures based on the idea of orthogonalization, which enjoys the feature that it does not require the zero and nonzero coefficients to be well-separated. Asymptotic null distribution and bootstrap implementation are both established. Moreover, we develop a multiple testing procedure for determining if the individual coefficients are relevant simultaneously, and show that it is able to control the false discovery rate asymptotically. Numerical results indicate that the new procedures can be highly competitive among existing methods, especially for heavy-tailed errors.

paragraphs: A single-index model assumes that a linear combination of predictors contains the information needed to relate them to the response. This offers flexibility and interpretability, but outliers and heavy-tailed errors can undermine estimation efficiency. The paper develops a robust inference procedure for this model when the number of predictors is high.

The method transforms the responses and recasts the problem as a pseudo-linear model. This permits more general error distributions than the sub-Gaussian conditions used in less robust formulations. Within this framework, orthogonalization supports inference about groups of coefficients without requiring zero and nonzero coefficients to be clearly separated.

The authors establish asymptotically honest group inference, derive the null distribution, and provide a bootstrap implementation. They also introduce simultaneous testing of individual coefficients with asymptotic false discovery rate control. These guarantees concern large-sample behavior. Numerical results indicate that the procedures can compete strongly with existing methods, especially under heavy-tailed errors, connecting the relaxed error assumptions to useful gains in robust statistical inference.
summary.tldr: A transformed-response approach enables robust group inference and simultaneous coefficient testing for high-dimensional single-index models with more general errors.

title: Robust group and simultaneous inferences for high-dimensional single index model

abstract: Conformal prediction converts nearly any point estimator into a prediction interval under standard assumptions while ensuring valid coverage. However, the extensive computational demands of full conformal prediction are daunting in practice, as it necessitates a comprehensive number of trainings across the entire latent label space. Unfortunately, existing efforts to expedite conformalization often carry strong assumptions and are developed specifically for certain models, or they only offer approximate solution sets. To address this gap, we develop a method for fast exact conformalization of generalized statistical estimation. Our analysis reveals that the structure of the solution path is inherently piecewise smooth, and indicates that utilizing second-order information of difference equations suffices to approximate the entire solution spectrum arbitrarily. We provide a unified view that not only encompasses existing work but also attempts to offer geometric insights. Practically, our framework integrates seamlessly with well-studied numerical solvers. The significant speedups of our algorithm as compared to the existing standard methods are demonstrated across numerous benchmarks.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction turns point predictions into intervals with valid coverage under standard assumptions. Full conformal prediction can be expensive because it considers candidate labels across the possible output space and repeatedly trains the estimator. Existing acceleration methods often impose strong assumptions, apply only to particular models, or provide approximate prediction sets.

This paper develops a framework for fast exact conformalization across generalized statistical estimation problems. Its analysis follows how the fitted solution changes as the candidate label varies. The authors establish that this solution path is piecewise smooth and show that second-order information from difference equations is sufficient to approximate the full range of solutions to arbitrary accuracy.

That structure provides a way to organize the computation around a connected solution path. The framework offers a unified interpretation of earlier work, adds geometric insight, and integrates with established numerical solvers. Experiments across numerous benchmarks demonstrate substantial speedups over standard methods. The intended benefit is to make full conformal procedures more practical while retaining the exact-conformalization objective.
summary.tldr: Piecewise-smooth solution paths enable a general framework for accelerating exact conformalization, with substantial benchmark speedups.

title: Generalized Fast Exact Conformalization

abstract: We provide new lower bounds on the privacy guarantee of _multi-epoch_ Adaptive Batch Linear Queries (ABLQ) mechanism with _shuffled batch sampling_, demonstrating substantial gaps when compared to _Poisson subsampling_; prior analysis was limited to a single epoch.Since the privacy analysis of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) is obtained by analyzing the ABLQ mechanism, this brings into serious question the common practice of implementing Shuffling based DP-SGD, but reporting privacy parameters as if Poisson subsampling was used.To understand the impact of this gap on the utility of trained machine learning models, we introduce a novel practical approach to implement Poisson subsampling _at scale_ using massively parallel computation, and efficiently train models with the same.We provide a comparison between the utility of models trained with Poisson subsampling based DP-SGD, and the optimistic estimates of utility when using shuffling, via our new lower bounds on the privacy guarantee of ABLQ with shuffling.

paragraphs: The privacy accounting for differentially private stochastic gradient descent depends on how training batches are sampled. This paper examines the common practice of implementing batches through shuffling while reporting privacy parameters calculated for Poisson subsampling. Its analysis shows substantial gaps between these sampling schemes in the mechanism used to analyze DP-SGD privacy.

The theoretical contribution gives new lower bounds for multi-epoch Adaptive Batch Linear Queries with shuffled batch sampling. Earlier analysis covered only one epoch. Extending the analysis to repeated passes makes the mismatch relevant to multi-epoch training and raises serious questions about applying Poisson-based accounting to a shuffled implementation.

The authors also introduce a practical way to perform Poisson subsampling at scale using massively parallel computation and use it to train models efficiently. They compare those models' utility with optimistic utility estimates for shuffling, informed by the new lower bounds. This connects the privacy-accounting issue to model usefulness while providing a scalable implementation of the sampling scheme assumed by Poisson-based analysis.
summary.tldr: Multi-epoch privacy bounds challenge using Poisson accounting for shuffled DP-SGD, while a parallel implementation makes Poisson sampling scalable.

title: Scalable DP-SGD: Shuffling vs. Poisson Subsampling

abstract: Time series data are ubiquitous across a wide range of real-world domains. Whilereal-world time series analysis (TSA) requires human experts to integrate numerical series data with multimodal domain-specific knowledge, most existing TSAmodels rely solely on numerical data, overlooking the significance of information beyond numerical series. This oversight is due to the untapped potentialof textual series data and the absence of a comprehensive, high-quality multimodal dataset. To overcome this obstacle, we introduce Time-MMD, the firstmulti-domain, multimodal time series dataset covering 9 primary data domains.Time-MMD ensures fine-grained modality alignment, eliminates data contamination, and provides high usability. Additionally, we develop MM-TSFlib, thefirst-cut multimodal time-series forecasting (TSF) library, seamlessly pipeliningmultimodal TSF evaluations based on Time-MMD for in-depth analyses. Extensiveexperiments conducted on Time-MMD through MM-TSFlib demonstrate significant performance enhancements by extending unimodal TSF to multimodality,evidenced by over 15% mean squared error reduction in general, and up to 40%in domains with rich textual data. More importantly, our datasets and libraryrevolutionize broader applications, impacts, research topics to advance TSA. Thedataset is available at https://github.com/AdityaLab/Time-MMD.

paragraphs: Time-series analysis often involves interpreting numerical changes alongside domain-specific information. Human experts use that broader context, but many forecasting models operate on numerical sequences alone. Time-MMD addresses this gap by providing a dataset that connects time-series numbers with textual information across nine primary domains.

The dataset emphasizes fine-grained alignment between modalities, contamination prevention, and usability. The authors also introduce MM-TSFlib, a library that organizes multimodal forecasting evaluations using Time-MMD. Together, the dataset and library make it possible to study the contribution of text through a shared evaluation pipeline rather than treating every domain as an entirely separate integration problem.

The reported experiments show mean squared error reductions of more than 15% in general when extending numerical-only forecasting to multiple modalities. Reductions reach up to 40% in domains with abundant textual data. These findings indicate that aligned text can provide useful forecasting information in the tested settings, with especially strong gains where textual context is rich.
summary.tldr: Time-MMD and MM-TSFlib support multimodal forecasting across nine domains, with experiments showing substantial error reductions from adding textual information.

title: Time-MMD: Multi-Domain Multimodal Dataset for Time Series Analysis

abstract: Neural networks excel at discovering statistical patterns inhigh-dimensional data sets. In practice, higher-order cumulants, which quantifythe non-Gaussian correlations between three or more variables, are particularlyimportant for the performance of neural networks. But how efficient are neuralnetworks at extracting features from higher-order cumulants? We study thisquestion in the spiked cumulant model, where the statistician needs to recover aprivileged direction or "spike'' from the order-$p\ge 4$ cumulantsof $d$-dimensional inputs. We first discuss the fundamental statistical andcomputational limits of recovering the spike by analysing the number of samples $n$ required to strongly distinguish between inputs from the spikedcumulant model and isotropic Gaussian inputs. Existing literature established the presence of a wide statistical-to-computational gap in this problem. We deepen this line of work by finding an exact formula for the likelihood ratio norm which proves that statisticaldistinguishability requires $n\gtrsim d$ samples, while distinguishing the twodistributions in polynomial time requires $n \gtrsim d^2$ samples for a wideclass of algorithms, i.e. those covered by the low-degree conjecture. Numerical experiments show that neural networks do indeed learn to distinguishthe two distributions with quadratic sample complexity, while ``lazy'' methodslike random features are not better than random guessing in this regime. Ourresults show that neural networks extract information from higher-ordercorrelations in the spiked cumulant model efficiently, and reveal a large gap inthe amount of data required by neural networks and random features to learn fromhigher-order cumulants.

paragraphs: Some statistical signals appear in relationships among several variables rather than simple pairwise correlations. This paper studies such information through a spiked cumulant model, where a hidden direction is encoded in cumulants of order four or higher. The authors investigate the data requirements for distinguishing these inputs from isotropic Gaussian data.

An exact likelihood-ratio norm formula sharpens the distinction between statistical possibility and efficient computation. Statistical distinguishability requires at least order d samples, where d is input dimension. For the broad algorithmic class covered by the low-degree conjecture, polynomial-time distinguishability requires at least order d² samples. The computational conclusion is tied to that conjectural framework and algorithmic scope.

Numerical experiments show neural networks learning to distinguish the distributions with quadratic sample complexity. Random-feature methods, representing a lazy-learning approach, perform no better than chance in that regime. Within this model, the results indicate that neural networks can efficiently extract higher-order information and reveal a substantial difference in the data needed by neural networks and random features.
summary.tldr: In a spiked cumulant model, neural networks empirically learn higher-order signals with quadratic sample complexity where random features fail.

title: Learning from higher-order correlations, efficiently: hypothesis tests, random features, and neural networks

abstract: Parameter-efficient transfer learning (PETL) methods show promise in adapting a pre-trained model to various downstream tasks while training only a few parameters. In the computer vision (CV) domain, numerous PETL algorithms have been proposed, but their direct employment or comparison remains inconvenient. To address this challenge, we construct a Unified Visual PETL Benchmark (V-PETL Bench) for the CV domain by selecting 30 diverse, challenging, and comprehensive datasets from image recognition, video action recognition, and dense prediction tasks. On these datasets, we systematically evaluate 25 dominant PETL algorithms and open-source a modular and extensible codebase for fair evaluation of these algorithms. V-PETL Bench runs on NVIDIA A800 GPUs and requires approximately 310 GPU days. We release all the benchmark, making it more efficient and friendly to researchers. Additionally, V-PETL Bench will be continuously updated for new PETL algorithms and CV tasks.

To address this challenge, we construct a Unified Visual PETL Benchmark (V-PETL Bench) for the CV domain by selecting 30 diverse, challenging, and comprehensive datasets from image recognition, video action recognition, and dense prediction tasks. V-PETL Bench runs on NVIDIA A800 GPUs and requires approximately 310 GPU days. We release all the benchmark, making it more efficient and friendly to researchers. Additionally, V-PETL Bench will be continuously updated for new PETL algorithms and CV tasks.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient transfer learning adapts a pretrained model while training only a small portion of its parameters. Many such methods exist for computer vision, but using them and comparing their results consistently can be inconvenient. V-PETL Bench provides a common evaluation framework to make these comparisons more accessible and systematic.

The benchmark includes 30 datasets covering image recognition, video action recognition, and dense prediction. The authors evaluate 25 major algorithms within a modular, extensible codebase intended to support fair comparison. This breadth makes the resource relevant to several kinds of visual adaptation, rather than restricting evaluation to a single task category.

The reported benchmark effort uses NVIDIA A800 GPUs and approximately 310 GPU days. Releasing the benchmark and code makes that substantial evaluation effort available as a shared research resource. The authors also state an intention to add new algorithms and tasks over time. The contribution is the unified infrastructure and systematic evaluation; the abstract does not identify one method as the overall winner.
summary.tldr: V-PETL Bench provides shared code and systematic evaluation of 25 parameter-efficient visual adaptation methods across 30 datasets.

title: V-PETL Bench: A Unified Visual Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning Benchmark

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate content that contains factual errors when responding to fact-seeking prompts on open-ended topics. To benchmark a model’s long-form factuality in open domains, we first use GPT-4 to generate LongFact, a prompt set comprising thousands of questions spanning 38 topics. We then propose that LLM agents can be used as automated evaluators for long-form factuality through a method which we call Search-Augmented Factuality Evaluator (SAFE). SAFE utilizes an LLM to break down a long-form response into a set of individual facts and to evaluate the accuracy of each fact using a multi-step reasoning process comprising sending search queries to Google Search and determining whether a fact is supported by the search results. Furthermore, we propose extending F1 score as an aggregated metric for long-form factuality. To do so, we balance the percentage of supported facts in a response (precision) with the percentage of provided facts relative to a hyperparameter representing a user’s preferred response length (recall).Empirically, we demonstrate that LLM agents can outperform crowdsourced human annotators—on a set of∼16k individual facts, SAFE agrees with crowdsourced human annotators 72% of the time, and on a random subset of 100 disagreement cases, SAFE wins 76% of the time. At the same time, SAFE is more than 20 times cheaper than human annotators. We also benchmark thirteen language models on LongFact across four model families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, and PaLM-2), finding that larger language models generally achieve better long-form factuality. LongFact, SAFE, and all experimental code are available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/long-form-factuality.
