Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness and versatility of our approach across diverse contextual bandit settings.

paragraphs: The paper examines online decision-making in contextual bandits, where decisions depend on the available context and learning proceeds as feedback arrives. The authors focus on a difficulty with approaches that lack informative prior knowledge: they can be inefficient in the computation or statistical evidence needed to make useful decisions.

Their approach uses pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors. The purpose is to represent complex dependencies among actions, giving the decision process a richer starting point. The paper pairs this choice with a practical algorithm for approximating the posterior under a diffusion-model prior. That posterior incorporates incoming evidence, so efficient approximation is central to making the prior useful during ongoing decision-making.

The algorithm supports both fast updates and sampling, connecting the expressive prior to operations needed in an online setting. Empirical results across diverse contextual bandit settings support the approach's effectiveness and versatility. The contribution is the combination of a flexible pretrained model with a practical inference procedure: representing action dependencies and updating beliefs efficiently are treated as linked parts of the same decision-making method.
summary.tldr: Pretrained diffusion models provide expressive priors for contextual bandits, paired with approximate posterior inference that supports fast updates and sampling.

title: Diffusion Models Meet Contextual Bandits

abstract: Plasticity and stability denote the ability to assimilate new tasks while preserving previously acquired knowledge, representing two important concepts in continual learning. Recent research addresses stability by leveraging pre-trained models to provide informative representations, yet the efficacy of these methods is highly reliant on the choice of the pre-trained backbone, which may not yield optimal plasticity. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a streamlined and potent framework that orchestrates multiple different pre-trained backbones to derive semantically rich multi-source representations. We propose an innovative Multi-Scale Interaction and Dynamic Fusion (MSIDF) technique to process and selectively capture the most relevant parts of multi-source features through a series of learnable attention modules, thereby helping to learn better decision boundaries to boost performance. Furthermore, we introduce a novel Multi-Level Representation Optimization (MLRO) strategy to adaptively refine the representation networks, offering adaptive representations that enhance plasticity. To mitigate over-regularization issues, we propose a novel Adaptive Regularization Optimization (ARO) method to manage and optimize a switch vector that selectively governs the updating process of each representation layer, which promotes the new task learning. The proposed MLRO and ARO approaches are collectively optimized within a unified optimization framework to achieve an optimal trade-off between plasticity and stability. Our extensive experimental evaluations reveal that the proposed framework attains state-of-the-art performance. The source code of our algorithm is available at https://github.com/CL-Coder236/LMSRR.

paragraphs: Continual learning must balance acquiring new tasks with retaining earlier knowledge. Pretrained models can help preserve useful representations, but the choice of a single backbone can restrict adaptation. This paper builds a framework that combines several different pretrained backbones to obtain richer representations from multiple sources.

Its Multi-Scale Interaction and Dynamic Fusion component uses learnable attention modules to select relevant information from the different feature sources. A Multi-Level Representation Optimization strategy then adapts the representation networks to improve their capacity to learn new tasks. Together, these components address both which features to use and how those features should change.

The framework also introduces Adaptive Regularization Optimization, which controls a switch vector governing updates to individual representation layers. This is designed to reduce excessive regularization that would otherwise hinder new learning. Joint optimization coordinates adaptation and preservation, and the reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance. The approach treats continual learning as a problem of selecting, refining, and selectively updating representations across multiple pretrained sources.
summary.tldr: Combining multiple pretrained backbones with selective feature fusion and layer adaptation improves the reported balance between learning new tasks and preserving knowledge.

title: Learning Multi-Source and Robust Representations for Continual Learning

abstract: In this paper we extend temporal difference policy evaluation algorithms to performance criteria that include the variance of the cumulative reward. Such criteria are useful for risk management, and are important in domains such as finance and process control. We propose variants of both TD(0) and LSTD(λ) with linear function approximation, prove their convergence, and demonstrate their utility in a 4-dimensional continuous state space problem.
originalAbstract: In this paper we extend temporal difference policy evaluation algorithms to performance criteria that include the variance of the cumulative reward. Such criteria are useful for risk management, and are important in domains such as finance and process control. We propose variants of both TD(0) and LSTD(λ) with linear function approximation, prove their convergence, and demonstrate their utility in a 4-dimensional continuous state space problem.

paragraphs: Evaluating a policy can involve more than its expected cumulative reward. The variance of that reward describes how much the outcome fluctuates, making it relevant to performance criteria that account for risk. This paper extends temporal difference policy evaluation to include that variability, with finance and process control identified as motivating domains.

The authors propose variants of TD(0) and LSTD(λ) using linear function approximation. This places variance-related evaluation within two temporal difference approaches while representing the quantities being learned through linear approximations. The work concerns assessing a policy through reward criteria that incorporate variance, giving the evaluation a way to describe uncertainty in cumulative outcomes.

The paper proves convergence of the proposed algorithms and demonstrates their utility on a problem with a four-dimensional continuous state space. The theoretical and experimental contributions serve different purposes: convergence supports the learning procedures, while the example shows them operating in a continuous setting. Together, they extend temporal difference evaluation toward risk-sensitive performance assessment.
summary.tldr: Convergent extensions of TD(0) and LSTD(λ) evaluate reward criteria that include cumulative-reward variance using linear function approximation.

title: Temporal Difference Methods for the Variance of the Reward To Go

abstract: Representing examples in a way that is compatible with the underlying classifier can greatly enhance the performance of a learning system. In this paper we investigate scalable techniques for inducing discriminative features by taking advantage of simple second order structure in the data. We focus on multiclass classification and show that features extracted from the generalized eigenvectors of the class conditional second moments lead to classifiers with excellent empirical performance. Moreover, these features have attractive theoretical properties, such as inducing representations that are invariant to linear transformations of the input. We evaluate classifiers built from these features on three different tasks, obtaining state of the art results.

Moreover, these features have attractive theoretical properties, such as inducing representations that are invariant to linear transformations of the input. paragraphs: A classifier's performance depends partly on how its examples are represented. This paper investigates scalable ways to construct features that help distinguish multiple classes, using simple second-order structure in the data. Such structure summarizes relationships between pairs of input components rather than treating each component entirely separately.

The proposed features come from generalized eigenvectors of class-conditional second moments. In plain terms, the method uses second-order summaries computed within classes to identify directions for a new representation. The approach therefore connects feature construction directly to class-specific data structure and to the needs of the downstream classification problem.

The authors establish theoretical properties of these representations, including invariance to linear transformations of the input. They also evaluate classifiers using the extracted features on three tasks and report state-of-the-art results. Together, these findings show that relatively simple statistical structure can support effective discriminative representations. The empirical success concerns the evaluated tasks, while the invariance property offers a separate mathematical reason to study the representation.
summary.tldr: Generalized eigenvectors of class-specific second moments yield discriminative features with theoretical invariance properties and strong reported classification results.

title: Discriminative Features via Generalized Eigenvectors

abstract: We propose a probabilistic matrix factorization model for collaborative filtering that learns from data that is missing not at random(MNAR). Matrix factorization models exhibit state-of-the-art predictive performance in collaborative filtering. However, these models usually assume that the data is missing at random (MAR), and this is rarely the case. For example, the data is not MAR if users rate items they like more than ones they dislike. When the MAR assumption is incorrect, inferences are biased and predictive performance can suffer. Therefore, we model both the generative process for the data and the missing data mechanism. By learning these two models jointly we obtain improved performance over state-of-the-art methods when predicting the ratings and when modeling the data observation process. We present the first viable MF model for MNAR data. Our results are promising and we expect that further research on NMAR models will yield large gains in collaborative filtering.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering learns preferences from observed user ratings, but the ratings that appear may be a selective sample. Users might rate items they like more often than items they dislike. In that situation, treating missing ratings as missing at random can bias inference and harm predictions.

This paper proposes a probabilistic matrix factorization model that learns two processes together: how ratings are generated and how they become observed. The missingness mechanism is therefore part of the model, allowing the learning procedure to account for a relationship between preferences and rating availability. The authors present this as a viable matrix factorization approach for data missing not at random.

Joint learning improves both rating prediction and modeling of the observation process relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. These findings support treating selective observation as part of the recommendation problem itself. The authors regard the results as promising and anticipate further gains from future work on such models; those anticipated gains are an expectation rather than an established experimental result.
summary.tldr: Jointly modeling ratings and their selective observation improves collaborative filtering when data is missing not at random.

title: Probabilistic Matrix Factorization with Non-random Missing Data

abstract: We consider the problem of automatic macro-action discovery in imitation learning, which we cast as one of change-point detection. Unlike prior work in change-point detection, the present work leverages discriminative learning algorithms. Our main contribution is a novel supervised learning algorithm which extends the classical Boosting framework by combining it with dynamic programming. The resulting process alternatively improves the performance of individual strong predictors and the estimated change-points in the training sequence. Empirical evaluation is presented for the proposed method on tasks where change-points arise naturally as part of a classification problem. Finally we show the applicability of the algorithm to macro-action discovery in imitation learning and demonstrate it allows us to solve complex image-based goal-planning problems with thousands of features.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can benefit from identifying larger action units within demonstrated behavior. This paper treats the discovery of these macro-actions as a change-point detection problem: finding positions in a training sequence where one meaningful segment ends and another begins. The central challenge is learning those boundaries together with useful predictors.

The proposed supervised algorithm combines boosting with dynamic programming. It alternates between improving individual strong predictors and refining the estimated change-points. This links segmentation to discriminative learning, so the predictors and the division of the sequence are improved through the same overall process. The approach extends the classical boosting framework to accommodate uncertain boundaries.

The authors evaluate the method on classification tasks with naturally occurring change-points and then apply it to macro-action discovery in imitation learning. They demonstrate its use in complex image-based goal-planning problems involving thousands of features. These results show that the combined learning and segmentation procedure can support planning from rich visual inputs in the examined tasks.
summary.tldr: Combining boosting with dynamic programming jointly improves predictors and sequence boundaries for discovering macro-actions in imitation learning.

title: Dynamic Programming Boosting for Discriminative Macro-Action Discovery

abstract: In various applications involving hidden Markov models (HMMs), some of the hidden states are aliased, having identical output distributions. The minimality, identifiability and learnability of such aliased HMMs have been long standing problems, with only partial solutions provided thus far. In this paper we focus on parametric-output HMMs, whose output distributions come from a parametric family, and that have exactly two aliased states. For this class, we present a complete characterization of their minimality and identifiability. Furthermore, for a large family of parametric output distributions, we derive computationally efficient and statistically consistent algorithms to detect the presence of aliasing and learn the aliased HMM transition and emission parameters. We illustrate our theoretical analysis by several simulations.

For this class, we present a complete characterization of their minimality and identifiability. paragraphs: In a hidden Markov model, distinct hidden states can produce exactly the same output distribution. These aliased states complicate the question of what can be learned from observations. This paper focuses on models with exactly two aliased states and output distributions drawn from a parametric family, giving the analysis a precise scope.

For that class, the authors completely characterize minimality and identifiability. Minimality concerns whether a model needs its full hidden-state structure, while identifiability concerns whether observations distinguish its underlying parameters. These questions matter before designing a learning algorithm: they establish when the hidden description is essential and when recovering it is possible.

For a large family of parametric output distributions, the paper also provides efficient algorithms to detect aliasing and learn transition and emission parameters. The algorithms are statistically consistent, meaning their estimates approach the target parameters as data increase under the applicable conditions. Simulations illustrate the theory. The contribution combines structural characterization with constructive learning methods for a specific, difficult form of hidden-state ambiguity.
summary.tldr: For parametric-output HMMs with exactly two aliased states, the paper characterizes identifiability and develops efficient, consistent learning algorithms.

title: Learning Parametric-Output HMMs with Two Aliased States

abstract: We discuss a multiple-play multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem in which several arms are selected at each round. Recently, Thompson sampling (TS), a randomized algorithm with a Bayesian spirit, has attracted much attention for its empirically excellent performance, and it is revealed to have an optimal regret bound in the standard single-play MAB problem. In this paper, we propose the multiple-play Thompson sampling (MP-TS) algorithm, an extension of TS to the multiple-play MAB problem, and discuss its regret analysis. We prove that MP-TS has the optimal regret upper bound that matches the regret lower bound provided by Anantharam et al.\,(1987). Therefore, MP-TS is the first computationally efficient algorithm with optimal regret. A set of computer simulations was also conducted, which compared MP-TS with state-of-the-art algorithms. We also propose a modification of MP-TS, which is shown to have better empirical performance.

Recently, Thompson sampling (TS), a randomized algorithm with a Bayesian spirit, has attracted much attention for its empirically excellent performance, and it is revealed to have an optimal regret bound in the standard single-play MAB problem. In this paper, we propose the multiple-play Thompson sampling (MP-TS) algorithm, an extension of TS to the multiple-play MAB problem, and discuss its regret analysis. We prove that MP-TS has the optimal regret upper bound that matches the regret lower bound provided by Anantharam et al.\,(1987). Therefore, MP-TS is the first computationally efficient algorithm with optimal regret. A set of computer simulations was also conducted, which compared MP-TS with state-of-the-art algorithms. paragraphs: In a multiple-play bandit problem, a learner selects several arms in each round rather than just one. This paper extends Thompson sampling to that setting through an algorithm called MP-TS. The motivation is to carry a randomized, Bayesian-inspired approach with strong single-play results into a problem requiring several simultaneous selections.

The main theoretical result is a regret upper bound matching the established lower bound for the problem. This establishes optimal regret for MP-TS in the studied setting. The authors identify it as the first computationally efficient algorithm with this optimality property, combining a statistical guarantee with a method intended to be practical to run.

Computer simulations compare MP-TS with state-of-the-art algorithms. The paper also introduces a modified version that performs better empirically. These contributions have distinct roles: the regret analysis establishes the stated optimality of MP-TS, while the simulation findings motivate the modification as a practical improvement without presenting that empirical gain as a separate universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: Multiple-play Thompson sampling achieves an optimal regret bound, and a proposed modification improves empirical performance.

title: Optimal Regret Analysis of Thompson Sampling in Stochastic Multi-armed Bandit Problem with Multiple Plays

abstract: A central problem in machine learning involves modeling complex data-sets using highly flexible families of probability distributions in which learning, sampling, inference, and evaluation are still analytically or computationally tractable. Here, we develop an approach that simultaneously achieves both flexibility and tractability. The essential idea, inspired by non-equilibrium statistical physics, is to systematically and slowly destroy structure in a data distribution through an iterative forward diffusion process. We then learn a reverse diffusion process that restores structure in data, yielding a highly flexible and tractable generative model of the data. This approach allows us to rapidly learn, sample from, and evaluate probabilities in deep generative models with thousands of layers or time steps, as well as to compute conditional and posterior probabilities under the learned model. We additionally release an open source reference implementation of the algorithm.

Here, we develop an approach that simultaneously achieves both flexibility and tractability. The essential idea, inspired by non-equilibrium statistical physics, is to systematically and slowly destroy structure in a data distribution through an iterative forward diffusion process. We then learn a reverse diffusion process that restores structure in data, yielding a highly flexible and tractable generative model of the data. This approach allows us to rapidly learn, sample from, and evaluate probabilities in deep generative models with thousands of layers or time steps, as well as to compute conditional and posterior probabilities under the learned model. We additionally release an open source reference implementation of the algorithm.

paragraphs: Flexible probability models can describe complicated data, but their usefulness also depends on whether learning and computation remain manageable. This paper develops a generative approach intended to combine that flexibility with tractable sampling, inference, and probability evaluation. Its organizing idea comes from nonequilibrium statistical physics.

The method first applies a gradual forward diffusion process that repeatedly destroys structure in the data distribution. It then learns a reverse process that restores structure. The sequence of transformations is central: the generative model is built through many stages of reversing the gradual destruction, allowing a deep model to represent complex data while retaining manageable computations.

The authors state that this construction supports rapid learning, sampling, and probability evaluation in models with thousands of layers or time steps. It also permits computation of conditional and posterior probabilities under the learned model. These capabilities matter because the model serves both generation and probabilistic inference. An open-source reference implementation accompanies the work, providing an implementation of the proposed algorithm.
summary.tldr: Learning to reverse a gradual diffusion process produces flexible deep generative models with tractable sampling and probabilistic inference.

title: Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics

abstract: We consider the problem of including additional knowledge in estimating sparse Gaussian graphical models (sGGMs) from aggregated samples, arising often in bioinformatics and neuroimaging applications. Previous joint sGGM estimators either fail to use existing knowledge or cannot scale-up to many tasks (large $K$) under a high-dimensional (large $p$) situation. In this paper, we propose a novel \underline{J}oint \underline{E}lementary \underline{E}stimator incorporating additional \underline{K}nowledge (JEEK) to infer multiple related sparse Gaussian Graphical models from large-scale heterogeneous data. Using domain knowledge as weights, we design a novel hybrid norm as the minimization objective to enforce the superposition of two weighted sparsity constraints, one on the shared interactions and the other on the task-specific structural patterns. This enables JEEK to elegantly consider various forms of existing knowledge based on the domain at hand and avoid the need to design knowledge-specific optimization. JEEK is solved through a fast and entry-wise parallelizable solution that largely improves the computational efficiency of the state-of-the-art $O(p^5K^4)$ to $O(p^2K^4)$. We conduct a rigorous statistical analysis showing that JEEK achieves the same convergence rate $O(\log(Kp)/n_{tot})$ as the state-of-the-art estimators that are much harder to compute. Empirically, on multiple synthetic datasets and one real-world data from neuroscience, JEEP outperforms the speed of the state-of-arts significantly while achieving the same level of prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn several related networks of statistical relationships while incorporating existing domain knowledge. The setting involves sparse Gaussian graphical models, where relatively few interactions are retained. Applications such as neuroscience can involve many variables and many related tasks, making both the use of prior knowledge and computational scalability important.

The proposed estimator, JEEK, represents domain knowledge through weights. Its optimization objective combines two sparsity constraints: one for interactions shared across tasks and another for patterns specific to individual tasks. This gives the method a common way to incorporate different kinds of knowledge without requiring a separate optimization design for each kind.

JEEK also permits parallel computation for individual matrix entries. The stated computational complexity improves from O(p^5 K^4) to O(p^2 K^4), while the statistical analysis establishes the same convergence rate as harder-to-compute estimators. Experiments on synthetic data and neuroscience data report substantially faster computation with comparable prediction accuracy, supporting the value of the computational simplification.
summary.tldr: JEEK incorporates domain knowledge into related sparse graphical models while substantially reducing computation and retaining established statistical convergence rates.

title: A Fast and Scalable Joint Estimator for Integrating Additional Knowledge in Learning Multiple Related Sparse Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: Value-function approximation methods that operate in batch mode have foundational importance to reinforcement learning (RL). Finite sample guarantees for these methods often crucially rely on two types of assumptions: (1) mild distribution shift, and (2) representation conditions that are stronger than realizability. However, the necessity (“why do we need them?”) and the naturalness (“when do they hold?”) of such assumptions have largely eluded the literature. In this paper, we revisit these assumptions and provide theoretical results towards answering the above questions, and make steps towards a deeper understanding of value-function approximation.

paragraphs: This paper examines the assumptions behind theoretical guarantees for batch reinforcement learning with value-function approximation. Such methods learn from a batch of experience and use a representation to estimate values. Understanding their guarantees requires asking what the data and representation must provide, beyond simply stating that a method works under a list of conditions.

The abstract highlights two recurring requirements. One limits distribution shift, so the relevant distributions cannot differ too severely. The other imposes representation conditions stronger than realizability, meaning that the usual ability to represent the desired value function is not the only property being required. These assumptions often play crucial roles in guarantees based on a finite amount of data.

The authors revisit both requirements through theoretical results about their necessity and naturalness: why they are needed and when they hold. The contribution is an investigation of the foundations of existing guarantees. Its stated outcome is progress toward understanding value-function approximation, rather than a claim that all such assumptions have been completely characterized or removed.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates why batch reinforcement learning guarantees rely on distribution-shift and representation assumptions, and when those assumptions hold.

title: Information-Theoretic Considerations in Batch Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs) are capable of learning latent representations for high dimensional data. However, due to the i.i.d. assumption, VAEs only optimize the singleton variational distributions and fail to account for the correlations between data points, which might be crucial for learning latent representations from dataset where a priori we know correlations exist. We propose Correlated Variational Auto-Encoders (CVAEs) that can take the correlation structure into consideration when learning latent representations with VAEs. CVAEs apply a prior based on the correlation structure. To address the intractability introduced by the correlated prior, we develop an approximation by average of a set of tractable lower bounds over all maximal acyclic subgraphs of the undirected correlation graph. Experimental results on matching and link prediction on public benchmark rating datasets and spectral clustering on a synthetic dataset show the effectiveness of the proposed method over baseline algorithms.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders learn compact latent representations of high dimensional data. Their usual assumption that observations are independent means they optimize distributions for individual examples without accounting for correlations between them. This paper addresses datasets where relationships between examples are known beforehand and may matter for the representations being learned.

Correlated variational autoencoders incorporate those relationships through a prior based on the correlation structure. That change makes inference intractable, so the authors develop an approximation using an undirected graph of the relationships. They average tractable lower bounds associated with all maximal acyclic subgraphs. In this way, simpler graph structures provide manageable pieces for approximating the objective involving the correlated prior.

The experiments evaluate matching and link prediction on public rating benchmarks, along with spectral clustering on synthetic data. The reported results show effectiveness relative to baseline algorithms. The contribution is a way to make known relationships between examples participate in representation learning, together with an approximation that addresses the computational difficulty those relationships introduce.
summary.tldr: Correlated variational autoencoders incorporate known relationships between examples through a structured prior and a tractable approximation to the resulting objective.

title: Correlated Variational Auto-Encoders

abstract: In this paper, we focus on a theory-practice gap for Adam and its variants (AMSGrad, AdamNC, etc.). In practice, these algorithms are used with a constant first-order moment parameter $\beta_{1}$ (typically between $0.9$ and $0.99$). In theory, regret guarantees for online convex optimization require a rapidly decaying $\beta_{1}\to0$ schedule. We show that this is an artifact of the standard analysis, and we propose a novel framework that allows us to derive optimal, data-dependent regret bounds with a constant $\beta_{1}$, without further assumptions. We also demonstrate the flexibility of our analysis on a wide range of different algorithms and settings.

We also demonstrate the flexibility of our analysis on a wide range of different algorithms and settings.

paragraphs: Adam and related optimization algorithms use a first-moment parameter to control how past gradients influence current updates. Practitioners usually keep this parameter fixed, but earlier regret guarantees for online convex optimization required it to shrink rapidly toward zero. This mismatch left the usual practical configuration outside those theoretical guarantees.

The paper develops a new analysis framework that permits a constant first-moment parameter. It derives optimal, data-dependent regret bounds without adding further assumptions to the setting studied. Regret measures accumulated performance relative to a comparison decision, so these results explain how the algorithms can remain competitive over a sequence of convex optimization problems.

The central contribution is a change in the analysis: the authors show that the decaying-parameter requirement came from the standard proof approach. They also apply their framework across different algorithms and settings. This brings the theory closer to practical parameter choices while keeping the stated guarantees within the online convex optimization context.
summary.tldr: A new analysis gives optimal, data-dependent regret bounds for Adam-type algorithms with the constant momentum parameter commonly used in practice.

title: A new regret analysis for Adam-type algorithms

abstract: Many machine learning algorithms are trained and evaluated by splitting data from a single source into training and test sets. While such focus on in-distribution learning scenarios has led to interesting advancement, it has not been able to tell if models are relying on dataset biases as shortcuts for successful prediction (e.g., using snow cues for recognising snowmobiles), resulting in biased models that fail to generalise when the bias shifts to a different class. The cross-bias generalisation problem has been addressed by de-biasing training data through augmentation or re-sampling, which are often prohibitive due to the data collection cost (e.g., collecting images of a snowmobile on a desert) and the difficulty of quantifying or expressing biases in the first place. In this work, we propose a novel framework to train a de-biased representation by encouraging it to be different from a set of representations that are biased by design. This tactic is feasible in many scenarios where it is much easier to define a set of biased representations than to define and quantify bias. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method across a variety of synthetic and real-world biases; our experiments show that the method discourages models from taking bias shortcuts, resulting in improved generalisation. Source code is available at https://github.com/clovaai/rebias.

paragraphs: A model can perform well on training and test data from the same source while relying on misleading shortcuts. A visual cue associated with one class may cease to be reliable when the association changes. This paper addresses that cross-bias generalization problem, where ordinary evaluation can conceal dependence on dataset-specific correlations.

The proposed framework deliberately constructs biased representations and encourages the desired representation to differ from them. The motivation is practical: specifying a representation that favors a shortcut can be easier than explicitly defining and measuring the bias itself. This provides an alternative to collecting or resampling data to break unwanted correlations, which can be costly or difficult.

Experiments spanning synthetic and real-world biases show that the method discourages shortcut use and improves generalization. The findings support using deliberately biased representations as a reference for learning less biased ones in the tested settings. The approach is particularly motivated by scenarios where those reference representations are easier to design than a complete description of the unwanted bias.
summary.tldr: Encouraging learned representations to differ from deliberately biased ones reduces shortcut reliance and improves generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Learning De-biased Representations with Biased Representations

abstract: We present a Bayesian non-parametric way of inferring stochastic differential equations for both regression tasks and continuous-time dynamical modelling. The work has high emphasis on the stochastic part of the differential equation, also known as the diffusion, and modelling it by means of Wishart processes. Further, we present a semiparametric approach that allows the framework to scale to high dimensions. This successfully leads us onto how to model both latent and autoregressive temporal systems with conditional heteroskedastic noise. We provide experimental evidence that modelling diffusion often improves performance and that this randomness in the differential equation can be essential to avoid overfitting.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations describe continuous-time behavior with a random component called diffusion. This paper proposes a Bayesian nonparametric approach to learning such equations for regression and dynamical modeling. It places particular emphasis on learning the diffusion, making the randomness itself a central part of the model.

The framework models diffusion using Wishart processes. A semiparametric extension allows it to scale to high-dimensional settings. The authors use this approach for both latent temporal systems and autoregressive temporal systems with conditional heteroskedastic noise, meaning that the amount of noise can vary with the conditions rather than remaining fixed.

Experiments provide evidence that explicitly modeling diffusion often improves performance. They also show that randomness in the differential equation can be essential for avoiding overfitting. The findings give the stochastic component a role beyond merely acknowledging noise: learning its changing structure can matter to the quality of the fitted model and its ability to avoid fitting the data too closely.
summary.tldr: Wishart-process diffusion models learn changing randomness in stochastic differential equations, often improving performance and sometimes preventing overfitting.

title: Stochastic Differential Equations with Variational Wishart Diffusions

abstract: Task-specific fine-tuning on pre-trained transformers has achieved performance breakthroughs in multiple NLP tasks. Yet, as both computation and parameter size grows linearly with the number of sub-tasks, it is increasingly difficult to adopt such methods to the real world due to unrealistic memory and computation overhead on computing devices. Previous works on fine-tuning focus on reducing the growing parameter size to save storage cost by parameter sharing. However, compared to storage, the constraint of computation is a more critical issue with the fine-tuning models in modern computing environments. In this work, we propose LeTS, a framework that leverages both computation and parameter sharing across multiple tasks. Compared to traditional fine-tuning, LeTS proposes a novel neural architecture that contains a fixed pre-trained transformer model, plus learnable additive components for sub-tasks. The learnable components reuse the intermediate activations in the fixed pre-trained model, decoupling computation dependency. Differentiable neural architecture search is used to determine a task-specific computation sharing scheme, and a novel early stage pruning is applied to additive components for sparsity to achieve parameter sharing. Extensive experiments show that with 1.4% of extra parameters per task, LeTS reduces the computation by 49.5% on GLUE benchmarks with only 0.2% accuracy loss compared to full fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a separate transformer for each language task increases both stored parameters and computation as tasks accumulate. Sharing parameters can reduce storage, but the paper emphasizes that computation also needs attention. Learn-to-Share, or LeTS, addresses both costs through a framework that shares a fixed pretrained transformer across tasks.

Each task receives learnable additive components that reuse intermediate activations from the shared model. This architecture decouples computation dependencies and creates opportunities to share work. Differentiable neural architecture search determines the computation-sharing arrangement for each task, while early pruning makes the additive components sparse to support parameter sharing.

On GLUE benchmarks, the reported configuration adds 1.4% extra parameters per task and reduces computation by 49.5%, with a reported accuracy loss of 0.2% relative to full fine-tuning. These results show a favorable tradeoff in the evaluated setting. The broader contribution is to treat shared computation as an explicit design objective alongside parameter storage, using learned task-specific components to adapt a common transformer.
summary.tldr: LeTS shares transformer parameters and intermediate computation across tasks, reducing reported GLUE computation by 49.5% with a 0.2% accuracy loss.

title: Learn-to-Share: A Hardware-friendly Transfer Learning Framework Exploiting Computation and Parameter Sharing

abstract: Several recent end-to-end text-to-speech (TTS) models enabling single-stage training and parallel sampling have been proposed, but their sample quality does not match that of two-stage TTS systems. In this work, we present a parallel end-to-end TTS method that generates more natural sounding audio than current two-stage models. Our method adopts variational inference augmented with normalizing flows and an adversarial training process, which improves the expressive power of generative modeling. We also propose a stochastic duration predictor to synthesize speech with diverse rhythms from input text. With the uncertainty modeling over latent variables and the stochastic duration predictor, our method expresses the natural one-to-many relationship in which a text input can be spoken in multiple ways with different pitches and rhythms. A subjective human evaluation (mean opinion score, or MOS) on the LJ Speech, a single speaker dataset, shows that our method outperforms the best publicly available TTS systems and achieves a MOS comparable to ground truth.

paragraphs: A written sentence can be spoken with different pitches and rhythms, so text-to-speech must model more than a single fixed audio output. This paper introduces a parallel, end-to-end speech-generation method that explicitly represents that variability. It addresses a quality gap identified between earlier single-stage systems and systems that generate speech in two stages.

The method combines variational inference, normalizing flows, and adversarial training to increase the expressive power of its generative model. A stochastic duration predictor adds variation in timing, allowing the same text to produce different rhythms. Together, uncertainty in the latent variables and variability in duration capture multiple plausible ways of speaking an input.

Human listeners evaluate the generated speech using mean opinion scores on LJ Speech, a single-speaker dataset. In that evaluation, the method outperforms the best publicly available text-to-speech systems and receives scores comparable to ground-truth audio. This supports the quality of the proposed combination in the tested setting; the comparison concerns listener ratings on that dataset.
summary.tldr: A parallel end-to-end speech model captures variable pitch and rhythm and achieves human quality ratings comparable to ground-truth audio on LJ Speech.

title: Conditional Variational Autoencoder with Adversarial Learning for End-to-End Text-to-Speech

abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) is the task of finding a reward function that generates a desired optimal policy for a given Markov Decision Process (MDP). This paper develops an information-theoretic lower bound for the sample complexity of the finite state, finite action IRL problem. A geometric construction of $\beta$-strict separable IRL problems using spherical codes is considered. Properties of the ensemble size as well as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the generated trajectories are derived. The resulting ensemble is then used along with Fano’s inequality to derive a sample complexity lower bound of $O(n \log n)$, where $n$ is the number of states in the MDP.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function that makes a desired policy optimal in a given decision-making environment. This paper studies how much data that inference can require when the environment has finitely many states and actions. Its contribution is an information-theoretic lower bound, describing a fundamental obstacle to learning rather than proposing a faster reward-learning algorithm.

The argument constructs a collection of reward-inference problems using spherical codes, a geometric way of arranging separated possibilities. The constructed problems satisfy a specified strict-separation condition. The authors analyze both the size of this collection and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the trajectories it generates. These quantities capture how many alternatives must be distinguished and how informative the observations are for distinguishing them.

Combining this construction with Fano’s inequality yields the sample-complexity lower bound reported in the abstract as O(n log n), where n is the number of states. The finding links the difficulty of reward inference to environment size through the information available in trajectories, rather than through the computational design of a particular algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper derives an information-theoretic lower bound, reported as O(n log n), for finite-state inverse reinforcement learning.

title: A Lower Bound for the Sample Complexity of Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning faithful graph representations as sets of vertex embeddings has become a fundamental intermediary step in a wide range of machine learning applications. We propose the systematic use of symmetric spaces in representation learning, a class encompassing many of the previously used embedding targets. This enables us to introduce a new method, the use of Finsler metrics integrated in a Riemannian optimization scheme, that better adapts to dissimilar structures in the graph. We develop a tool to analyze the embeddings and infer structural properties of the data sets. For implementation, we choose Siegel spaces, a versatile family of symmetric spaces. Our approach outperforms competitive baselines for graph reconstruction tasks on various synthetic and real-world datasets. We further demonstrate its applicability on two downstream tasks, recommender systems and node classification.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings represent vertices as points in a geometric space, making graph information available to downstream learning tasks. This paper proposes systematically using symmetric spaces as the embedding target. That class includes many spaces used previously, giving the approach a broader geometric framework for representing different graph structures.

Within this framework, the authors combine Finsler metrics with a Riemannian optimization scheme. The stated benefit is better adaptation to dissimilar structures within a graph. They also develop a tool for analyzing the learned embeddings and inferring structural properties of the underlying datasets. For implementation, they choose Siegel spaces, a versatile family within the symmetric-space class.

Experiments show better graph reconstruction than competitive baselines on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The paper additionally demonstrates applications to recommender systems and node classification. These results connect the geometric proposal to both faithful graph representation and downstream uses. The contribution therefore extends beyond choosing a new embedding space: it combines a distance framework, an optimization approach, and a way to inspect what the learned representations reveal about graph structure.
summary.tldr: Symmetric-space embeddings combine Finsler metrics and Riemannian optimization to better represent varied graph structures.

title: Symmetric Spaces for Graph Embeddings: A Finsler-Riemannian Approach

abstract: We create classical (non-quantum) dynamic data structures supporting queries for recommender systems and least-squares regression that are comparable to their quantum analogues. De-quantizing such algorithms has received a flurry of attention in recent years; we obtain sharper bounds for these problems. More significantly, we achieve these improvements by arguing that the previous quantum-inspired algorithms for these problems are doing leverage or ridge-leverage score sampling in disguise; these are powerful and standard techniques in randomized numerical linear algebra. With this recognition, we are able to employ the large body of work in numerical linear algebra to obtain algorithms for these problems that are simpler or faster (or both) than existing approaches. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed data structures also work well on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper develops classical dynamic data structures for recommendation and least-squares regression with query capabilities comparable to quantum counterparts. It contributes to de-quantization: understanding how classical methods can reproduce capabilities associated with quantum algorithms. The authors obtain sharper bounds for these problems.

The key observation is that earlier quantum-inspired methods implicitly perform leverage-score or ridge-leverage-score sampling. These are established techniques from randomized numerical linear algebra. Recognizing that connection allows the authors to use an existing body of mathematical results and algorithmic tools to improve the data structures.

The resulting algorithms are simpler, faster, or both compared with previous approaches, and experiments show that the proposed structures work well on real-world datasets. The broader methodological contribution is the identification of a familiar sampling principle beneath seemingly specialized quantum-inspired procedures. That connection explains where improvements can come from and makes numerical linear algebra directly useful in developing stronger classical solutions for the two application areas studied.
summary.tldr: Recognizing standard sampling techniques inside quantum-inspired algorithms yields simpler or faster classical methods for recommendation and regression.

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithms from Randomized Numerical Linear Algebra

abstract: In compressed sensing, the goal is to reconstruct the signal from an underdetermined system of linear measurements. Thus, prior knowledge about the signal of interest and its structure is required. Additionally, in many scenarios, the signal has an unknown orientation prior to measurements. To address such recovery problems, we propose using equivariant generative models as a prior, which encapsulate orientation information in their latent space. Thereby, we show that signals with unknown orientations can be recovered with iterative gradient descent on the latent space of these models and provide additional theoretical recovery guarantees. We construct an equivariant variational autoencoder and use the decoder as generative prior for compressed sensing. We discuss additional potential gains of the proposed approach in terms of convergence and latency.

Thereby, we show that signals with unknown orientations can be recovered with iterative gradient descent on the latent space of these models and provide additional theoretical recovery guarantees. We construct an equivariant variational autoencoder and use the decoder as generative prior for compressed sensing. We discuss additional potential gains of the proposed approach in terms of convergence and latency.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs a signal from too few linear measurements to determine it uniquely without additional knowledge. A prior supplies information about the kinds of signals that are plausible. This paper addresses an added difficulty: the signal may have an unknown orientation before the measurements are taken, so recovery must accommodate that uncertainty.

The authors propose equivariant generative models as priors, with orientation information represented in their latent space. They construct an equivariant variational autoencoder and use its decoder to generate candidate signals. Reconstruction then proceeds through iterative gradient descent in the model’s latent space, searching for a representation that recovers the signal despite its unknown orientation.

The paper shows recovery with this approach and provides additional theoretical guarantees. Its central contribution is to make orientation part of the generative representation used for reconstruction. The authors also discuss possible improvements in convergence and latency. Those computational benefits are presented as potential gains, while latent-space recovery and the accompanying guarantees form the stated core results.
summary.tldr: Equivariant generative priors enable latent-space reconstruction of compressed signals with unknown orientation, supported by theoretical recovery guarantees.

title: Equivariant Priors for compressed sensing with unknown orientation

abstract: The modern strategy for training deep neural networks for classification tasks includes optimizing the network’s weights even after the training error vanishes to further push the training loss toward zero. Recently, a phenomenon termed “neural collapse" (NC) has been empirically observed in this training procedure. Specifically, it has been shown that the learned features (the output of the penultimate layer) of within-class samples converge to their mean, and the means of different classes exhibit a certain tight frame structure, which is also aligned with the last layer’s weights. Recent papers have shown that minimizers with this structure emerge when optimizing a simplified “unconstrained features model" (UFM) with a regularized cross-entropy loss. In this paper, we further analyze and extend the UFM. First, we study the UFM for the regularized MSE loss, and show that the minimizers’ features can have a more delicate structure than in the cross-entropy case. This affects also the structure of the weights. Then, we extend the UFM by adding another layer of weights as well as ReLU nonlinearity to the model and generalize our previous results. Finally, we empirically demonstrate the usefulness of our nonlinear extended UFM in modeling the NC phenomenon that occurs with practical networks.

paragraphs: Deep classifiers often keep training after they classify every training example correctly, further reducing the loss. Simplified unconstrained features models have helped explain this behavior.

This paper first studies that simplified model with regularized mean squared error instead of regularized cross-entropy. Its analysis shows that minimizing features can have a more intricate structure than in the cross-entropy setting, with corresponding changes to the weights. The result makes the choice of loss relevant to the geometry predicted by the model.

The authors then add another weight layer and a ReLU nonlinearity, extending their earlier results to this richer model. Experiments demonstrate that the nonlinear extension is useful for modeling neural collapse in practical networks. The work therefore develops a more expressive analytical setting while showing why the simplest geometric description need not capture every loss-dependent structure.
summary.tldr: An extended features model explains richer neural-collapse geometry under mean squared error and incorporates an additional nonlinear layer.

title: Extended Unconstrained Features Model for Exploring Deep Neural Collapse

abstract: A central problem in sequential decision making is to develop algorithms that are practical and computationally efficient, yet support the use of flexible, general-purpose models. Focusing on the contextual bandit problem, recent progress provides provably efficient algorithms with strong empirical performance when the number of possible alternatives (“actions”) is small, but guarantees for decision making in large, continuous action spaces have remained elusive, leading to a significant gap between theory and practice. We present the first efficient, general-purpose algorithm for contextual bandits with continuous, linearly structured action spaces. Our algorithm makes use of computational oracles for (i) supervised learning, and (ii) optimization over the action space, and achieves sample complexity, runtime, and memory independent of the size of the action space. In addition, it is simple and practical. We perform a large-scale empirical evaluation, and show that our approach typically enjoys superior performance and efficiency compared to standard baselines.

paragraphs: Contextual bandit algorithms choose actions using information about the current situation and learn from the resulting feedback. Methods that work well with a small menu of actions can become difficult to use when the choices are extremely numerous or continuous. The paper targets this gap between flexible prediction models and efficient decision making.

The authors introduce a general-purpose algorithm for continuous action spaces with linear structure. It relies on two computational components: a supervised learning oracle and an oracle for optimization over the action space. Together, these components let the method use general-purpose models while handling action selection through a separate optimization operation.

The stated guarantees make sample complexity, runtime, and memory independent of the number of available actions. This is meaningful for continuous spaces, where enumerating every choice is impossible, but the result specifically concerns the stated linear structure and oracle access. A large-scale empirical evaluation finds that the method typically improves both performance and efficiency relative to standard baselines.
summary.tldr: An oracle-based contextual bandit algorithm handles continuous, linearly structured actions with complexity independent of action-space size.

title: Contextual Bandits with Large Action Spaces: Made Practical

abstract: We study statistical/computational tradeoffs for the following density estimation problem: given $k$ distributions $v_1, \ldots, v_k$ over a discrete domain of size $n$, and sampling access to a distribution $p$, identify $v_i$ that is "close" to $p$. Our main result is the first data structure that, given a sublinear (in $n$) number of samples from $p$, identifies $v_i$ in time sublinear in $k$. We also give an improved version of the algorithm of Acharya et al. (2018) that reports $v_i$ in time linear in $k$. The experimental evaluation of the latter algorithm shows that it achieves a significant reduction in the number of operations needed to achieve a given accuracy compared to prior work.

paragraphs: The paper considers selecting a distribution from a collection of candidates using samples from an unknown target distribution. The candidates share a discrete domain. The challenge has two separate scales: the number of possible domain values and the number of candidate distributions that could match the target.

The main result is a data structure that uses a number of target samples sublinear in the domain size and identifies a close candidate in time sublinear in the number of candidates. This combines a statistical saving with a computational one. The stated sample and query-time improvements concern different quantities, making their simultaneous achievement the central theoretical contribution.

The authors also improve an earlier algorithm whose running time is linear in the candidate count. Experiments evaluate this latter algorithm and show a substantial reduction in operations needed to reach a given accuracy compared with prior work. Thus, the paper offers both a sublinear-time data-structure result and experimental evidence for a separate, improved linear-time approach.
summary.tldr: A density-estimation data structure combines sublinear sample use with sublinear candidate search, while a separate linear-time algorithm improves empirical efficiency.

title: Data Structures for Density Estimation

abstract: Understanding the neural implementation of complex human behaviors is one of the major goals in neuroscience. To this end, it is crucial to find a true representation of the neural data, which is challenging due to the high complexity of behaviors and the low signal-to-ratio (SNR) of the signals. Here, we propose a novel unsupervised learning framework, Neural Latent Aligner (NLA), to find well-constrained, behaviorally relevant neural representations of complex behaviors. The key idea is to align representations across repeated trials to learn cross-trial consistent information. Furthermore, we propose a novel, fully differentiable time warping model (TWM) to resolve the temporal misalignment of trials. When applied to intracranial electrocorticography (ECoG) of natural speaking, our model learns better representations for decoding behaviors than the baseline models, especially in lower dimensional space. The TWM is empirically validated by measuring behavioral coherence between aligned trials. The proposed framework learns more cross-trial consistent representations than the baselines, and when visualized, the manifold reveals shared neural trajectories across trials.

paragraphs: Neural recordings of complex behavior contain substantial noise, making behaviorally meaningful structure difficult to recover. Neural Latent Aligner uses repeated trials as a source of structure. Its unsupervised framework learns representations that agree across repetitions, emphasizing information that remains consistent from trial to trial.

Repetitions can differ in timing, so directly aligning them can obscure shared patterns. The authors introduce a fully differentiable time-warping model to handle temporal misalignment. Combining temporal alignment with representation learning lets the framework seek common neural information even when corresponding events occur at different times.

Applied to intracranial electrocorticography recordings of natural speech, NLA learns representations that support better behavioral decoding than the evaluated baselines, especially in lower-dimensional spaces. Behavioral coherence between aligned trials provides empirical validation of the time-warping component. The learned representations are also more consistent across trials, and visualizations reveal shared neural trajectories. These results support repeated-trial alignment as a useful constraint for extracting meaningful structure from complex, noisy recordings.
summary.tldr: Neural Latent Aligner combines cross-trial consistency and learned time warping to extract behaviorally useful representations from neural recordings.

title: Neural Latent Aligner: Cross-trial Alignment for Learning Representations of Complex, Naturalistic Neural Data

abstract: We show that taking the width and depth to infinity in a deep neural network with skip connections, when branches are scaled by $1/\sqrt{depth}$, result in the same covariance structure no matter how that limit is taken. This explains why the standard infinite-width-then-depth approach provides practical insights even for networks with depth of the same order as width. We also demonstrate that the pre-activations, in this case, have Gaussian distributions which has direct applications in Bayesian deep learning. We conduct extensive simulations that show an excellent match with our theoretical findings.
originalAbstract: We show that taking the width and depth to infinity in a deep neural network with skip connections, when branches are scaled by $1/\sqrt{depth}$, result in the same covariance structure no matter how that limit is taken. This explains why the standard infinite-width-then-depth approach provides practical insights even for networks with depth of the same order as width. We also demonstrate that the pre-activations, in this case, have Gaussian distributions which has direct applications in Bayesian deep learning. We conduct extensive simulations that show an excellent match with our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Theoretical analyses often simplify neural networks by letting their width become infinite before considering infinite depth. But actual networks can have width and depth of comparable size, raising the question of whether that order of analysis is informative. This paper examines the issue for networks with skip connections under a specific scaling of their residual branches.

When branches are scaled by the inverse square root of depth, the authors show that the limiting covariance structure is the same regardless of how width and depth approach infinity. Covariance describes relationships among the network’s signals. The result explains why the conventional width-first analysis can still provide insight when depth grows on the same order as width.

The paper also establishes Gaussian distributions for pre-activations in this setting, with direct relevance to Bayesian deep learning. Extensive simulations closely match the theoretical predictions. The branch scaling is central to the stated result: the paper establishes agreement of these limits for the specified residual-network setup, rather than asserting that width and depth limits commute for every neural architecture.
summary.tldr: With residual branches scaled by inverse square-root depth, infinite-width and infinite-depth limits yield the same covariance structure regardless of their order.

title: Width and Depth Limits Commute in Residual Networks

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning framework where many clients collaboratively train models while keeping the training data decentralized. Despite recent advances in FL, the uncertainty quantification topic (UQ) remains partially addressed. Among UQ methods, conformal prediction (CP) approaches provides distribution-free guarantees under minimal assumptions. We develop a new federated conformal prediction method based on quantile regression and take into account privacy constraints. This method takes advantage of importance weighting to effectively address the label shift between agents and provides theoretical guarantees for both valid coverage of the prediction sets and differential privacy. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate that this method outperforms current competitors.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients train a shared model while keeping training data decentralized. This paper addresses how such a system can express uncertainty about its predictions. The authors use conformal prediction, which constructs prediction sets with coverage guarantees under minimal assumptions, and adapt it to a setting with both client differences and privacy constraints.

Their method combines quantile regression with importance weighting. The weighting addresses label shift between agents, meaning that the relative prevalence of labels differs across clients. Accounting for this variation matters because an uncertainty procedure must accommodate the populations represented by the different participants, alongside the requirement to protect their information.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for valid prediction-set coverage and differential privacy within its proposed method. It also reports extensive experiments in which the approach outperforms current competitors. The contribution brings these requirements into one federated uncertainty procedure: handling label imbalance across agents, providing prediction sets with theoretical coverage support, and incorporating a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: A federated conformal prediction method uses quantile regression and importance weighting to provide coverage and privacy guarantees under label shift.

title: Conformal Prediction for Federated Uncertainty Quantification Under Label Shift

abstract: Macro-AUC is the arithmetic mean of the class-wise AUCs in multi-label learning and is commonly used in practice. However, its theoretical understanding is far lacking. Toward solving it, we characterize the generalization properties of various learning algorithms based on the corresponding surrogate losses w.r.t. Macro-AUC. We theoretically identify a critical factor of the dataset affecting the generalization bounds: the label-wise class imbalance . Our results on the imbalance-aware error bounds show that the widely-used univariate loss-based algorithm is more sensitive to the label-wise class imbalance than the proposed pairwise and reweighted loss-based ones, which probably implies its worse performance. Moreover, empirical results on various datasets corroborate our theory findings. To establish it, technically, we propose a new (and more general) McDiarmid-type concentration inequality, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Macro-AUC averages the AUC scores computed separately for each label in a multi-label problem. Although widely used, its generalization behavior has received limited theoretical treatment. This paper examines how the surrogate losses used to train different learning algorithms relate to performance on that evaluation measure beyond the training data.

The analysis identifies label-wise class imbalance as a critical factor in generalization bounds. For a given label, the balance between positive and negative examples affects the guarantees. The authors find that bounds for the widely used univariate-loss approach are more sensitive to this imbalance than those for their proposed pairwise and reweighted-loss approaches.

That difference suggests potentially worse performance for the univariate approach; the bound comparison alone does not make the performance ordering universal. Experiments across several datasets corroborate the theoretical findings. To establish the analysis, the authors also introduce a more general McDiarmid-type concentration inequality. The work connects a dataset property, the training loss, and the generalization behavior of a practical multi-label metric.
summary.tldr: Imbalance-aware bounds suggest that pairwise and reweighted losses generalize more favorably for Macro-AUC than a common univariate loss.

title: Towards Understanding Generalization of Macro-AUC in Multi-label Learning

abstract: Distributed Mean Estimation (DME), in which $n$ clients communicate vectors to a parameter server that estimates their average, is a fundamental building block in communication-efficient federated learning. In this paper, we improve on previous DME techniques that achieve the optimal $O(1/n)$ Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) guarantee by asymptotically improving the complexity for either encoding or decoding (or both). To achieve this, we formalize the problem in a novel way that allows us to use off-the-shelf mathematical solvers to design the quantization. Using various datasets and training tasks, we demonstrate how QUIC-FL achieves state of the art accuracy with faster encoding and decoding times compared to other DME methods.

paragraphs: Federated learning often requires a server to estimate the average of vectors held by many clients. Sending and processing these vectors efficiently makes distributed mean estimation an important part of the training system. This paper targets the computational work involved in preparing client messages and reconstructing their average at the server.

Earlier methods already achieve an optimal normalized mean squared error rate of O(1/n), where n is the number of clients. The authors improve the asymptotic complexity of encoding, decoding, or both while retaining that error guarantee. Their key methodological change is a new formulation of the problem that lets existing mathematical solvers design the quantization used to represent communicated values.

The resulting method, QUIC-FL, is evaluated across multiple datasets and training tasks. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy alongside faster encoding and decoding than other distributed mean estimation methods. The contribution therefore addresses the computation surrounding communication: maintaining a strong accuracy guarantee while reducing the effort needed to turn client vectors into an estimated average.
summary.tldr: QUIC-FL accelerates distributed mean estimation while retaining an optimal error rate and achieving strong federated-learning accuracy.

title: Accelerating Federated Learning with Quick Distributed Mean Estimation

abstract: It is widely held that one cause of downstream bias in classifiers is bias present in the training data. Rectifying such biases may involve context-dependent interventions such as training separate models on subgroups, removing features with bias in the collection process, or even conducting real-world experiments to ascertain sources of bias. Despite the need for such data bias investigations, few automated methods exist to assist practitioners in these efforts. In this paper, we present one such method that given a dataset $X$ consisting of protected and unprotected features, outcomes $y$, and a regressor $h$ that predicts $y$ given $X$, outputs a tuple $(f_j, g)$, with the following property: $g$ corresponds to a subset of the training dataset $(X, y)$, such that the $j^{th}$ feature $f_j$ has much larger (or smaller) influence in the subgroup $g$, than on the dataset overall, which we call feature importance disparity (FID). We show across $4$ datasets and $4$ common feature importance methods of broad interest to the machine learning community that we can efficiently find subgroups with large FID values even over exponentially large subgroup classes and in practice these groups correspond to subgroups with potentially serious bias issues as measured by standard fairness metrics.

paragraphs: Investigating training-data bias often requires identifying where a model behaves differently across subgroups. This paper proposes an automated way to find such leads by looking for feature importance disparities. A disparity occurs when a feature has much more or much less influence within a subgroup than it does across the dataset overall.

The method takes a dataset containing protected and unprotected features, observed outcomes, and a regressor that predicts those outcomes. It returns a feature together with a subgroup in which that feature’s influence differs substantially from its overall influence. This gives practitioners a specific relationship to investigate, connecting a model input to a particular part of the training population.

Across four datasets and four common feature importance methods, the authors efficiently identify large disparities even when the candidate subgroup class is exponentially large. In practice, the resulting groups correspond to potentially serious bias issues under standard fairness metrics. The findings support the method as an aid to investigation: a detected disparity points toward a concern, while the appropriate intervention remains dependent on context.
summary.tldr: Searching for subgroup differences in feature importance can efficiently identify promising leads for investigating data bias.

title: Feature Importance Disparities for Data Bias Investigations

abstract: Building upon score-based learning, new interest in stochastic localization techniques has recently emerged. In these models, one seeks to noise a sample from the data distribution through a stochastic process, called observation process, and progressively learns a denoiser associated to this dynamics. Apart from specific applications, the use of stochastic localization for the problem of sampling from an unnormalized target density has not been explored extensively. This work contributes to fill this gap. We consider a general stochastic localization framework and introduce an explicit class of observation processes, associated with flexible denoising schedules. We provide a complete methodology, Stochastic Localization via Iterative Posterior Sampling (SLIPS), to obtain approximate samples of these dynamics, and as a by-product, samples from the target distribution. Our scheme is based on a Markov chain Monte Carlo estimation of the denoiser and comes with detailed practical guidelines. We illustrate the benefits and applicability of SLIPS on several benchmarks of multi-modal distributions, including Gaussian mixtures in increasing dimensions, Bayesian logistic regression and a high-dimensional field system from statistical-mechanics.

paragraphs: Sampling from an unnormalized density means generating examples when the target distribution is specified without its normalizing constant. This paper approaches that problem through stochastic localization, where a stochastic observation process adds noise and an associated denoiser describes how to recover information about the underlying sample.

The authors introduce an explicit family of observation processes with flexible denoising schedules. Their complete sampling method, SLIPS, approximately samples the resulting dynamics and thereby obtains samples from the target distribution. A central component is estimating the denoiser using Markov chain Monte Carlo, connecting the localization process to a practical posterior-sampling procedure.

The paper also supplies implementation guidance and illustrates SLIPS on several multimodal sampling benchmarks. These include Gaussian mixtures of increasing dimension, Bayesian logistic regression, and a high-dimensional statistical-mechanics field system. The examples demonstrate benefits and applicability across different distributional settings. The contribution extends stochastic localization toward a general sampling task while providing a concrete procedure for approximating the required dynamics.
summary.tldr: SLIPS uses Monte Carlo denoiser estimates within stochastic localization to approximately sample unnormalized target distributions.

title: Stochastic Localization via Iterative Posterior Sampling

abstract: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) aims to find subspaces spanned by the so-called principal components that best represent the variance in the dataset. The deflation method is a popular meta-algorithm that sequentially finds individual principal components, starting from the most important ones and working towards the less important ones. However, as deflation proceeds, numerical errors from the imprecise estimation of principal components propagate due to its sequential nature. This paper mathematically characterizes the error propagation of the inexact Hotelling’s deflation method. We consider two scenarios: $i)$ when the sub-routine for finding the leading eigenvector is abstract and can represent various algorithms; and $ii)$ when power iteration is used as the sub-routine. In the latter case, the additional directional information from power iteration allows us to obtain a tighter error bound than the sub-routine agnostic case. For both scenarios, we explicitly characterize how the errors progress and affect subsequent principal component estimations.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis seeks directions that capture the variation in a dataset. Deflation finds these directions sequentially, beginning with the most important component and continuing to less important ones. Because each stage depends on earlier estimates, numerical inaccuracies can carry forward and affect components computed later.

This paper mathematically characterizes that error propagation for inexact Hotelling’s deflation. One analysis treats the procedure for estimating the leading eigenvector as an abstract subroutine.
