Using information about the directions of the errors produced by that method, the authors obtain a tighter bound than the algorithm-independent analysis permits. Both cases explicitly describe how inaccuracies progress through successive component estimates. The contribution clarifies the consequences of sequential approximation and shows why accounting for a particular subroutine’s error structure can sharpen the analysis of the overall PCA procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes error propagation in sequential PCA and derives tighter bounds when deflation uses power iteration.

title: On the Error-Propagation of Inexact Hotelling’s Deflation for Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Automated machine learning (AutoML) was formed around the fundamental objectives of automatically and efficiently configuring machine learning (ML) workflows, aiding the research of new ML algorithms, and contributing to the democratization of ML by making it accessible to a broader audience. Over the past decade, commendable achievements in AutoML have primarily focused on optimizing predictive performance. This focused progress, while substantial, raises questions about how well AutoML has met its broader, original goals. In this position paper, we argue that a key to unlocking AutoML's full potential lies in addressing the currently underexplored aspect of user interaction with AutoML systems, including their diverse roles, expectations, and expertise. We envision a more human-centered approach in future AutoML research, promoting the collaborative design of ML systems that tightly integrates the complementary strengths of human expertise and AutoML methodologies.

This position paper argues that progress has concentrated heavily on predictive performance, leaving open how fully the field has served those broader purposes.

The authors identify interaction between people and AutoML systems as an underexplored research priority. Users bring different roles, expectations, and levels of expertise, so improving a system's predictions alone does not address the full range of ways people need to work with it. Their proposal places those differences at the center of future research.

The envisioned approach treats machine-learning system design as a collaboration between human expertise and automated methods. Its significance is a proposed change in what AutoML research pays attention to: useful automation includes how people contribute to and interact with the resulting workflow. As a position paper, it offers an argument and research direction, rather than reporting an experimental demonstration that a particular interface or collaboration method has solved these challenges.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that AutoML should prioritize human interaction and collaborative design alongside predictive performance.

title: Position: A Call to Action for a Human-Centered AutoML Paradigm

abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing research interest in decision-focused learning, which embeds optimization problems as a layer in learning pipelines and demonstrates a superior performance than the prediction-focused approach. However, for distributionally robust optimization (DRO), a popular paradigm for decision-making under uncertainty, it is still unknown how to embed it as a layer, i.e., how to differentiate decisions with respect to an ambiguity set. In this paper, we develop such differentiable DRO layers for generic mixed-integer DRO problems with parameterized second-order conic ambiguity sets and discuss its extension to Wasserstein ambiguity sets. To differentiate the mixed-integer decisions, we propose a novel dual-view methodology by handling continuous and discrete parts of decisions via different principles. Specifically, we construct a differentiable energy-based surrogate to implement the dual-view methodology and use importance sampling to estimate its gradient. We further prove that such a surrogate enjoys the asymptotic convergency under regularization. As an application of the proposed differentiable DRO layers, we develop a novel decision-focused learning pipeline for contextual distributionally robust decision-making tasks and compare it with the prediction-focused approach in experiments

paragraphs: Decision-focused learning trains a model through the decisions produced by an optimization problem. Distributionally robust optimization makes decisions while considering a set of possible probability distributions, called an ambiguity set. This paper addresses how to differentiate those decisions with respect to that set, allowing robust optimization to become part of a learning pipeline.

The authors develop differentiable layers for mixed-integer problems with parameterized second-order conic ambiguity sets and discuss extensions to Wasserstein ambiguity sets. Mixed-integer decisions contain both continuous and discrete components. Their dual-view methodology treats these components using different principles, implemented through a differentiable energy-based surrogate whose gradient is estimated with importance sampling.

They prove an asymptotic convergence property for the surrogate under regularization. They also build a contextual decision-focused learning pipeline and compare it experimentally with a prediction-focused approach. The contribution supplies machinery for training through robust decisions, including discrete choices, so that learning can respond to the optimization outcome and the uncertainty description that shapes it.
summary.tldr: Differentiable robust-optimization layers enable learning through mixed continuous and discrete decisions and the ambiguity sets that shape them.

title: Differentiable Distributionally Robust Optimization Layers

abstract: Large Language Models have recently gained significant attention in scientific discovery for their extensive knowledge and advanced reasoning capabilities. However, they encounter challenges in effectively simulating observational feedback and grounding it with language to propel advancements in physical scientific discovery. Conversely, human scientists undertake scientific discovery by formulating hypotheses, conducting experiments, and revising theories through observational analysis. Inspired by this, we propose to enhance the knowledge-driven, abstract reasoning abilities of LLMs with the computational strength of simulations. We introduce Scientific Generative Agent (SGA), a bilevel optimization framework: LLMs act as knowledgeable and versatile thinkers, proposing scientific hypotheses and reason about discrete components, such as physics equations or molecule structures; meanwhile, simulations function as experimental platforms, providing observational feedback and optimizing via differentiability for continuous parts, such as physical parameters. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate our framework’s efficacy in constitutive law discovery and molecular design, unveiling novel solutions that differ from conventional human expectations yet remain coherent upon analysis.

This paper builds that division of work into Scientific Generative Agent, or SGA. Its motivation is that language models offer scientific knowledge and abstract reasoning, but have difficulty generating and grounding the observational feedback needed for physical discovery.

SGA combines a language model with simulation in a bilevel optimization framework. The language model handles discrete choices, such as the form of a physical equation or a molecular structure. The simulator supplies observational feedback and uses differentiability to optimize continuous quantities, such as physical parameters. These roles connect structural hypotheses with numerical testing and adjustment.

Experiments examine constitutive-law discovery and molecular design. The authors report effective discovery and novel solutions that differ from conventional human expectations while remaining coherent under analysis. The approach matters because it gives generated hypotheses a computational testing process. Its stated findings concern discovery through this combination of language-based reasoning and simulation, with each component contributing a different kind of optimization.
summary.tldr: SGA pairs language-model hypothesis generation with differentiable simulation to optimize scientific structures and their continuous parameters.

title: LLM and Simulation as Bilevel Optimizers: A New Paradigm to Advance Physical Scientific Discovery

abstract: Bilevel optimization (BO) has recently gained prominence in many machine learning applications due to its ability to capture the nested structure inherent in these problems. Recently, many hypergradient methods have been proposed as effective solutions for solving large-scale problems. However, current hypergradient methods for the lower-level constrained bilevel optimization (LCBO) problems need very restrictive assumptions, namely, where optimality conditions satisfy the differentiability and invertibility conditions, and lack a solid analysis of the convergence rate. What’s worse, existing methods require either double-loop updates, which are sometimes less efficient. To solve this problem, in this paper, we propose a new hypergradient of LCBO leveraging the theory of nonsmooth implicit function theorem instead of using the restrive assumptions. In addition, we propose a single-loop single-timescale algorithm based on the double-momentum method and adaptive step size method and prove it can return a $(\delta, \epsilon)$-stationary point with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(d_2^2\epsilon^{-4})$ iterations. Experiments on two applications demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization contains one optimization problem inside another. When the inner problem has constraints, computing how its solution affects the outer objective becomes difficult. Existing hypergradient methods can depend on restrictive differentiability and invertibility conditions, and some use nested update loops that can reduce efficiency.

This paper derives a new hypergradient using a nonsmooth implicit function theorem. The approach replaces the restrictive conditions highlighted for earlier methods with a framework that accommodates nonsmooth behavior. The authors then build an algorithm combining double momentum with adaptive step sizes. It uses a single loop and a single timescale, simplifying the organization of updates across the nested problem.

The theoretical result bounds the iterations required to reach a specified approximate stationarity criterion. The stated bound is proportional to d₂ squared and ε to the negative fourth power, up to suppressed logarithmic factors. This is a guarantee about approximate stationarity rather than global optimality. Experiments on two applications also support the method's effectiveness, connecting the new gradient construction with a practical optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: A nonsmooth hypergradient enables a single-loop double-momentum algorithm with an iteration guarantee for constrained bilevel optimization.

title: Double Momentum Method for Lower-Level Constrained Bilevel Optimization

abstract: In-context learning is a powerful emergent ability in transformer models. Prior work in mechanistic interpretability has identified a circuit element that may be critical for in-context learning – the induction head (IH), which performs a match-and-copy operation. During training of large transformers on natural language data, IHs emerge around the same time as a notable phase change in the loss. Despite the robust evidence for IHs and this interesting coincidence with the phase change, relatively little is known about the diversity and emergence dynamics of IHs. Why is there more than one IH, and how are they dependent on each other? Why do IHs appear all of a sudden, and what are the subcircuits that enable them to emerge? We answer these questions by studying IH emergence dynamics in a controlled setting by training on synthetic data. In doing so, we develop and share a novel optogenetics-inspired causal framework for modifying activations throughout training. Using this framework, we delineate the diverse and additive nature of IHs. By "clamping" subsets of activations throughout training, we then identify three underlying subcircuits that interact to drive IH formation, yielding the phase change. Furthermore, these subcircuits shed light on data-dependent properties of formation, such as phase change timing, already showing the promise of this more in-depth understanding of subcircuits that need to "go right" for an induction head.

Their appearance during language-model training coincides with a marked change in loss. This paper investigates how these heads form, why several can coexist, and which underlying components enable their emergence.

The authors study transformers trained on synthetic data in a controlled setting. They develop a causal intervention framework inspired by optogenetics that modifies activations throughout training. By clamping selected activations, they can investigate how different parts of the developing computation contribute to the emergence of induction heads.

The analysis finds that induction heads are diverse and additive, and identifies three interacting subcircuits that drive their formation and the associated phase change. Those subcircuits also help explain data-dependent properties, including when the transition occurs. The contribution is a more detailed causal account of circuit formation in the controlled setting, moving from observing an abrupt training transition to investigating the interacting computations that produce it.
summary.tldr: Training-time activation interventions reveal three interacting subcircuits that drive induction-head formation and its associated phase change in a synthetic setting.

title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation

abstract: We tackle the problem of estimating risk measures of the infinite-horizon discounted cost of a Markov cost process. The risk measures we study include variance, Value-at-Risk (VaR), and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR). First, we show that estimating any of these risk measures with $\epsilon$-accuracy, either in expected or high-probability sense, requires at least $\Omega(1/\epsilon^2)$ samples. Then, using a truncation scheme, we derive an upper bound for the CVaR and variance estimation. This bound matches our lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Finally, we discuss an extension of our estimation scheme that covers more general risk measures satisfying a certain continuity criterion, such as spectral risk measures and utility-based shortfall risk. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to provide lower and upper bounds for estimating any risk measure beyond the mean within a Markovian setting. Our lower bounds also extend to the infinite-horizon discounted costs’ mean. Even in that case, our lower bound of $\Omega(1/\epsilon^2) $ improves upon the existing $\Omega(1/\epsilon)$ bound (Metelli et al. 2023.

paragraphs: The average cost of a process does not fully describe its variability or costly outcomes. This paper studies estimation of variance, Value-at-Risk, and Conditional Value-at-Risk for the infinite-horizon discounted cost of a Markov cost process. Its central question is how many samples are needed to estimate these quantities accurately.

The authors prove that achieving error ε requires at least order 1/ε² samples for each of these risk measures, whether accuracy is defined in expectation or with high probability. They then use a truncation scheme to obtain upper bounds for variance and Conditional Value-at-Risk estimation. Those bounds match the lower bound up to logarithmic factors, closely characterizing the sample requirements for these two measures.

The estimation scheme also extends to more general risk measures that satisfy a specified continuity criterion, including spectral measures and utility-based shortfall risk. The lower bound additionally applies to mean discounted cost, strengthening the previously stated order 1/ε bound. The result distinguishes unavoidable sampling difficulty from what an explicit estimation scheme can achieve, while keeping the broader extension conditional on continuity.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes risk-estimation sample lower bounds and nearly matching upper bounds for variance and CVaR in Markov cost processes.

title: Risk Estimation in a Markov Cost Process: Lower and Upper Bounds

abstract: Research on the theoretical expressiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has developed rapidly, and many methods have been proposed to enhance the expressiveness. However, most methods do not have a uniform expressiveness measure except for a few that strictly follow the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman ($k$-WL) test hierarchy, leading to difficulties in quantitatively comparing their expressiveness. Previous research has attempted to use datasets for measurement, but facing problems with difficulty (any model surpassing 1-WL has nearly 100% accuracy), granularity (models tend to be either 100% correct or near random guess), and scale (only several essentially different graphs involved). To address these limitations, we study the realized expressive power that a practical model instance can achieve using a novel expressiveness dataset, BREC, which poses greater difficulty (with up to 4-WL-indistinguishable graphs), finer granularity (enabling comparison of models between 1-WL and 3-WL), a larger scale (consisting of 800 1-WL-indistinguishable graphs that are non-isomorphic to each other). We synthetically test 23 models with higher-than-1-WL expressiveness on BREC. Our experiment gives the first thorough measurement of the realized expressiveness of those state-of-the-art beyond-1-WL GNN models and reveals the gap between theoretical and realized expressiveness. Dataset and evaluation codes are released at: https://github.com/GraphPKU/BREC.

paragraphs: A graph neural network’s theoretical expressiveness describes which graph structures it can potentially distinguish. Comparing that potential across architectures is difficult, and existing datasets often make practical comparisons uninformative: models either solve nearly everything or perform close to guessing. This paper instead measures realized expressiveness, meaning the distinctions that an actual model instance succeeds in making.

The authors introduce BREC, a dataset containing 800 mutually non-isomorphic graphs that the basic 1-WL graph comparison test cannot distinguish. It includes harder cases reaching beyond what 4-WL can distinguish, while also providing finer comparisons among models between the 1-WL and 3-WL levels. These properties address difficulty, measurement granularity, and dataset scale together.

The study evaluates 23 models whose theoretical expressiveness exceeds 1-WL. Its experiments reveal a gap between theoretical capabilities and realized performance. BREC therefore provides a way to examine whether stronger architectural expressiveness translates into usable distinctions in practice, rather than treating a theoretical position in an expressiveness hierarchy as a complete performance assessment.
summary.tldr: BREC benchmarks 23 expressive graph neural networks and reveals gaps between their theoretical distinguishing power and realized performance.

title: An Empirical Study of Realized GNN Expressiveness

abstract: With the advancement of neural networks, diverse methods for neural Granger causality have emerged, which demonstrate proficiency in handling complex data, and nonlinear relationships. However, the existing framework of neural Granger causality has several limitations. It requires the construction of separate predictive models for each target variable, and the relationship depends on the sparsity on the weights of the first layer, resulting in challenges in effectively modeling complex relationships between variables as well as unsatisfied estimation accuracy of Granger causality. Moreover, most of them cannot grasp full-time Granger causality. To address these drawbacks, we propose a Jacobian Regularizer-based Neural Granger Causality (JRNGC) approach, a straightforward yet highly effective method for learning multivariate summary Granger causality and full-time Granger causality by constructing a single model for all target variables. Specifically, our method eliminates the sparsity constraints of weights by leveraging an input-output Jacobian matrix regularizer, which can be subsequently represented as the weighted causal matrix in the post-hoc analysis. Extensive experiments show that our proposed approach achieves competitive performance with the state-of-the-art methods for learning summary Granger causality and full-time Granger causality while maintaining lower model complexity and high scalability.

paragraphs: JRNGC learns Granger-causal relationships among variables in multivariate time series. These relationships concern whether one variable’s history helps predict another. The authors target shortcomings in existing neural approaches, including the need for a separate predictive model for each target and the reliance on sparse first-layer weights to represent dependencies.

Their method uses one model for all target variables and regularizes its input-output Jacobian. The Jacobian describes how model outputs respond to changes in inputs, giving a way to express dependencies through the model’s behavior. This removes the need for the weight-sparsity constraints described in the existing framework. The resulting Jacobian can also be represented as a weighted causal matrix during post-hoc analysis.

The approach supports both summary Granger causality and full-time Granger causality, extending its scope beyond methods that capture only summary relationships. Experiments report performance competitive with leading methods while maintaining lower model complexity and high scalability. The contribution is a shared predictive model with a dependency regularizer tied directly to input-output sensitivity.
summary.tldr: JRNGC uses a single neural model and Jacobian regularization to learn multivariate Granger-causal dependencies.

title: Jacobian Regularizer-based Neural Granger Causality

abstract: We introduce the linear-transformation model, a distributed model of differentially private data analysis. Clients have access to a trusted platform capable of applying a public matrix to their inputs. Such computations can be securely distributed across multiple servers using simple and efficient secure multiparty computation techniques. The linear-transformation model serves as an intermediate model between the highly expressive central model and the minimal local model. In the central model, clients have access to a trusted platform capable of applying any function to their inputs. However, this expressiveness comes at a cost, as it is often expensive to distribute such computations, leading to the central model typically being implemented by a single trusted server. In contrast, the local model assumes no trusted platform, which forces clients to add significant noise to their data. The linear-transformation model avoids the single point of failure for privacy present in the central model, while also mitigating the high noise required in the local model. We demonstrate that linear transformations are very useful for differential privacy, allowing for the computation of linear sketches of input data. These sketches largely preserve utility for tasks such as private low-rank approximation and private ridge regression, while introducing only minimal error, critically independent of the number of clients.

paragraphs: Private data analysis faces a tradeoff between trust and noise. A central platform can perform arbitrary computations on client inputs, but distributing that flexibility securely can be expensive. Local privacy avoids a trusted platform by having clients protect their own data, at the cost of substantial noise. This paper introduces a model between these two arrangements.

In the linear-transformation model, the trusted capability is restricted to applying a public matrix to client inputs. The authors explain how this computation can be distributed securely across multiple servers using efficient secure multiparty computation. Restricting the available operation makes secure distribution more manageable while retaining a useful form of collective processing.

The resulting linear sketches support tasks including private low-rank approximation and private ridge regression. The paper reports that they largely preserve utility while introducing only small additional error that does not depend on the number of clients. The approach thus reduces reliance on a single trusted server while mitigating the noise burden associated with purely local analysis.
summary.tldr: A distributed privacy model based on public linear transformations enables useful data sketches with small error independent of client count.

title: Distributed Differentially Private Data Analytics via Secure Sketching

abstract: Designing learning agents that explore efficiently in a complex environment has been widely recognized as a fundamental challenge in reinforcement learning. While a number of works have demonstrated the effectiveness of techniques based on randomized value functions on a single agent, it remains unclear, from a theoretical point of view, whether injecting randomization can help a society of agents concurently explore an environment. The theoretical results established in this work tender an affirmative answer to this question. We adapt the concurrent learning framework to randomized least-squares value iteration (RLSVI) with aggregated state representation. We demonstrate polynomial worst-case regret bounds in both finite- and infinite-horizon environments. In both setups the per-agent regret decreases at an optimal rate of $\Theta\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\right)$, highlighting the advantage of concurent learning. Our algorithm exhibits significantly lower space complexity compared to Russo (2019) and Agrawal et. al (2021). We reduce the space complexity by a factor of $K$ while incurring only a $\sqrt{K}$ increase in the worst-case regret bound, compared to Russo (2019) and Agrawal et. al (2021). Interestingly, our algorithm improves the worst-case regret bound of Russo (2019) by a factor of $H^{1/2}$, matching the improvement in Agrawal et. al (2021). However, this result is achieved through a fundamentally different algorithmic enhancement and proof technique. Additionally, we conduct numerical experiments to demonstrate our theoretical findings.

The authors additionally obtain a square-root-of-H improvement over one earlier bound through a different algorithmic and proof approach. Numerical experiments accompany the theory, linking the formal analysis to observed behavior.
summary.tldr: Randomized value iteration with aggregated states gives concurrent agents provable exploration benefits and a quantified tradeoff between memory and regret.

title: Concurrent Reinforcement Learning with Aggregated States via Randomized Least Squares Value Iteration

abstract: Text-to-visual retrieval often struggles with semantic redundancy and granularity mismatches between textual queries and visual content. Unlike existing methods that address these challenges during training, we propose VISual Abstraction (VISA), a test-time approach that enhances retrieval by transforming visual content into textual descriptions using off-the-shelf large models. The generated text descriptions, with their dense semantics, naturally filter out low-level redundant visual information. To further address granularity issues, VISA incorporates a question-answering process, enhancing the text description with the specific granularity information requested by the user. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VISA brings substantial improvements in text-to-image and text-to-video retrieval for both short- and long-context queries, offering a plug-and-play enhancement to existing retrieval systems.

paragraphs: Searching for images or videos using text can fail when visual content contains distracting detail or represents information at a different level of specificity from the query. This paper introduces VISA, a test-time method for addressing both problems. It uses existing large models to convert visual content into textual descriptions.

Those descriptions concentrate semantic information and filter out low-level visual redundancy. VISA then adds a question-answering process to refine the descriptions with details at the granularity requested by the user. The approach therefore combines a general textual abstraction of the content with information tailored to what the query is asking.

Experiments report substantial improvements in both image and video retrieval, across short and long queries. Because the method operates at test time, the authors position it as a plug-and-play addition to existing retrieval systems. The contribution is a way to improve matching through the representation used during retrieval: descriptions emphasize meaning, while query-guided questions help align the level of detail between the request and the visual content.
summary.tldr: VISA improves image and video retrieval at test time by generating textual descriptions and refining them with query-specific questions.

title: Visual Abstraction: A Plug-and-Play Approach for Text-Visual Retrieval

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) has enjoyed great success in machine learning as a principled way to align datasets via a least-cost correspondence, driven in large part by the runtime efficiency of the Sinkhorn algorithm (Cuturi, 2013). However, Sinkhorn has quadratic space and time complexity in the number of points, limiting scalability to larger datasets. Low-rank OT achieves linear complexity, but by definition, cannot compute a one-to-one correspondence between points. When the optimal transport problem is an assignment problem between datasets then an optimal mapping, known as the Monge map, is guaranteed to be a bijection. In this setting, we show that the factors of an optimal low-rank coupling co-cluster each point with its image under the Monge map. We leverage this invariant to derive an algorithm, Hierarchical Refinement (HiRef), that dynamically constructs a multiscale partition of each dataset using low-rank OT subproblems, culminating in the bijective Monge map. Hierarchical Refinement runs in log-linear time and linear space, retaining the advantages of low-rank OT while overcoming its limited resolution. We demonstrate the advantages of Hierarchical Refinement on several datasets, including ones containing over a million points, scaling full-rank OT to problems previously beyond Sinkhorn’s reach.

Low-rank approaches reduce complexity to linear, but their compressed representation cannot directly express a one-to-one correspondence between individual points.

Demonstrations include datasets with more than a million points, showing that the approach can extend full-rank transport to problem sizes previously beyond Sinkhorn's reach in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Refinement uses low-rank transport subproblems to recover bijective optimal assignments in log-linear time and linear space.

title: Hierarchical Refinement: Optimal Transport to Infinity and Beyond

abstract: Existing approaches based on context prompting or reinforcement learning (RL) to improve the reasoning capacities of large language models (LLMs) depend on the LLMs’ internal knowledge to produce reliable Chain-Of-Thought (CoT). However, no matter the size of LLMs, certain problems cannot be resolved in a single forward pass. Meanwhile, agent-based reasoning systems require access to a comprehensive nonparametric knowledge base, which is often costly or not feasible for use in scientific and niche domains. We present Graph Inspired Veracity Extrapolation (GIVE), a novel reasoning method that merges parametric and non-parametric memories to improve accurate reasoning with minimal external input. GIVE guides the LLM agent to select the most pertinent expert data ($\textbf{observe}$), engage in query-specific associative thinking ($\textbf{reflect}$), and then synthesize this information to produce the final output ($\textbf{speak}$). Extensive experiments demonstrated the following benefits of our framework: (1) GIVE increases the performance of LLMs across various sizes. (2) In some scenarios, GIVE allows smaller LLMs to surpass larger, more sophisticated ones in scientific tasks ($\textbf{GPT3.5T + GIVE > GPT4}$). (3) GIVE is effective on scientific and open-domain assessments. (4) GIVE is a training-free method that enables LLMs to tackle new problems that extend beyond their training data (up to $\textbf{43.5}$% $\rightarrow$ $\textbf{88.2}$% accuracy improvement). (5) GIVE allows LLM agents to reason using both restricted (very small) and noisy (very large) knowledge sources, accommodating knowledge graphs (KG) ranging from $\textbf{135}$ to more than $\textbf{840k}$ nodes. (6) The reasoning process involved in GIVE is fully interpretable. Our code is available at https://github.com/Jason-Tree/GIVE

paragraphs: GIVE addresses reasoning tasks where a language model’s internal knowledge is insufficient and a comprehensive external knowledge base may be expensive or unavailable. It combines information stored in model parameters with external knowledge, aiming to improve reasoning while requiring only limited outside input. The method works without additional model training.

Its reasoning process has three stages. The agent first selects relevant expert information, then develops associations specific to the query, and finally combines that information into an answer. This observe-reflect-speak structure organizes how internal and external knowledge contribute to the result. The authors describe the resulting reasoning process as fully interpretable.

title: GIVE: Structured Reasoning of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graph Inspired Veracity Extrapolation

abstract: Ainsworth et al. empirically demonstrated that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can be achieved between two independently trained neural networks (NNs) by applying an appropriate parameter permutation. LMC is satisfied if a linear path with non-increasing test loss exists between the models, suggesting that NNs trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) converge to a single approximately convex low-loss basin under permutation symmetries. However, Ainsworth et al. verified LMC for two models and provided only limited discussion on its extension to multiple models. In this paper, we conduct a more detailed empirical analysis. First, we show that existing permutation search methods designed for two models can fail to transfer multiple models into the same convex low-loss basin. Next, we propose a permutation search method using a straight-through estimator for multiple models (STE-MM). We then experimentally demonstrate that even when multiple models are given, the test loss of the merged model remains nearly the same as the losses of the original models when using STE-MM, and the loss barriers between all permuted model pairs are also small. Additionally, from the perspective of the trace of the Hessian matrix, we show that the loss sharpness around the merged model decreases as the number of models increases with STE-MM, indicating that LMC for multiple models is more likely to hold. The source code implementing our method is available at https://github.com/e5-a/STE-MM.

paragraphs: Independently trained networks can use different parameter orderings while representing comparable solutions. Permuting their parameters can reveal low-loss linear connections that were previously hidden. This paper asks whether methods that align two networks also place several networks together in an approximately convex region of low test loss.

The empirical analysis finds that existing pairwise permutation-search methods can fail at this multi-model task. The authors introduce STE-MM, which searches for permutations across multiple models using a straight-through estimator. In their experiments, merging models aligned this way produces test loss close to that of the original models, while loss barriers between every aligned pair remain small.

The authors additionally examine local loss sharpness through the trace of the Hessian matrix. With STE-MM, sharpness around the merged model decreases as more models are included. These observations provide empirical support for multi-model linear connectivity after suitable alignment. They also show why successful alignment of an individual pair does not automatically establish compatible alignment for an entire collection.
summary.tldr: STE-MM jointly aligns multiple networks through parameter permutations, empirically enabling low-loss merging and small barriers between aligned model pairs.

title: Linear Mode Connectivity between Multiple Models modulo Permutation Symmetries

abstract: Process and outcome supervision represent two fundamental approaches to reinforcement learning, especially for complex reasoning tasks in large language models. While process supervision offers intuitive advantages for long-term credit assignment, the precise relationship between these paradigms has remained an open question. Conventional wisdom suggests that outcome supervision is fundamentally more challenging due to the trajectory-level coverage problem, leading to significant investment in collecting fine-grained process supervision data. In this paper, we provide a possible theoretical resolution to this debate. Perhaps surprisingly, our main theorem shows that: under standard data coverage assumptions, reinforcement learning through outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult than through process supervision. At the core of this result lies the novel Change of Trajectory Measure Lemma—a powerful technical tool that bridges return-based trajectory measure and step-level distribution shift. Furthermore, for settings with access to a verifier or a rollout capability, we prove that any policy’s advantage function can serve as an optimal process reward model, providing a simple yet powerful connection between outcome and process supervision. These findings suggest that the empirically observed performance gap between outcome and process supervision likely stems from algorithmic limitations rather than inherent statistical difficulties, potentially transforming how we approach data and algorithm design for reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Process supervision evaluates intermediate steps, while outcome supervision evaluates the overall result. For reasoning tasks, step-level feedback seems helpful because it identifies which decisions contributed to success. This paper asks whether outcome-only feedback is inherently more statistically difficult, or whether practical performance differences can arise from the algorithms used.

The main theorem states that, under standard data coverage assumptions, reinforcement learning with outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult than with process supervision. The proof uses a new Change of Trajectory Measure Lemma to connect return-based measures over complete trajectories with distribution shifts at individual steps. The data coverage condition is central to the stated result.

A second result applies when a verifier or rollout capability is available: any policy’s advantage function can serve as an optimal process reward model. This establishes a theoretical connection between outcome information and useful intermediate feedback. The findings suggest that observed performance gaps likely reflect algorithmic limitations rather than inherent statistical difficulty, motivating attention to algorithm design alongside the collection of step-level labels.
summary.tldr: Under standard data coverage assumptions, outcome supervision is no more statistically difficult than process supervision in the paper’s theoretical analysis.

title: Do We Need to Verify Step by Step? Rethinking Process Supervision from a Theoretical Perspective

abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has shown promise in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by generating natural language (NL) rationales that lead to the final answer. However, it struggles with numerical computation, which has somehow led to the development of program-aided techniques. Despite their potential, a persistent challenge remains: inconsistencies between LLM-reported reasoning steps and the logic in generated programs, which we term “reasoning hallucinations." This stems from the inherent ambiguities of NL and the statistical nature of LLMs, which often lack rigorous logical coherence. To address this challenge, we propose a novel test-time scaling framework, Reasoning-as-Logic-Units (RaLU), which constructs a more reliable reasoning path by aligning logical units between the generated program and their corresponding NL descriptions. By decomposing the initially generated program into discrete units using static analysis, RaLU engages in an iterative dialogue with the LLM to judge, refine, and explain each unit. A rewind-and-correct mechanism ensures alignment between code statements and task requirements in each unit, ultimately forming a cohesive reasoning path under the program’s logic, from which the model reaches a final solution. Our experiments demonstrate that RaLU significantly outperforms existing baselines in mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH) and algorithmic reasoning (HumanEval+, MBPP+), underscoring its potential to advance LLM reasoning and programming by offering enhanced accuracy and interpretability.

Experiments report significant improvements over existing baselines on mathematical reasoning tasks GSM8K and MATH, and algorithmic reasoning tasks HumanEval+ and MBPP+. These results support spending additional inference effort on local alignment between code and explanations. The method's interpretability contribution is to organize the solution around inspectable program units, making the connection between stated reasoning and implemented operations more explicit.
summary.tldr: RaLU improves reasoning by iteratively aligning small program units with their explanations and the task requirements.

title: Reasoning-as-Logic-Units: Scaling Test-Time Reasoning in Large Language Models Through Logic Unit Alignment

abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning faces significant challenges in effectively organizing agent relationships and facilitating information exchange, particularly when agents need to adapt their coordination patterns dynamically. This paper presents a novel framework that integrates dynamic spectral clustering with hypergraph neural networks to enable adaptive group formation and efficient information processing in multi-agent systems. The proposed framework dynamically constructs and updates hypergraph structures through spectral clustering on agents’ state histories, enabling higher-order relationships to emerge naturally from agent interactions. The hypergraph structure is enhanced with attention mechanisms for selective information processing, providing an expressive and efficient way to model complex agent relationships. This architecture can be implemented in both value-based and policy-based paradigms through a unified objective combining task performance with structural regularization. Extensive experiments on challenging cooperative tasks demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in both sample efficiency and final performance. The code is available at: https://github.com/mysteryelder/HYGMA.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents need to decide both whom to coordinate with and what information to exchange. These relationships may change as a task unfolds. HYGMA addresses this problem by combining dynamic grouping with a hypergraph neural network, allowing the representation of coordination to adapt to the agents’ interactions.

The framework applies spectral clustering to histories of agent states and uses the resulting groups to construct and update a hypergraph. Hypergraphs represent relationships involving groups of agents, giving the model a way to capture coordination beyond individual pairs. Attention mechanisms then selectively process information within this structure, helping the network focus on relevant relationships.

HYGMA combines task performance and structural regularization in one training objective. The architecture supports both value-based and policy-based reinforcement learning, extending its use across two learning paradigms. Experiments on challenging cooperative tasks show significant improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods in sample efficiency and final performance. The results support adapting the organization of agent relationships as part of learning, alongside learning the actions themselves.
summary.tldr: HYGMA dynamically groups cooperating agents and models their group relationships with attention-enhanced hypergraphs, improving efficiency and performance.

title: HYGMA: Hypergraph Coordination Networks with Dynamic Grouping for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Is there really much more to say about sparse autoencoders (SAEs)? Autoencoders in general, and SAEs in particular, represent deep architectures that are capable of modeling low-dimensional latent structure in data. Such structure could reflect, among other things, correlation patterns in large language model activations, or complex natural image manifolds. And yet despite the wide-ranging applicability, there have been relatively few changes to SAEs beyond the original recipe from decades ago, namely, standard deep encoder/decoder layers trained with a classical/deterministic sparse regularizer applied within the latent space. One possible exception is the variational autoencoder (VAE), which adopts a stochastic encoder module capable of producing sparse representations when applied to manifold data. In this work we formalize underappreciated weaknesses with both canonical SAEs, as well as analogous VAEs applied to similar tasks, and propose a hybrid alternative model that circumvents these prior limitations. In terms of theoretical support, we prove that global minima of our proposed model recover certain forms of structured data spread across a union of manifolds. Meanwhile, empirical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets substantiate the efficacy of our approach in accurately estimating underlying manifold dimensions and producing sparser latent representations without compromising reconstruction error. In general, we are able to exceed the performance of equivalent-capacity SAEs and VAEs, as well as recent diffusion models where applicable, within domains such as images and language model activation patterns.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders aim to represent data using a compact set of active latent features. This paper revisits their ability to capture low-dimensional structure, including natural-image structure and patterns in language-model activations. The authors formalize weaknesses in conventional sparse autoencoders and in related variational autoencoders applied to these tasks, then propose a hybrid alternative.

The theoretical result concerns global minima of the proposed model: they recover certain forms of structured data distributed across a union of manifolds. The qualification matters because the guarantee applies to specified data structures and global solutions. It provides a formal connection between the model's objective and recovery of the underlying structure.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support more accurate estimates of manifold dimensions and sparser latent representations without worsening reconstruction error. The authors report stronger performance than equal-capacity sparse and variational autoencoders, and than recent diffusion models where applicable. Across images and language-model activation patterns, the results support revisiting the modeling recipe behind sparse representations.
summary.tldr: A hybrid autoencoder improves latent sparsity and manifold estimation, with structured-data recovery guarantees at global minima.

title: Sparse Autoencoders, Again?

abstract: Interpretability is crucial for ensuring RL systems align with human values. However, it remains challenging to achieve in complex decision making domains. Existing methods frequently attempt interpretability at the level of fundamental model units, such as neurons or decision nodes: an approach which scales poorly to large models. Here, we instead propose an approach to interpretability at the level of functional modularity. We show how encouraging sparsity and locality in network weights leads to the emergence of functional modules in RL policy networks. To detect these modules, we develop an extended Louvain algorithm which uses a novel ‘correlation alignment’ metric to overcome the limitations of standard network analysis techniques when applied to neural network architectures. Applying these methods to 2D and 3D MiniGrid environments reveals the consistent emergence of distinct navigational modules for different axes, and we further demonstrate how these functions can be validated through direct interventions on network weights prior to inference.

paragraphs: Understanding a reinforcement learning policy one neuron at a time becomes difficult as models grow. This paper instead studies groups of network components that carry out recognizable functions. Its proposed pipeline addresses three connected tasks: encouraging such modules to emerge, finding them within a trained network, and checking what roles they perform.

The authors encourage sparsity and locality in network weights, which leads to functional modules in the policy networks they study. To identify the modules, they extend the Louvain community-detection algorithm with a correlation alignment metric. The extension addresses limitations that standard network analysis methods encounter when applied to neural network architectures.

In two-dimensional and three-dimensional MiniGrid environments, the method consistently reveals separate navigation modules associated with different axes. The authors then intervene directly on network weights before inference to validate the modules’ functions. This links structural groupings to changes in policy behavior and supports functional modules as a useful scale for interpreting the tested reinforcement learning systems.
summary.tldr: A pipeline encourages, detects, and experimentally validates functional navigation modules in reinforcement learning policy networks.

title: Inducing, Detecting and Characterising Neural Modules: A Pipeline for Functional Interpretability in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Subgraph representation learning has attracted growing interest due to its wide applications in various domains. However, existing methods primarily focus on local neighborhood structures while overlooking the significant impact of global structural information, in particular the influence of multi-hop neighbors beyond immediate neighborhoods. This presents two key challenges: how to effectively capture the structural relationships between distant nodes, and how to prevent excessive aggregation of global structural information from weakening the discriminative ability of subgraph representations. To address these challenges, we propose GPEN (Global Position Encoding Network). GPEN leverages a hierarchical tree structure to encode each node’s global position based on its path distance to the root node, enabling a systematic way to capture relationships between distant nodes. Furthermore, we introduce a boundary-aware convolution module that selectively integrates global structural information while maintaining the unique structural patterns of each subgraph. Extensive experiments on eight public datasets identify that GPEN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in subgraph representation learning.

paragraphs: A subgraph's meaning can depend on its position within the larger graph, including relationships beyond its immediate neighborhood. Methods that emphasize local structure may overlook this information. However, aggregating too much global information can also blur the structural differences that make individual subgraphs distinguishable.

GPEN addresses these two concerns with complementary components. It uses a hierarchical tree to encode each node's global position through its path distance to the root. This provides a systematic representation of relationships involving distant nodes. A boundary-aware convolution module then selectively incorporates global structure while preserving the distinctive patterns within each subgraph.

The design matters because access to broader graph context and preservation of local identity are treated as separate requirements. Position encoding supplies distant structural information, while selective integration controls how that information affects the subgraph representation. Experiments on eight public datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the usefulness of incorporating global position without allowing broad aggregation to overwhelm the structure being represented.
summary.tldr: GPEN combines global position encoding with boundary-aware convolution to improve subgraph representations while preserving their distinctive structure.

title: GPEN: Global Position Encoding Network for Enhanced Subgraph Representation Learning

abstract: Current fake image detectors trained on large synthetic image datasets perform satisfactorily on limited studied generative models. However, these detectors suffer a notable performance decline over unseen models. Besides, collecting adequate training data from online generative models is often expensive or infeasible. To overcome these issues, we propose Few-Shot Detector (FSD), a novel AI-generated image detector which learns a specialized metric space for effectively distinguishing unseen fake images using very few samples. Experiments show that FSD achieves state-of-the-art performance by $+11.6%$ average accuracy on the GenImage dataset with only $10$ additional samples. More importantly, our method is better capable of capturing the intra-category commonality in unseen images without further training. Our code is available at https://github.com/teheperinko541/Few-Shot-AIGI-Detector.

Experiments show that FSD achieves state-of-the-art performance by $+11.6%$ average accuracy on the GenImage dataset with only $10$ additional samples. More importantly, our method is better capable of capturing the intra-category commonality in unseen images without further training. Our code is available at https://github.com/teheperinko541/Few-Shot-AIGI-Detector.

paragraphs: An image detector can perform well on the generators represented in its training data yet struggle with images from an unseen generator. Gathering a large new synthetic dataset may also be expensive or infeasible, particularly for online generative models. This paper addresses both issues by making small amounts of additional data useful for detection.

The proposed Few-Shot Detector, or FSD, learns a specialized metric space for distinguishing AI-generated images. The central idea is to learn a representation in which very few samples can support detection of previously unseen fake images. The researchers also report that the method better captures common characteristics within categories of unseen images without requiring further training.

On GenImage, the experiments report a state-of-the-art result with an average accuracy improvement of 11.6% using only 10 additional samples. This finding supports the paper's emphasis on sample-efficient generalization across generators. The result is tied to the evaluated setting, while the broader methodological contribution is a learned comparison space that makes limited new examples more informative for image detection.
summary.tldr: FSD learns a metric space that supports detection of images from unseen generators using very few additional samples.

title: Few-Shot Learner Generalizes Across AI-Generated Image Detection

abstract: Identifying the most representative subset for a close-to-submodular objective while satisfying the predefined partition constraint is a fundamental task with numerous applications in machine learning. However, the existing distorted local-search methods are often hindered by their prohibitive query complexities and the rigid requirement for prior knowledge of difficult-to-obtain structural parameters. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel algorithm titled Multinoulli-SCG, which not only is parameter-free, but also can achieve the same approximation guarantees as the distorted local-search methods with significantly fewer function evaluations. The core of our Multinoulli-SCG algorithm is an innovative continuous-relaxation framework named Multinoulli Extension(ME), which can effectively convert the discrete subset selection problem subject to partition constraints into a solvable continuous maximization focused on learning the optimal multinoulli priors across the considered partition. In sharp contrast with the well-established multi-linear extension for submodular subset selection, a notable advantage of our proposed ME is its intrinsic capacity to provide a lossless rounding scheme for any set function. Finally, we validate the practical efficacy of our proposed algorithms by applying them to video summarization, bayesian A-optimal design and coverage maximization.

The contribution combines a broadly applicable rounding property with an algorithmic improvement for the stated constrained selection setting.

title: Multinoulli Extension: A Lossless Yet Effective Probabilistic Framework for Subset Selection over Partition Constraints

abstract: We introduce SWE-Flow, a novel data synthesis framework grounded in Test-Driven Development (TDD). Unlike existing software engineering data that rely on human-submitted issues, SWE-Flow automatically infers incremental development steps directly from unit tests, which inherently encapsulate high-level requirements. The core of SWE-Flow is the construction of a Runtime Dependency Graph (RDG), which precisely captures function interactions, enabling the generation of a structured, step-by-step development schedule. At each step, SWE-Flow produces a partial codebase, the corresponding unit tests, and the necessary code modifications, resulting in fully verifiable TDD tasks. With this approach, we generated 16,061 training instances and 2,020 test instances from real-world GitHub projects, creating the SWE-Flow-Eval benchmark. Our experiments show that fine-tuning open model on this dataset significantly improves performance in TDD-based coding. To facilitate further research, we release all code, datasets, models, and Docker images at Github.

paragraphs: SWE-Flow creates software engineering tasks from unit tests, using the requirements encoded in those tests to infer incremental development steps. This provides a source of training data that does not depend on human-submitted issue descriptions. The framework follows test-driven development, organizing each task around tests and the code changes needed to satisfy them.

Its central representation is a Runtime Dependency Graph that captures interactions between functions. From this graph, SWE-Flow constructs an ordered development schedule. At each step, it supplies a partial codebase, relevant unit tests, and the required modifications. The findings support using existing tests and runtime dependencies to synthesize structured, verifiable development tasks for both training and evaluation.
summary.tldr: SWE-Flow turns unit tests and runtime dependencies into verifiable development tasks that improve test-driven coding after fine-tuning.

title: Synthesizing Software Engineering Data in a Test-Driven Manner

abstract: Long-tailed distribution datasets are prevalent in many machine learning tasks, yet existing neural network models still face significant challenges when handling such data. This paper proposes a novel adaptive pruning strategy, LTAP (Long-Tailed Adaptive Pruner), aimed at balancing model efficiency and performance to better address the challenges posed by long-tailed data distributions. LTAP introduces multi-dimensional importance scoring criteria and designs a dynamic weight adjustment mechanism to adaptively determine the pruning priority of parameters for different classes. By focusing on protecting parameters critical for tail classes, LTAP significantly enhances computational efficiency while maintaining model performance. This method combines the strengths of long-tailed learning and neural network pruning, overcoming the limitations of existing approaches in handling imbalanced data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LTAP outperforms existing methods on various long-tailed datasets, achieving a good balance between model compression rate, computational efficiency, and classification accuracy. This research provides new insights into solving model optimization problems in long-tailed learning and is significant for improving the performance of neural networks on imbalanced datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/DataLab-atom/LT-VOTE.

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network becomes especially delicate when some classes have many examples and others have very few. Parameters that appear less important overall may still matter for those rare classes. This paper introduces Long-Tailed Adaptive Pruner, or LTAP, to make pruning decisions sensitive to that imbalance while pursuing a smaller, more efficient model.

LTAP scores parameter importance along multiple dimensions and dynamically adjusts the weights used in those scores. This lets it adapt which parameters receive priority for removal according to their importance for different classes. Protecting parameters needed by tail classes is central to the approach: compression decisions explicitly account for the parts of the classification problem that have fewer examples.

The reported experiments show LTAP outperforming existing methods across several long-tailed datasets while balancing compression, computation, and classification accuracy. The practical contribution is a way to connect efficiency decisions with class-specific needs. Its findings support treating class imbalance as part of the pruning problem itself, since maintaining performance requires attention to which capabilities survive compression.
summary.tldr: LTAP adapts parameter pruning to protect rare classes while improving model efficiency and preserving classification performance.

title: Balancing Model Efficiency and Performance: Adaptive Pruner for Long-tailed Data

abstract: Evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) is very expensive, due to high computational cost and the wide variety of tasks. The good news is that if we already have some observed performance scores, we may be able to infer unknown ones. In this study, we propose a new framework for predicting unknown performance scores based on observed ones from other LVLMs or tasks. We first formulate the performance prediction as a matrix completion task. Specifically, we construct a sparse performance matrix $\boldsymbol{R}$, where each entry $R_{mn}$ represents the performance score of the $m$-th model on the $n$-th dataset. By applying probabilistic matrix factorization (PMF) with Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we can complete the performance matrix, i.e., predict unknown scores. Additionally, we estimate the uncertainty of performance prediction based on MCMC. Practitioners can evaluate their models on untested tasks with higher uncertainty first, which quickly reduces the prediction errors. We further introduce several improvements to enhance PMF for scenarios with sparse observed performance scores. Our experiments demonstrate the accuracy of PMF in predicting unknown scores, the reliability of uncertainty estimates in ordering evaluations, and the effectiveness of our enhancements for handling sparse data. Our code is available at https://github.com/Qinyu-Allen-Zhao/CrossPred-LVLM.

paragraphs: Evaluating every large vision-language model on every relevant task can be expensive. This paper asks whether scores already collected for some model-task combinations can help predict the missing ones. It organizes the available evidence into a sparse matrix, with models along one dimension, datasets along the other, and measured performance in the filled entries.

The proposed framework uses probabilistic matrix factorization to infer missing scores from patterns in that matrix. Markov chain Monte Carlo supplies both predictions and estimates of their uncertainty. That uncertainty has a practical role: evaluators can prioritize untested tasks whose predicted scores are less certain, adding measurements that help reduce subsequent prediction errors.

The authors also modify the factorization approach for cases where very few scores are available. Experiments support the accuracy of the inferred scores, the usefulness of uncertainty for ordering evaluations, and the improvements under sparse observations. The contribution therefore combines performance estimation with a strategy for deciding what to measure next, making existing evaluation results more useful for planning further evaluations.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic matrix completion predicts missing vision-language evaluation scores and uses uncertainty to prioritize further testing.

title: Can We Predict Performance of Large Models across Vision-Language Tasks?

abstract: Recent work suggests that (stochastic) gradient descent self-organizes near the instability boundary, shaping both optimization and the solutions found. Momentum and mini-batch gradients are widely used in practical deep learning optimization, but it remains unclear whether they operate in a comparable regime of instability. We demonstrate that SGD with momentum exhibits an Edge of Stochastic Stability (EoSS)-like regime with batch-size–dependent behavior that cannot be explained by a single momentum-adjusted stability threshold. Batch Sharpness (the expected directional mini-batch curvature) stabilizes in two distinct regimes: at small batch sizes it converges to a lower plateau $2(1-\beta)/\eta$, reflecting amplification of stochastic fluctuations by momentum and favoring flatter regions than vanilla SGD; at large batch sizes it converges to a higher plateau $2(1+\beta)/\eta$, where momentum recovers its classical stabilizing effect and favors sharper regions consistent with full-batch dynamics. We further show this aligns with linear stability thresholds and we discuss the implications on hyperparameters tuning and coupling.

paragraphs: Gradient-based training can operate near the boundary where updates become unstable. This paper studies how momentum changes that behavior when gradients are estimated from mini-batches. Its central finding is that batch size determines which stability regime appears, so a single momentum-adjusted threshold does not explain the observed behavior.

The authors track Batch Sharpness, the expected curvature along mini-batch update directions. For small batches, it settles near 2(1−β)/η, where β is momentum and η is the learning rate. In this regime, momentum amplifies stochastic fluctuations and favors flatter regions than ordinary SGD. For large batches, the plateau is instead 2(1+β)/η, consistent with momentum’s classical stabilizing effect and sharper regions.

These two plateaus align with linear stability thresholds. The result connects noisy mini-batch training and full-batch-like dynamics within one account, while emphasizing their different responses to momentum. It also explains why learning rate, momentum, and batch size should be considered together when tuning: their interaction determines which curvature constraint governs the observed training regime.
summary.tldr: Momentum produces distinct small- and large-batch sharpness plateaus, revealing two different stochastic stability regimes.

title: Momentum Further Constrains Sharpness at the Edge of Stochastic Stability

abstract: The generalized Ising problem captures a broad spectrum of hard combinatorial problems, including MAX-CUT, Number Partitioning (NPP), and Maximum Independent Set. In this work, we consider the notion of one-flip local minima for this problem. We construct a polynomial relaxation and prove the landscape equivalence theorem: there exists a one-to-one correspondence between the local minima of the relaxation and the one-flip local minima of the original Ising problem. This guarantee reduces the Ising problem to finding the local minima of a smooth function, allowing us to leverage scalable gradient-based optimizers such as ADAM. We demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance across challenging benchmarks, including spin-glass models, MAX-CUT, and NPP.

paragraphs: Many difficult discrete optimization problems can be expressed as generalized Ising problems, including MAX-CUT, number partitioning, and maximum independent set. This paper focuses on one-flip local minima: configurations whose objective cannot be improved by changing just one variable. The challenge is to connect these discrete solutions to a smooth objective that gradient-based methods can search.

The authors construct a polynomial relaxation and prove a landscape-equivalence theorem. Every local minimum of the relaxed function corresponds to a one-flip local minimum of the original Ising problem, and the correspondence works in both directions. This gives the continuous landscape a precise relationship to the discrete one, rather than merely hoping that solutions transfer usefully after relaxation.

The smooth formulation permits scalable optimizers such as ADAM, and experiments report strong performance on spin-glass, MAX-CUT, and number-partitioning benchmarks. The guarantee concerns local minima, so it does not make every recovered solution globally optimal. Its significance is preserving a meaningful discrete notion of local optimality while opening the problem to gradient-based optimization.
summary.tldr: A polynomial relaxation exactly matches its local minima to one-flip Ising minima, enabling gradient-based search with a precise discrete interpretation.

title: Local-Minima-Preserving Polynomial Relaxation of Ising Problems

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard for privacy-preserving LLM fine-tuning. However, existing personalized methods predominantly operated under a restrictive Flat-Model Assumption: they addressed client-side statistical heterogeneity but treated the model as a monolithic block, ignoring the functional heterogeneity across LLM layers. We argue that these two statistical (horizontal) and functional (vertical) dimensions, are orthogonal in source yet coupled in interaction, implying that the optimal depth of parameter sharing is functionally dependent on client similarity. To address this, we propose FedTreeLoRA, a framework employing tree-structured aggregation for fine-grained, layer-wise alignment. By dynamically constructing an aggregation hierarchy, FedTreeLoRA allows clients to share broad consensus on shallow ’trunks‘ while progressively specializing on deep ‘branches’. Experiments on NLU and NLG benchmarks demonstrate that FedTreeLoRA significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods by effectively reconciling generalization and personalization.

paragraphs: Personalized federated fine-tuning must account for differences between clients’ data. This paper argues that it must also account for differences between the functions performed by language-model layers. Treating the entire model as a single block overlooks how those two kinds of variation interact.

FedTreeLoRA organizes the aggregation of low-rank adaptation parameters into a tree. The hierarchy is constructed dynamically so that clients share broader consensus in shallow layers and become progressively more specialized in deeper layers. The guiding idea is that the appropriate depth of sharing depends on client similarity, allowing the aggregation structure to reflect both data differences and layer roles.

Experiments on natural-language-understanding and natural-language-generation benchmarks report significant gains over state-of-the-art methods. The authors attribute these improvements to a better reconciliation of generalization and personalization. The contribution is a finer-grained sharing mechanism: the framework can represent broad agreement among clients while accommodating increasingly specific adaptations across deeper parts of the model.
summary.tldr: FedTreeLoRA dynamically organizes federated parameter sharing into a tree that combines shallow consensus with deeper client specialization.

title: FedTreeLoRA: Reconciling Statistical and Functional Heterogeneity in Federated LoRA Fine-Tuning

abstract: Open-vocabulary navigation requires embodied agents to manage significant perception uncertainty stemming from semantic ambiguity and model errors. However, most existing works settle for local optimal deterministic approaches, depriving complex navigation decision-making over multiple composite possibilities that are critical for globally better solutions. In this paper, we propose Probabilistic Scene Graph Navigation (PSG-Nav), which constructs a 3D Probabilistic Scene Graph that uses full semantic categorical distributions to account for perception uncertainty. To efficiently use the local distributions to compose and reason about the optimal navigation landmarks, we propose Multiverse Decision to sample multiple most likely world settings from the joint distribution, and evaluate navigation landmarks based on the compatibility between landmarks and multiverses. To mitigate false positives due to epistemic uncertainty in open-vocabulary navigation, we introduce the Evidential Experience Calibrator, which enables online lifelong adaptation by cross-validating detections against memories of past successes and failures. Extensive experiments on widely-used benchmarks MP3D, HM3D, and HSSD demonstrate that PSG-Nav establishes new state-of-the-art results, achieving Success Rates of 66.1%, 44.8%, and 67.9%, respectively. Code is available at: https://psg-nav.github.io

paragraphs: PSG-Nav addresses navigation when an embodied agent is uncertain about the semantic identity of what it sees. Ambiguous observations and model errors can make a single confident interpretation misleading. The method constructs a three-dimensional scene graph that retains categorical probability distributions over semantic interpretations.

Its Multiverse Decision component samples several likely world configurations from the joint distribution. It then evaluates candidate navigation landmarks according to their compatibility with those possible worlds. This allows a navigation decision to reflect combinations of uncertain interpretations. An additional Evidential Experience Calibrator checks detections against memories of previous successes and failures, supporting ongoing adaptation and reducing false positives associated with model uncertainty.

The authors evaluate PSG-Nav on MP3D, HM3D, and HSSD and report new state-of-the-art success rates of 66.1%, 44.8%, and 67.9%, respectively. These results support retaining uncertainty throughout scene representation and landmark selection. The memory component adds a complementary source of evidence by incorporating what the agent has learned from past navigation outcomes.
summary.tldr: PSG-Nav improves navigation by reasoning across probable scene interpretations and calibrating detections using past successes and failures.

title: PSG-Nav: Probabilistic Scene Graph Navigation via Multiverse Decision Making

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) training is prohibitively expensive, driving interest in low-precision fully-quantized training (FQT). While novel 4-bit formats like NVFP4 offer substantial efficiency gains, achieving near-lossless training at such low precision remains challenging. We introduce TetraJet-v2, an end-to-end 4-bit FQT method that leverages NVFP4 for activations, weights and gradients in all linear layers. We identify two critical issues hindering low-precision LLM training: weight oscillation and outliers. To address these, we propose: 1) an unbiased double-block quantization method for NVFP4 linear layers, 2) OsciReset, an algorithm to suppress weight oscillation, and 3) OutControl, an algorithm to retain outlier accuracy. TetraJet-v2 outperforms prior methods on FP4 pre-training for LLMs across models up to 370M parameters trained up to 212B tokens, reducing the performance gap to BF16 by an average of $51.3$% while enabling an $1.67\times$ end-to-end speedup over FP8.

paragraphs: Training language models with four-bit numbers can improve efficiency, but such limited precision makes it difficult to preserve training quality. TetraJet-v2 uses the NVFP4 format for activations, weights, and gradients throughout all linear layers. The paper identifies weight oscillation and outliers as two central obstacles to accurate training at this precision.

The method combines three responses. An unbiased double-block quantization scheme handles NVFP4 linear layers. OsciReset suppresses weight oscillation, while OutControl aims to retain accuracy for outlying values. Together, these components target both unstable weight behavior and the difficulty of representing unusually large values within a very compact numerical format.
