TetraJet-v2 outperforms prior FP4 pretraining methods, reducing the performance gap to BF16 by an average of 51.3%, and delivers a 1.67-times end-to-end speedup over FP8. The results show a substantial narrowing of the accuracy gap rather than its elimination, alongside a measured training-speed benefit within the reported evaluation scale.
summary.tldr: TetraJet-v2 targets weight oscillation and outliers to improve four-bit LLM training accuracy while achieving a 1.67-times speedup over FP8.

title: TetraJet-v2: Accurate NVFP4 Training for Large Language Models with Oscillation Suppression and Outlier Control

abstract: We study clustered multitask learning in a semiparametric setting where tasks share a latent cluster structure in their target parameters but exhibit heterogeneous, potentially infinite-dimensional nuisance components. Such heterogeneity poses a major challenge for existing multitask learning methods, which typically rely on aligned feature spaces or homogeneous task structures. To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive fused orthogonal estimator that integrates Neyman-orthogonal losses with data-driven pairwise fusion penalties. Our framework leverages task-specific pilot estimates to calibrate the fusion penalties and combines adaptive aggregation with orthogonalization to mitigate the impact of nuisance-parameter estimation error. Theoretically, we show that the proposed estimator achieves exact recovery of the latent clustering with high probability and attains pooled parametric convergence rates proportional to cluster size. Moreover, we establish asymptotic normality and show that, asymptotically, our estimator matches the performance of an oracle procedure that knows the true clustering in advance. Empirically, we show that the proposed method consistently outperforms strong baselines in various simulation setups. A real-world application to U.S. residential energy consumption further demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach in uncovering meaningful regional clustering in electricity price elasticity, showcasing the efficacy of our method.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to share information across related learning tasks when their similarities are partly hidden. Tasks belong to unknown groups with shared target parameters, but other components can differ substantially across tasks. Those nuisance components may even be infinite-dimensional, making ordinary assumptions about aligned features or homogeneous tasks unsuitable.

The proposed estimator combines two mechanisms. Adaptive pairwise fusion penalties encourage appropriate tasks to share target estimates, with initial task-specific estimates determining how fusion is calibrated. Neyman-orthogonal losses reduce sensitivity to errors in estimating nuisance components. Together, these mechanisms aim to discover which tasks should pool information while limiting interference from their differences.

The theoretical results establish exact cluster recovery with high probability, pooled parametric convergence rates linked to cluster size, and asymptotic normality. Asymptotically, the estimator matches an oracle that already knows the groups. Simulations report improvements over strong baselines, while an application to residential energy consumption identifies meaningful regional groupings in electricity price elasticity.
summary.tldr: An adaptive estimator discovers shared task groups while reducing the influence of errors in task-specific nuisance estimates.

title: Adaptive Estimation and Inference in Semi-parametric Heterogeneous Clustered Multitask Learning via Neyman Orthogonality

abstract: Standard Set Representation Learning methods typically excel on curated data but often overlook the challenge of Inference-time Element Corruption. This refers to scenarios where deployed models encounter element-level degradations, such as outliers or missing components, that may distort set representation and degrade performance. We propose SW-DRSO, a distributionally robust optimization framework tailored for sets. Rather than minimizing loss solely on observed training data, SW-DRSO optimizes a tractable surrogate of the worst-case expected loss over a family of plausible inference-time variations. We introduce a barycentric adversary that approximates the intractable search over corrupted sets by a differentiable training-time optimization over simplex weights. Extensive experiments across four tasks demonstrate that SW-DRSO effectively enhances robustness against corruption while maintaining high overall performance.

paragraphs: Set representation models must summarize collections of elements into useful representations. A model trained on curated sets may encounter outliers or missing components after deployment, distorting that summary and harming performance. This paper focuses on those element-level changes at inference time, rather than assuming deployed inputs will remain as clean as the training data.

SW-DRSO changes the training objective to account for a family of plausible input variations. It optimizes a tractable surrogate for the worst-case expected loss within that family. This asks the model to prepare for adverse variations during learning instead of minimizing errors only on the observed training sets.

Searching directly over corrupted sets is intractable in the proposed formulation, so the method introduces a barycentric adversary. It approximates that search through differentiable optimization over simplex weights, allowing the adversarial component to participate in training. Experiments across four tasks show improved robustness to corruption while maintaining high overall performance. The contribution is a practical training approach for making set representations less vulnerable to changes in their constituent elements.
summary.tldr: SW-DRSO trains set representations against plausible element corruptions using a tractable approximation to worst-case loss.

title: Distributionally Robust Set Representation Learning Under Inference-Time Element Corruption

abstract: Entropic optimal transport (EOT) in continuous spaces with quadratic cost is a classical tool for solving the domain translation problem. In practice, recent approaches optimize a weak dual EOT objective depending on a single potential, but doing so is computationally not efficient due to the intractable log-partition term. Existing methods typically resolve this obstacle in one of two ways: by significantly restricting the transport family to obtain closed-form normalization (via Gaussian-mixture parameterizations), or by using general neural parameterizations that require simulation-based training procedures. We propose Variational Entropic Optimal Transport (VarEOT), based on an exact variational reformulation of the log-partition $\log \mathbb{E}[\exp(\cdot)]$ as a tractable minimization over an auxiliary positive normalizer. This yields a differentiable learning objective optimized with stochastic gradients and avoids the necessity of MCMC simulations during the training. We provide theoretical guarantees, including finite-sample generalization bounds and approximation results under universal function approximation. Experiments on synthetic data and unpaired image-to-image translation demonstrate competitive or improved translation quality, while comparisons within the solvers that use the same weak dual EOT objective support the benefit of the proposed optimization principle.

paragraphs: Entropic optimal transport provides a way to translate between distributions in continuous spaces. For quadratic transport costs, a commonly used weak dual objective depends on one potential but contains a difficult log-partition term. Existing approaches handle it through restricted families with tractable normalization or flexible neural models requiring simulation-based training.

VarEOT replaces this computational obstacle with an exact variational reformulation. It expresses the log-partition term as a tractable minimization over an additional positive normalizer. The resulting objective is differentiable and can be optimized with stochastic gradients, avoiding the need for MCMC simulations during training. The reformulation changes how the objective is optimized while preserving its exact mathematical basis.

The authors provide finite-sample generalization bounds and approximation results under universal function approximation. Experiments on synthetic data and unpaired image translation show competitive or improved translation quality. Comparisons among solvers using the same weak dual objective further support the proposed optimization principle, helping connect the observed benefits to the reformulation rather than simply to choosing a different transport objective.
summary.tldr: VarEOT exactly reformulates a difficult normalization term to train entropic transport models with stochastic gradients and no required MCMC training simulations.

title: Variational Entropic Optimal Transport

abstract: The increasing complexity of AI tasks has shifted the paradigm from monolithic models toward multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. However, these collaborative architectures introduce a critical bottleneck: redundant prefill computation for shared content generated by previous agents, which significantly increases KV cache memory usage and time-to-first-token (TTFT). While various KV cache methods have been proposed to mitigate prefill redundancy, they either fail to maintain accuracy on agent-generated outputs or exhibit low reuse rates due to rigid constraints. We present RelayCaching, a training-free inference method that directly reuses decoding phase KV caches from previous agents in subsequent prefill phases. Our key insight is that KV caches for identical content are highly consistent across phases, while prefix-induced deviations are sparse and localized within a limited range of layers and token positions. By selectively recomputing KV caches at these positions, RelayCaching preserves model accuracy with minimal overhead, yielding a superior accuracy–efficiency trade-off over existing methods. Experiments on diverse collaborative LLM tasks spanning mathematical reasoning, general knowledge, and code generation demonstrate that RelayCaching achieves over $80$% KV cache reuse, reduces TTFT by up to $4.7\times$ compared to the standard pipeline, all with negligible accuracy degradation.

paragraphs: When language model agents collaborate, one agent's generated text often becomes another agent's input. Processing that shared content again creates redundant prefill computation, increasing memory use and time before the next agent produces its first token. RelayCaching aims to reuse work already performed while the earlier agent generated the text.

The method transfers decoding-phase key-value caches into subsequent prefill phases without additional training. Its central observation is that caches for identical content are highly consistent across these phases. Differences caused by the surrounding prefix are sparse and concentrated in limited layers and token positions, so selective recomputation can correct them with modest overhead.

Across collaborative tasks involving mathematics, general knowledge, and code generation, RelayCaching reuses more than 80% of the KV cache. It reduces time to first token by up to a factor of 4.7 compared with the standard pipeline, with negligible accuracy degradation. The result makes cache reuse more flexible by correcting localized differences instead of requiring every reused entry to remain unchanged.
summary.tldr: RelayCaching selectively repairs and reuses caches from earlier agents, reducing repeated processing with negligible accuracy degradation in evaluated collaboration tasks.

title: RelayCaching: Accelerating LLM Collaboration via Decoding KV Cache Reuse

abstract: Subsampled natural gradient descent (SNG) has been used to enable high-precision scientific machine learning, but standard analyses based on stochastic preconditioning fail to provide insight into realistic small-sample settings. We overcome this limitation by instead analyzing SNG as a sketch-and-project method. Motivated by this lens, we discard the usual theoretical proxy which decouples gradients and preconditioners using two independent mini-batches, and we replace it with a new proxy based on squared volume sampling. Under this new proxy the expectation of the SNG direction becomes equal to a preconditioned gradient descent step even in the presence of coupling, leading to (i) global convergence guarantees when using a single mini-batch of any size, and (ii) an explicit characterization of the convergence rate in terms of quantities related to the sketch-and-project structure. These findings in turn yield new insights into small-sample settings, for example by suggesting that the advantage of SNG over SGD is that it can more effectively exploit spectral decay in the model Jacobian. We also extend these ideas to explain a popular structured momentum scheme for SNG, known as SPRING, by showing that it arises naturally from accelerated sketch-and-project methods.

paragraphs: Subsampled natural gradient descent uses a small batch of data to construct an update that accounts for the model’s local geometry. Existing analyses struggle to explain its behavior with realistically small batches. The paper changes the mathematical viewpoint, treating each update as a sketch-and-project operation: a reduced problem that determines a projection-based step.

The analysis replaces a common theoretical simplification that uses independent batches for the gradient and its preconditioner. Instead, it introduces a proxy based on squared volume sampling, allowing those quantities to remain coupled. Under this proxy, the expected update equals a preconditioned gradient step. This yields global convergence guarantees for a single batch of any size and an explicit description of the convergence rate.

The results suggest that natural gradient methods can exploit declining spectral contributions in the model Jacobian more effectively than ordinary stochastic gradient descent. The paper also connects the structured momentum method SPRING to accelerated sketch-and-project algorithms. These conclusions explain small-batch behavior through the new analytical proxy.
summary.tldr: A sketch-and-project analysis explains small-batch natural gradient updates and connects their convergence and momentum to projection methods.

title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

abstract: Graph Edit Distance (GED), which aims to find an edit path with minimum number of edit operations to transform one graph into another, is a fundamental NP-hard problem and a widely used graph similarity measure. Recent matching-based hybrid approaches have demonstrated better scalability than A* search-based hybrids by reformulating GED as a graph matching problem. In these methods, a neural network predicts a single deterministic node matching matrix, from which top-$k$ node mappings are extracted iteratively to derive candidate edit paths. However, these methods often suffer from highly correlated candidates that easily lead to suboptimal solutions, while the iterative extraction becomes inefficient for large $k$. In this paper, we propose DiffGED, the first generative approach for GED computation. Specifically, we formulate the graph matching problem as a generative task, and employ a diffusion-based model to generate multiple diverse node matching matrices simultaneously, from which diverse node mappings can be efficiently extracted. The generative diversity introduced by the diffusion process enables DiffGED to avoid suboptimal solutions and achieve superior solution quality close to the exact solution. Experiments on real-world datasets show that DiffGED generates multiple diverse edit paths with accuracy comparable to exact solutions, while running faster than existing hybrid approaches.

paragraphs: Graph edit distance measures the smallest number of edits needed to transform one graph into another. Computing it is NP-hard. Some scalable hybrid methods predict a node-matching matrix and extract several candidate mappings, but candidates from the same deterministic matrix can be highly correlated, limiting the range of edit paths explored.

DiffGED treats node matching as a generative task. A diffusion model produces several diverse matching matrices simultaneously, from which candidate mappings can be extracted efficiently. This changes where diversity enters the process: the method generates different matching hypotheses instead of repeatedly extracting alternatives from one fixed prediction.

The authors report that the resulting diversity helps avoid suboptimal solutions and yields solution quality close to exact computation. On real-world datasets, DiffGED produces diverse edit paths with accuracy comparable to exact solutions while running faster than existing hybrid approaches. These are empirical results rather than a guarantee of exact recovery on every graph pair. The contribution is a way to broaden candidate exploration while reducing the inefficiency of repeated extraction.
summary.tldr: DiffGED generates diverse graph-matching hypotheses with diffusion, achieving near-exact empirical edit-distance quality faster than existing hybrid approaches.

title: Towards Generative Graph Matching for Graph Edit Distance Computation

abstract: Large language models are increasingly post-trained with reinforcement learning in verifiable domains such as code and math. Yet, current methods for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learn only from a scalar outcome reward per attempt, creating a severe credit-assignment bottleneck. Many verifiable environments actually provide rich textual feedback, such as runtime errors or judge evaluations, that explain why an attempt failed. We formalize this setting as reinforcement learning with rich feedback and introduce Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO), which converts tokenized feedback into a dense learning signal without any external teacher or explicit reward model. SDPO treats the current model conditioned on feedback as a self-teacher and distills its feedback-informed next-token predictions back into the policy. In this way, SDPO leverages the model’s ability to retrospectively identify its own mistakes in-context. Across scientific reasoning, tool use, and competitive programming on LiveCodeBench v6, SDPO improves sample efficiency and final accuracy over strong RLVR baselines. Notably, SDPO also outperforms baselines in standard RLVR environments that only return scalar feedback by using successful rollouts as implicit feedback for failed attempts. Finally, applying SDPO to individual questions at test time accelerates discovery on difficult binary-reward tasks, achieving the same discovery probability as best-of-k sampling or multi-turn conversations with 3x fewer attempts.

summary.tldr: SDPO turns feedback-informed predictions from the model itself into dense training signals, improving learning efficiency and accuracy in the evaluated tasks.

title: Reinforcement Learning via Self-Distillation

abstract: Generalizing pretrained models to unseen datasets without retraining is a central challenge toward foundation models. Achieving fully inductive inference on numerical data is particularly difficult due to large variations in feature dimensionality and semantics across datasets. We observe that, in the presence of graph structure, numerical data admits a distinct structure-induced representational axis beyond the feature space, which we formalize as the view space. This view space enables a unified representation of graphs with heterogeneous features and motivates Graph View Transformation (GVT), a class of parametric mappings that can be shared across arbitrary graphs. We instantiate this framework with Recurrent GVT, an architecture for fully inductive node representation learning in node classification. Pretrained on OGBN-Arxiv and evaluated on 27 benchmarks, Recurrent GVT outperforms GraphAny, the prior fully inductive graph model, by +8.93%, and surpasses 12 individually tuned GNNs by at least +3.30%. These results establish the view space as a principled and practical foundation for learning across graphs with heterogeneous feature spaces. Code and checkpoints are available in https://github.com/dooho00/graph-view-space.

paragraphs: A pretrained graph model may encounter new datasets whose node features differ in both meaning and dimensionality. Those differences make inference without retraining difficult. This paper identifies a representation axis induced by graph structure, called view space, that provides a shared basis for handling graphs with heterogeneous numerical features.

The framework introduces Graph View Transformation, a family of parametric mappings that can be shared across arbitrary graphs. Its concrete architecture, Recurrent GVT, learns node representations for fully inductive node classification. The central idea is to use structure-induced representations to bridge datasets whose raw feature spaces do not already align.

Pretrained on OGBN-Arxiv and evaluated on 27 benchmarks, Recurrent GVT outperforms GraphAny by a reported 8.93% and exceeds 12 individually tuned graph neural networks by at least 3.30%. These findings support view space as a practical basis for transfer across heterogeneous graphs. They demonstrate that a shared pretrained representation can perform strongly on unseen graph datasets without dataset-specific retraining.
summary.tldr: Recurrent GVT uses graph-induced view-space representations to transfer a pretrained node-classification model across datasets with different feature spaces.

title: View Space: Learning Representation across Arbitrary Graphs

abstract: Low-rank recurrent neural networks (lrRNNs) are a class of models that uncover low-dimensional latent dynamics underlying neural population activity. Although their functional connectivity is low-rank, it lacks independence interpretations, making it difficult to assign distinct computational roles to different latent dimensions. To address this, we propose the Factored Recurrent Neural Network (FacRNN), a generative lrRNN framework that assumes group-wise independence among latent dynamics while allowing flexible within-group entanglement. These independent latent groups allow latent dynamics to evolve separately, but are internally rich for complex computation. We reformulate the lrRNN under a variational autoencoder (VAE) framework, enabling us to introduce a partial correlation penalty that encourages independence between groups of latent dimensions. Experiments on synthetic, monkey M1, and mouse voltage imaging data show that FacRNN consistently improves the disentanglement and interpretability of learned neural latent trajectories in low-dimensional space and low-rank connectivity over baseline lrRNNs that do not encourage group-wise independence.

paragraphs: Neural population recordings contain many interacting signals, but low-rank recurrent networks seek a smaller set of underlying dynamics. A compact representation alone does not make those dynamics easy to interpret: different latent dimensions can remain entangled, making it difficult to assign them distinct computational roles. FacRNN adds an explicit structure to address that problem.

The framework assumes independence between groups of latent dynamics while allowing dimensions within each group to interact freely. This balances separation with flexibility: groups can evolve independently without requiring every individual dimension to represent an isolated process. The researchers formulate the recurrent model within a variational autoencoder and introduce a partial-correlation penalty that encourages separation between groups.

Experiments use synthetic data, monkey M1 recordings, and mouse voltage imaging. FacRNN consistently improves disentanglement and interpretability of both latent trajectories and low-rank connectivity compared with recurrent models lacking this independence encouragement. These findings support group-wise factorization as a useful modeling choice for making learned neural dynamics more understandable.
summary.tldr: FacRNN encourages independence between groups of neural latent dynamics to make recurrent models of brain activity more interpretable.

title: A Factorized Low-Rank RNN Framework for Uncovering Independent Neural Latent Dynamics and Connectivity

abstract: We present 4RC, a unified feed-forward framework for 4D reconstruction from monocular videos. Unlike existing methods that typically decouple motion from geometry or produce limited 4D attributes, such as sparse trajectories or two-view scene flow, 4RC learns a holistic 4D representation that jointly captures dense scene geometry and motion dynamics. At its core, 4RC introduces a novel encode-once, query-anywhere and anytime paradigm: a transformer backbone encodes the entire video into a compact spatio-temporal latent space, from which a conditional decoder can efficiently query 3D geometry and motion for any query frame at any target timestamp. To facilitate learning, we represent per-view 4D attributes in a minimally factorized form, decomposing them into base geometry and time-dependent relative motion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that 4RC outperforms prior methods across a wide range of 4D reconstruction tasks.

At its core, 4RC introduces a novel encode-once, query-anywhere and anytime paradigm: a transformer backbone encodes the entire video into a compact spatio-temporal latent space, from which a conditional decoder can efficiently query 3D geometry and motion for any query frame at any target timestamp. paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving scene from a single-camera video requires recovering both its three-dimensional shape and how that shape changes over time. 4RC addresses these together in one feed-forward framework. Its representation captures dense geometry and motion, extending beyond outputs such as a sparse collection of tracked points or motion between only two views.

The central design is to encode the video once and then query the resulting representation repeatedly. A transformer compresses the entire video into a compact representation of space and time. A conditional decoder uses this representation to return geometry and motion for a chosen query frame at a target timestamp. This separates the initial video encoding from subsequent requests for particular reconstruction outputs.

For learning, the method expresses each view’s changing scene through base geometry and relative motion that depends on time. This keeps geometry and motion jointly represented while giving them distinct roles. Experiments report improvements over prior methods across multiple reconstruction tasks, supporting the usefulness of a shared representation for recovering several aspects of dynamic scenes.
summary.tldr: 4RC encodes a single-camera video once into a joint geometry-and-motion representation that supports reconstruction queries across frames and time.

title: 4RC: 4D Reconstruction via Conditional Querying Anytime and Anywhere

abstract: Large language models exhibit complementary reasoning errors: on the same instance, one model may succeed with a particular decomposition while another fails. We propose Collaborative Reasoning (CoRe), a training-time collaboration framework that converts peer success into a learning signal via a cross-teaching protocol. Each problem is solved in two stages: a cold round of independent sampling, followed by a contexted rescue round in which failed models receive a hint extracted from a successful peer. CoRe optimizes a combined reward that balances (i) correctness, (ii) a lightweight DPP-inspired diversity term to reduce error overlap, and (iii) an explicit rescue bonus for successful recovery. We evaluate CoRe in low-data regimes across GSM8K, MATH, AIME, and GPQA. With only 1,000 training examples, a pair of small open-source models (3B+4B) reaches 99.54% oracle Team Pass@2 on GSM8K and 92.08% on MATH, compared to 82.50% and 74.82% for single-model training. On harder datasets, the same pair reaches 77.34% oracle Team Pass@2 on GPQA (trained on 348 examples) and 79.65% on AIME (trained on 792 examples), using a training-time budget of at most 1536 context tokens and 3072 generated tokens. A three-model non-oracle AIME evaluation further closes most of the oracle-selection gap (81.20% majority vote vs. 82.60% oracle Team Pass@2). Overall, these results show that training-time collaboration can reliably convert model complementarity into large gains without scaling model size.

paragraphs: Different language models can fail on different parts of the same reasoning problem. CoRe turns this complementarity into a training signal. Models first attempt a problem independently. In a second round, unsuccessful models receive a hint extracted from a successful peer and get an opportunity to recover.

Training combines rewards for correctness, diversity, and successful rescue. The diversity term encourages models to avoid overlapping errors, while the rescue bonus rewards useful learning from peer hints. Together, these objectives encourage both independent strengths and productive collaboration, rather than evaluating only whether each isolated attempt succeeds.

With 1,000 training examples, a 3B-plus-4B model pair achieves oracle Team Pass@2 of 99.54% on GSM8K and 92.08% on MATH. These are team results with oracle selection, not individual-model accuracy. The paper also reports results on GPQA and AIME. In a three-model AIME evaluation, majority voting reaches 81.20%, compared with 82.60% oracle Team Pass@2, showing that much of the team benefit persists without oracle selection in that setting.
summary.tldr: CoRe trains models to learn from successful peers while preserving complementary strengths, producing large reported gains in team reasoning.

title: CoRe: Collaborative Reasoning via Cross Teaching

abstract: We propose Log-Normal Multiplicative Dynamics (LMD), a new algorithm to stabilize low-precision deep learning. LMD is motivated by the robustness of biological neural networks where synaptic spine sizes follow a log-normal distribution and fluctuate via noisy multiplicative dynamics. So far, no algorithm has successfully incorporated all these synaptic properties to train large models. LMD incorporates these properties through a variational Bayesian formulation that uses a log-normal posterior over weights. We evaluate LMD with low-precision forward-pass matrix multiplications, including training a Vision Transformer and GPT-2 from scratch. Our findings demonstrate the utility of biologically inspired approaches for designing energy-efficient algorithms for stable low-precision deep learning.
originalAbstract: We propose Log-Normal Multiplicative Dynamics (LMD), a new algorithm to stabilize low-precision deep learning. LMD is motivated by the robustness of biological neural networks where synaptic spine sizes follow a log-normal distribution and fluctuate via noisy multiplicative dynamics. So far, no algorithm has successfully incorporated all these synaptic properties to train large models. LMD incorporates these properties through a variational Bayesian formulation that uses a log-normal posterior over weights. We evaluate LMD with low-precision forward-pass matrix multiplications, including training a Vision Transformer and GPT-2 from scratch. Our findings demonstrate the utility of biologically inspired approaches for designing energy-efficient algorithms for stable low-precision deep learning.

The paper uses these properties as a starting point for an algorithm, translating the biological motivation into a statistical training formulation.

LMD uses variational Bayesian learning with a log-normal posterior over weights. This makes the distributional assumption part of how the model learns, rather than leaving the biological analogy as an informal explanation. The method brings together the stated synaptic properties in an approach intended to support training large models under reduced numerical precision.

The evaluation uses low-precision matrix multiplications in the forward pass and includes training a Vision Transformer and GPT-2 from scratch. The authors interpret their findings as evidence that biologically inspired dynamics can help design stable, energy-efficient learning algorithms. The reported scope is specifically low-precision forward computation; the contribution is an algorithmic route toward stability supported by these training demonstrations.
summary.tldr: LMD translates biological synaptic dynamics into Bayesian weight learning to support stable training with low-precision forward computation.

title: Log-Normal Multiplicative Dynamics for Stable Low-Precision Deep Learning

abstract: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are powerful tools for complex decision-making tasks. While existing activation mechanisms often promote sparsity through thresholding, they lack explicit awareness of feature channel relevance, causing networks to continuously suffer from interference by noisy channels. Such irrelevant activation signals can propagate through the network and adversely affect the final decision. Inspired by observations that channel relevance can be reflected in both intrinsic activity levels and extrinsic decision weights, and that there is strong consensus between these two aspects, we propose AIEC (Activation with Intrinsic-Extrinsic Consensus), a novel activation mechanism that has the ability to identify and suppress irrelevant feature channels during training. With a basic threshold activation, AIEC integrates an intrinsic Activation-Counting Unit that tracks channel activation statistics, an extrinsic Decision-Making Unit that learns channel decision weights, and a Consensus Gatekeeping Unit that suppresses irrelevant channels based on the agreement between intrinsic and extrinsic channel relevance assessments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AIEC can effectively suppress irrelevant channels and encourage sparser representations. Furthermore, AIEC is compatible with a wide range of mainstream ANN architectures and achieves superior performance compared to existing activation mechanisms across multiple tasks and domains. Code is available at https://github.com/horrible-dong/AIEC.

This paper addresses the resulting interference from irrelevant channels by assessing relevance from two complementary perspectives: a channel’s own activity and its learned contribution to decisions.

The proposed AIEC mechanism combines a basic threshold activation with three units. An Activation-Counting Unit tracks channel activity statistics, while a Decision-Making Unit learns decision weights for channels. A Consensus Gatekeeping Unit then uses agreement between these internal and decision-related assessments to suppress irrelevant channels during training. The central idea is to make suppression depend on evidence of relevance, rather than activity magnitude alone.

Experiments report that AIEC suppresses irrelevant channels, produces sparser representations, and improves performance over existing activation mechanisms across multiple tasks and domains. Its compatibility with several mainstream network architectures suggests that relevance-aware activation can serve as a broadly applicable network component.

title: Activation with Intrinsic-Extrinsic Consensus

abstract: Irregular multivariate time series (IMTS) forecasting is challenging due to non-uniform sampling and variable asynchronicity. These irregularities violate the equidistant assumptions of standard models, hindering local temporal modeling and rendering classical frequency-domain methods ineffective for capturing global periodic structures. To address this challenge, we propose TFMixer, a joint time–frequency modeling framework for IMTS forecasting. Specifically, TFMixer incorporates a Global Frequency Module that employs a learnable Non-Uniform Discrete Fourier Transform (NUDFT) to directly extract spectral representations from irregular timestamps. In parallel, the Local Time Module introduces a query-based patch attention mechanism to adaptively aggregate informative temporal segments and alleviate information density imbalance. Finally, TFMixer fuses the time-domain and frequency-domain representations to generate forecasts and further leverages inverse NUDFT for explicit seasonal extrapolation. Extensive experiments on real-world IMTS benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of TFMixer under irregular sampling and missing data.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time series becomes difficult when observations arrive at uneven intervals and different variables are measured at different times. These conditions disrupt methods built around regularly spaced samples. They also complicate the combination of local changes with longer periodic patterns, because conventional frequency analysis does not directly fit irregular timestamps.

TFMixer addresses both views of the data. Its Global Frequency Module uses a learnable Non-Uniform Discrete Fourier Transform to extract frequency representations directly from irregular observations. In parallel, a Local Time Module uses query-based attention over patches to gather informative temporal segments and reduce the imbalance between densely and sparsely observed regions. The model combines these representations for forecasting and uses an inverse transform to explicitly extend seasonal patterns.

Experiments on real-world irregular time-series benchmarks show effective forecasting and robustness under irregular sampling and missing data. The approach matters because it gives local temporal evidence and global periodic structure distinct modeling mechanisms, while bringing them together in a single forecasting framework.
summary.tldr: TFMixer combines timestamp-aware frequency analysis with local temporal attention to forecast irregularly sampled multivariate time series.

title: Bridging Time and Frequency: A Joint Modeling Framework for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Language agents have shown strong promise for task automation. Realizing this promise for increasingly complex, long-horizon tasks has driven the rise of a subagent-as-tools paradigm for multi-turn task solving. However, existing designs still lack a dynamic abstraction view of sub-agents, thereby hurting adaptability: sub-agents are either context-isolated threads that lack specialization, or static roles that require human-engineering. We address this challenge with a unified, framework-agnostic agent abstraction that models any agent as a tuple (Model, Task, Tools, Context). This tuple acts as a compositional recipe for capabilities, enabling the system to spawn specialized executors for each task on demand. Building on this abstraction, we introduce an agentic system AOrchestra, where the central orchestrator concretizes the tuple at each step: it curates task-relevant context, selects tools and models, and delegates execution via on-the-fly automatic agent creation. Such designs enable reducing human engineering efforts, and remain framework-agnostic with plug-and-play support for diverse agents as task executors. It also enables a controllable performance–cost trade-off, allowing the system to approach Pareto-efficient. Across three challenging benchmarks and environments (GAIA, SWE-Bench, Terminal-Bench), AOrchestra achieves 16.28% relative improvement against the strongest baseline when paired with Gemini-3-Flash.

paragraphs: AOrchestra addresses how an AI system should delegate parts of a complex, extended task. Existing sub-agent arrangements can provide isolated conversation threads without much specialization, or fixed roles that people must design in advance. The paper introduces a common description of an agent using four components: its model, task, tools, and context.

A central orchestrator fills in these components as work proceeds. It selects relevant information, chooses a model and tools, and creates a specialized executor for the current task. This makes agent creation part of the system’s ongoing decisions. The abstraction is intended to work across frameworks and accommodate different kinds of executors with less human engineering.

The design also makes performance and computational cost controllable through these choices, allowing the system to approach efficient trade-offs. Across GAIA, SWE-Bench, and Terminal-Bench, the authors report a 16.28% relative improvement over the strongest baseline when using Gemini-3-Flash. This result supports the proposed approach in the evaluated settings; it is specifically tied to that model pairing.
summary.tldr: AOrchestra creates specialized sub-agents on demand by choosing their models, tasks, tools, and context during execution.

title: AOrchestra: Automating Sub-Agent Creation for Agentic Orchestration

abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) allow for fine-grained credit assignment in reinforcement learning (RL), and seemingly contrast with outcome reward models (ORMs), which assign a single reward to an entire trajectory. However, we provide theoretical proof in this work that the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) RL algorithm equipped with an ORM is in fact equivalent to a PRM-aware RL objective equipped with a non-trivial, Monte-Carlo-based PRM (given mild assumptions). Leveraging the framework of GRPO-as-a-PRM, we identify a flaw in the GRPO objective that interacts with imbalanced process steps and rewards to hinder both exploration and exploitation (under different conditions). We propose a simple modification to the algorithm to mitigate this defect ($\lambda$-GRPO), and show that LLMs tuned with $\lambda$-GRPO outperform LLMs tuned with standard GRPO on downstream reasoning tasks$—$and reach peak performance more rapidly. These results show that we can leverage the hidden, built-in PRM structure within the vanilla GRPO algorithm to boost model performance without employing an explicit PRM, and with a negligible impact on training time and cost.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can reward an entire answer or assign more detailed credit to intermediate steps. These approaches appear different because only the latter explicitly evaluates the process. This paper shows that, under mild assumptions, Group Relative Policy Optimization with an outcome reward is equivalent to a process-reward-aware objective with a nontrivial Monte Carlo-based process reward model.

This equivalence provides a way to examine how GRPO distributes credit within a trajectory. Using that perspective, the authors identify a defect involving imbalances in process steps and rewards. Depending on the conditions, the defect can obstruct exploration of alternatives or exploitation of useful behavior. They propose λ-GRPO, a simple modification intended to mitigate it.

Language models trained with λ-GRPO outperform those trained with standard GRPO on the reported downstream reasoning tasks and reach their best performance sooner. The change has negligible reported impact on training time and cost. The findings demonstrate how analyzing GRPO's implicit process-level structure can motivate improvements without introducing a separate, explicit process reward model.
summary.tldr: Under mild assumptions, GRPO contains an implicit process reward model, and λ-GRPO uses that insight to improve reasoning training.

title: GRPO is Secretly a Process Reward Model

abstract: We introduce PerceptionRubrics, a rubric-based evaluation framework that addresses the dissonance between benchmark saturation and real-world brittleness. Shifting evaluation from holistic semantic matching to rigorous atomic auditing, PerceptionRubrics pairs 1,038 information-dense images with over 12,000 instance-specific rubrics. These criteria are derived from golden captions that constructed via a novel Circular Peer-Review consensus pipeline and then distilled into a dual-stream system of Must-Right (essential facts) and Easy-Wrong (fine-grained details) rubrics. Crucially, PerceptionRubrics implements a Gated Scoring mechanism: unlike linear averages, failure on mandatory visual facts triggers sharp binary penalties. Extensive evaluation yields critical insights: (1) The Reliability Gap: models often verify fragmented elements correctly yet fail strict conjunctive constraints, exposing brittleness in dense domains; (2) Open-Closed Stratification: contrary to reasoning trends, we reveal a persistent 5% perception deficit between open-source and proprietary frontiers; and (3) Human-Aligned Rigor: our gated metrics substantially out-align conventional benchmarks, validating that strict perceptual fidelity is the prerequisite for reliable generation.

paragraphs: A model can score well on broad image-description matching while still missing essential visual facts. PerceptionRubrics evaluates perception through individual, image-specific checks instead of relying on an overall semantic resemblance. It pairs 1,038 information-dense images with more than 12,000 rubrics, aiming to expose errors that can be hidden by strong aggregate benchmark performance.

The rubrics come from reference captions constructed through a Circular Peer-Review consensus process. They divide into Must-Right criteria for essential facts and Easy-Wrong criteria for fine details. Gated scoring applies sharp binary penalties when mandatory facts are missed. Consequently, getting many separate details right cannot simply average away a failure on a required visual fact.

Evaluations reveal a reliability gap: models often recognize individual elements but struggle when several requirements must all hold together. The authors also report a persistent 5% perception deficit between open-source and proprietary frontier models in their evaluation. Their gated metrics align substantially better with human judgments than conventional benchmarks, supporting stricter assessment of perceptual fidelity when judging the reliability of generated descriptions.
summary.tldr: PerceptionRubrics uses image-specific factual checks and gated penalties to expose perceptual failures that broad benchmark scores can conceal.

title: PerceptionRubrics: Calibrating Multimodal Evaluation to Human Perception

abstract: The longitudinal management of blinding fundus diseases constitutes a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) necessitating a critical precision-risk trade-off between intervention and over-treatment, as true pathology is often obscured in static observations. However, existing paradigms fail to address this complexity. Traditional vision models remain uninterpretable and memoryless, and while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel in semantic understanding, they rely on unsafe open-loop text reasoning lacking the anatomical grounding essential for clinical safety. Furthermore, robust learning is hindered by the scarcity of process supervision in sparse clinical records. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Logic-Constrained Abductive Data Engine. Operating on a “Propose-and-Verify” paradigm, it validates MLLM-proposed biomarkers against clinical and temporal logic to reconstruct dense pathological states from sparse outcomes. Building on this foundation, we propose ORBIT, the first ophthalmic Prognostic World Model. Uniquely, ORBIT employs counterfactual visual foresight to imagine anatomical futures under different treatments, anchoring decisions in Closed-Loop Anatomical Verification rather than linguistic probabilities. Experiments demonstrate that ORBIT effectively captures disease evolution and establishes a new paradigm for human-in-the-loop longitudinal decision support and anatomically grounded treatment planning.

The paper frames management as decision-making under partial observability, with a trade-off between timely intervention and overtreatment. Its approach combines reconstruction of disease progression with visual predictions of possible treatment outcomes.

A multimodal language model proposes biomarkers, which are checked against clinical and temporal logic before being used to reconstruct more detailed pathological states. summary.tldr: ORBIT combines logic-checked disease-state reconstruction with imagined anatomical futures to support clinician-guided treatment planning over time.

title: ORBIT: A Prognostic World Model for Ocular Reasoning Based on Imagined Trajectories

abstract: Text-attributed Graphs (TAGs) incorporate textual node attributes with graph structures to describe rich relational semantics. Recent efforts to integrate Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for learning on TAGs, yet achieving well-aligned representations remains challenging. Prior studies largely rely on heuristics that perform coarse-grained matching. They lack sufficient constraints and ignore distributional alignment, leading to representation drift and limited generalization. Building on Energy-based Models (EBMs), we propose an Energy-based Representation Alignment (ERAlign) framework that projects GNN-encoded graph structure and LLM-derived text embeddings in a shared latent space to achieve distribution consistency. Concretely, layer-wise alignment is quantified by a distance metric and optimized via an EBM objective. By decreasing energy values, our framework yields well-aligned representations for downstream tasks. During training, we introduce Energy Discrepancy (ED) to avoid high sampling costs associated with intractable normalization. ED also carries theoretical guarantees of higher training efficiency and reduced energy landscape distortion. Empirical evaluations on eight TAG datasets demonstrate that ERAlign obtains state-of-the-art performance across varying levels of supervision and cross-task transfer scenarios.

title: ERAlign: Energy-based Representation Alignment of GNNs and LLMs on Text-attributed Graphs

abstract: LLM-conditioned segmentation has recently advanced rapidly by coupling large language models with iterative mask generation frameworks. However, we identify a persistent failure mode in current propose-then-select pipelines. Although high-quality mask candidates are often generated, the final prediction may fail to match the given linguistic condition. This failure arises because language semantics are typically used as static prompts or post-hoc matching signals, rather than participating in the iterative mask generation process. Through systematic analysis, we show that many errors stem from semantic misalignment rather than poor mask quality. To address this issue, we propose FlowSeg, which introduces dynamic semantic guidance via a bidirectional semantic flow between intermediate decoding states and LLM-derived condition embeddings throughout the generation process. Language conditions actively guide mask refinement at each stage, while condition embeddings are progressively updated by emerging visual evidence. This design yields semantically grounded mask representations and visually aligned language conditions, enabling more reliable matching. We further incorporate a lightweight boundary-aware refinement to selectively enhance uncertain regions without perturbing confident interiors. Extensive experiments on referring expression segmentation and reasoning segmentation tasks demonstrate that FlowSeg consistently improves language–mask alignment and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Project page: https://zkzhang98.github.io/FlowSeg_page

paragraphs: Language-conditioned segmentation requires selecting the image region described by a linguistic instruction. The paper identifies a failure in systems that generate candidate masks and then choose among them: good masks may already exist, yet the final choice can still mismatch the language. Its analysis attributes many such errors to semantic alignment rather than the quality of the candidate boundaries.

FlowSeg makes language participate throughout mask generation. Information moves in both directions between intermediate decoding states and language-model condition embeddings. The language guides each refinement step, while emerging visual evidence updates the representation of the condition. A lightweight boundary refinement component additionally focuses on uncertain areas without disturbing confident mask interiors.

Experiments on referring expression segmentation and reasoning segmentation report consistent improvements in language–mask alignment and state-of-the-art performance. The approach matters because it addresses the relationship between the requested meaning and the evolving visual region during construction. The reported gains support repeated interaction between visual and linguistic representations as a way to improve the final match.
summary.tldr: FlowSeg repeatedly exchanges visual and language information during mask generation to improve segmentation alignment with the requested meaning.

abstract: We describe a sparse Bayesian regression method for recovering 3D human bodymotion directly from silhouettes extracted from monocular video sequences. Nodetailed body shape model is needed, and realism is ensured by training onreal human motion capture data. The tracker estimates 3D body pose by usingRelevance Vector Machine regression to combine a learned autoregressivedynamical model with robust shape descriptors extracted automatically fromimage silhouettes. We studied several different combination methods, the mosteffective being to learn a nonlinear observation-update correction based onjoint regression with respect to the predicted state and the observations. Wedemonstrate the method on a 54-parameter full body pose model, bothquantitatively using motion capture based test sequences, and qualitatively ona test video sequence.

paragraphs: This paper estimates three-dimensional human body motion from silhouettes in video recorded by a single camera. It avoids requiring a detailed model of body shape and learns from real motion-capture data to support realistic motion estimates. The approach combines information about how a person is moving with information about their current outline.

A learned autoregressive dynamical model predicts the body’s state from its motion history. Automatically extracted silhouette descriptors supply visual evidence, and relevance vector machine regression combines the two. Among the combination methods studied, the most effective learns a nonlinear correction using both the predicted state and the observations together.

This correction matters because the tracker can use the new silhouette to update a motion-based prediction, rather than relying solely on either source of information. The authors demonstrate the approach with a full-body pose representation containing 54 parameters. They evaluate it quantitatively on motion-capture-based test sequences and qualitatively on a test video sequence.
summary.tldr: A sparse Bayesian tracker combines learned motion dynamics with silhouettes to estimate 3D body pose from single-camera video.

title: Learning to track 3D human motion from silhouettes

abstract: Traditional non-parametric statistical learning techniques are oftencomputationally attractive, but lack the same generalization and modelselection abilities as state-of-the-art Bayesian algorithms which, however,are usually computationally prohibitive. This paper makes several importantcontributions that allow Bayesian learning to scale to more complex,real-world learning scenarios. Firstly, we show that backfitting -- atraditional non-parametric, yet highly efficient regression tool -- can bederived in a novel formulation within an expectation maximization (EM)framework and thus can finally be given a probabilistic interpretation. Secondly, we show that the general framework of sparse Bayesian learning andin particular the relevance vector machine (RVM), can be derived as a highlyefficient algorithm using a Bayesian version of backfitting at its core. As wedemonstrate on several regression and classification benchmarks, Bayesianbackfitting offers a compelling alternative to current regression methods,especially when the size and dimensionality of the data challengecomputational resources.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the computational difficulty of Bayesian learning while seeking to retain its generalization and model-selection strengths. Its starting point is backfitting, an efficient regression technique from nonparametric statistics. The authors derive backfitting within an expectation-maximization framework, giving the procedure a probabilistic interpretation.

That interpretation becomes the basis for a Bayesian version of backfitting. The paper then uses this version to derive an efficient algorithm for sparse Bayesian learning, including the relevance vector machine. The approach connects a computationally attractive regression procedure with a Bayesian learning framework, making the backfitting step central to how the resulting model is trained.

Experiments on several regression and classification benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method as a compelling alternative to existing regression methods. The authors particularly emphasize settings where data size and dimensionality strain computational resources. The contribution therefore includes both a probabilistic explanation of backfitting and a practical algorithmic use of that explanation to make sparse Bayesian learning more computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic derivation of backfitting leads to an efficient Bayesian training algorithm for sparse models, including the relevance vector machine.

abstract: Group-Lasso estimators, useful in many applications, suffer from lack of meaningful variance estimates for regression coefficients. To overcome such problems, we propose a full Bayesian treatment of the Group-Lasso, extending the standard Bayesian Lasso, using hierarchical expansion. The method is then applied to Poisson models for contingency tables using a highly efficient MCMC algorithm. The simulated experiments validate the performance of this method on artificial datasets with known ground-truth. When applied to a breast cancer dataset, the method demonstrates the capability of identifying the differences in interactions patterns of marker proteins between different patient groups.

The authors propose a fully Bayesian treatment to address this issue. Their construction extends the standard Bayesian Lasso through a hierarchical expansion for the Group-Lasso setting.

The method is applied to Poisson models for contingency tables, which organize counts across categories. Inference uses an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. The Bayesian formulation brings coefficient uncertainty into the model, connecting the original motivation about variance estimates with a procedure for analyzing these count-based data.

Simulated experiments with known ground truth validate the method's performance on artificial datasets. An application to breast cancer data demonstrates its ability to identify differences in marker-protein interaction patterns between patient groups. That finding concerns statistical interaction patterns in the analyzed data. Together, the applications show how the Bayesian treatment can support both uncertainty-aware estimation and comparisons of relationships across groups.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian Group-Lasso formulation addresses coefficient uncertainty and identifies differing marker-protein interaction patterns in a breast cancer dataset.

title: The Bayesian group-Lasso for analyzing contingency tables

abstract: Many state-of-the-art approaches for Multi Kernel Learning (MKL) struggle at finding a compromise between performance, sparsity of the solution and speed of the optimization process. In this paper we look at the MKL problem at the same time from a learning and optimization point of view. So, instead of designing a regularizer and then struggling to find an efficient method to minimize it, we design the regularizer while keeping the optimization algorithm in mind. Hence, we introduce a novel MKL formulation, which mixes elements of p-norm and elastic-net kind of regularization. We also propose a fast stochastic gradient descent method that solves the novel MKL formulation. We show theoretically and empirically that our method has 1) state-of-the-art performance on many classification tasks; 2) exact sparse solutions with a tunable level of sparsity; 3) a convergence rate bound that depends only logarithmically on the number of kernels used, and is independent of the sparsity required; 4) independence on the particular convex loss function used.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning must balance predictive quality, a sparse solution, and the time needed for optimization. This paper approaches those goals together by designing the regularizer with its optimization algorithm in mind. The resulting formulation combines elements of p-norm and elastic-net regularization, accompanied by a fast stochastic gradient descent method.

The method produces exactly sparse solutions with an adjustable degree of sparsity. Its convergence-rate bound depends only logarithmically on the number of kernels and is independent of the requested sparsity level. These properties connect the choice of a compact solution to an optimization analysis that does not worsen with that sparsity requirement.

The authors also report that the approach is independent of the particular convex loss used and achieves state-of-the-art performance on many classification tasks. The theoretical and empirical results support the joint design strategy: the learning formulation accommodates sparsity and predictive performance while the associated algorithm addresses computational cost. The performance claim remains tied to the classification tasks evaluated.
summary.tldr: Jointly designing regularization and optimization yields fast multiple kernel learning with tunable exact sparsity and a logarithmic kernel-count convergence dependence.

title: Ultra-Fast Optimization Algorithm for Sparse Multi Kernel Learning

abstract: Applying supervised learning methods to new classification tasks requires domain experts to label sufficient training data for the classifier to achieve acceptable performance. It is desirable to mitigate this annotation effort. To this end, a pertinent observation is that instance labels are often an indirect form of supervision; it may be more efficient to impart domain knowledge directly to the model in the form of labeled features. We present a novel algorithm for exploiting such domain knowledge which we call the Constrained Weight Space SVM (CW-SVM). In addition to exploiting binary labeled features, our approach allows domain experts to provide ranked features, and, more generally, to express arbitrary expected relationships between sets of features. Our empirical results show that the CW-SVM outperforms both baseline supervised learning strategies and previously proposed methods for learning with labeled features.

paragraphs: Training a classifier for a new task often requires experts to label many examples. This paper explores a more direct way to express their knowledge: providing information about features themselves. The motivation is that example labels communicate domain knowledge indirectly, while a knowledgeable person may be able to state useful relationships among features.

The proposed Constrained Weight Space SVM incorporates this feature-level supervision. It supports binary feature labels, rankings of features, and more general expected relationships between sets of features. These options let an expert express richer guidance than assigning a class to each example, allowing the learning algorithm to use knowledge about how features should relate.

In the reported experiments, CW-SVM outperforms both baseline supervised-learning strategies and earlier methods using labeled features. The findings support the value of incorporating richer feature relationships into classifier training. The motivation is reduced annotation effort, while the stated empirical result concerns predictive performance against the compared methods; the abstract does not quantify how much expert labeling time is saved.
summary.tldr: CW-SVM incorporates expert feature labels, rankings, and relationships, outperforming compared supervised and feature-supervised methods in experiments.

title: The Constrained Weight Space SVM: Learning with Ranked Features

abstract: In this paper we present a fully Bayesian latent variable model which exploits conditional non- linear (in)-dependence structures to learn an efficient latent representation. The model is capable of learning from extremely high-dimensional data such as directly modelling high resolution images. The latent representation is factorized to represent shared and private information from multiple views of the data. Bayesian techniques allow us to automatically estimate the dimensionality of the latent spaces. We demonstrate the model by prediction of human pose in an ambiguous setting. Our Bayesian representation allows us to perform disambiguation in a principled manner by including priors which incorporate the dynamics structure of the data. We demonstrate the ability of the model to capture structure underlying extremely high dimensional spaces by learning a low-dimensional representation of a set of facial images under different illumination conditions. The model correctly automatically creates a factorized representation where the lighting variance is represented in a separate latent space from the variance associated with different faces. We show that the model is capable of generating morphed faces and images from novel light directions.

paragraphs: Multiple views of data can contain both common information and variation specific to each view. This paper introduces a fully Bayesian latent variable model that separates those sources into shared and private representations. It uses conditional nonlinear dependence and independence structure to learn an efficient hidden description of the observations.

Bayesian techniques automatically estimate the dimensions of the latent spaces. The model can work directly with extremely high-dimensional observations, including high-resolution images. In an ambiguous human-pose prediction task, priors incorporating the dynamics of the data allow the representation to resolve ambiguity in a principled way. This connects uncertainty in the representation with structural knowledge about how the data evolve.

A facial-image demonstration shows the model learning a low-dimensional representation under different lighting conditions. It automatically places lighting variation in a separate latent space from variation associated with different faces. The model also generates morphed faces and images under novel light directions, illustrating how the learned separation can support synthesis as well as representation.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian latent model automatically separates shared and private variation, estimates latent dimensions, and supports disambiguation and image generation.
